docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in microeconomics for readers with no background in the subject. It begins with scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, builds the model of demand and supply, elasticity, and consumer and producer surplus, and uses them to analyse taxes, subsidies and price controls. It then develops the theory of the consumer (utility, indifference curves and budget constraints, income and substitution effects) and of the firm (production and costs), and studies perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly with basic game theory. The last chapters cover the markets for labour, capital and land, market failure (externalities, public goods, common resources and asymmetric information), behavioural economics and international trade. Every chapter has worked numerical examples, diagrams drawn to scale from the same numbers, exercises with answers and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Behavioural Economics
docs.text:
What happens when real people depart from the rational model

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the main assumptions of the standard model of choice and explain what behavioural economics adds.
  2. Explain bounded rationality and describe common heuristics and the biases they can cause.
  3. Explain reference dependence, loss aversion and the shape of the value function in prospect theory.
  4. Describe the endowment effect, framing effects, mental accounting and the sunk cost fallacy.
  5. Show with numbers how present bias leads to preference reversals, and explain the role of commitment devices.
  6. Describe evidence on fairness and social preferences.
  7. Explain what a nudge is, give examples, and state the main arguments for and against nudges.

docs.title: 13.1 The standard model and its critics
docs.text:
The theory of the earlier chapters assumes that people:

  • have stable, consistent preferences (complete and transitive, Chapter 5);
  • maximise their utility, using all the relevant information and calculating correctly;
  • care about final outcomes (how much they end up with), not about how outcomes are described or what they had before;
  • weigh the future against the present consistently;
  • care mainly about their own consumption.

These assumptions make the theory simple and powerful, and the predictions they produce (people buy less when prices rise, firms enter profitable markets) are confirmed again and again. But psychologists and economists have also documented many situations in which people behave in systematic ways that the standard model does not predict. Behavioural economics brings these findings into economics, using insights from psychology to build models of how people actually choose.

The field has a long history. Herbert Simon, who received the Nobel prize in economics in 1978, argued in the 1950s that people have limited ability to process information. The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, from the 1970s on, documented systematic patterns in judgement and choice; Kahneman received the Nobel prize in 2002 (Tversky had died in 1996). Richard Thaler, who applied these ideas to many economic questions, received the prize in 2017.

The important word is systematic. Random mistakes would cancel out across many people and would not matter much for markets. Behavioural economics is concerned with mistakes and departures that are predictable: most people make them, in the same direction.

docs.title: 13.2 Bounded rationality and heuristics
docs.text:
Simon's idea of bounded rationality is that people try to make good decisions but face limits of information, time and computing power. Instead of finding the best option among all possible ones, they often satisfice: they search until they find an option that is good enough, and stop. A person buying a phone does not compare every model on the market; she looks at a few and picks one that meets her needs.

To cope with complexity, people use heuristics: mental short cuts or rules of thumb. Heuristics are usually sensible and save effort, but they can lead to systematic errors, called biases. Kahneman and Tversky described several.

  • Anchoring. People's estimates are pulled towards a number they have just seen, even an irrelevant one. In experiments, people asked first whether a quantity is more or less than a high number then give higher estimates of it than people first asked about a low number. In markets, a "recommended price" crossed out next to a sale price can act as an anchor, making the sale price look like a bargain.
  • Availability. People judge how likely an event is by how easily examples come to mind. After a widely reported air crash, many people overestimate the danger of flying, though road travel is far more dangerous per kilometre; vivid, recent and well-publicised events seem more common than they are.
  • Representativeness. People judge probabilities by how much a case resembles a typical example, and neglect base rates. A common form is the gambler's fallacy: after a coin has come up heads five times in a row, many people feel tails is "due", though the coin has no memory and the chance is still one half.
  • Overconfidence. Most people overrate their own abilities and the accuracy of their knowledge. Overconfidence may lead people to trade shares too often, start businesses with poor prospects, or underestimate how long a project will take.

docs.title: 13.3 Prospect theory: losses loom larger than gains
docs.text:
The standard theory of choice under risk assumes that people judge a gamble by the final wealth it may leave them with. Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) proposed instead that people judge outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, usually their current situation or what they expected. It has three main features.

  1. Reference dependence. What matters is the change, not the level. A salary of ₹60,000 a month feels good to someone who expected ₹50,000, and bad to someone who expected ₹70,000.
  2. Loss aversion. A loss hurts more than a gain of the same size pleases. Many studies estimate that losses weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains.
  3. Diminishing sensitivity. The difference between gaining ₹100 and ₹200 feels larger than the difference between gaining ₹10,100 and ₹10,200. The same is true of losses.

These features give the value function its characteristic shape.

Figure 13.1 The value function of prospect theory. The value function of prospect theory. Outcomes are measured as gains or losses from a reference point. The curve is concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses than for gains: a loss is felt more strongly than a gain of the same size.

Example 13.1 Why people refuse a fair bet

You are offered a bet on the toss of a coin: heads, you win ₹1,000; tails, you lose ₹1,000. Suppose losses weigh twice as much as gains, so that a gain of \(x\) is valued at \(x\) and a loss of \(x\) at \(-2x\). Would you accept? How large would the win have to be?

Solution. The expected money value of the bet is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1{,}000) + \tfrac{1}{2}(-1{,}000) = 0\). But its value, with loss aversion, is

\[ \tfrac{1}{2}(1{,}000) + \tfrac{1}{2}(-2 \times 1{,}000) = 500 - 1{,}000 = -500. \]

You would refuse. To accept, the possible win \(G\) must satisfy \(\tfrac{1}{2}G - \tfrac{1}{2}(2{,}000) \ge 0\), that is, \(G \ge 2{,}000\). This matches the common finding that many people will accept such a bet only if the possible gain is about twice the possible loss.

Diminishing sensitivity also means that people tend to be risk-averse for gains (preferring a sure gain to a gamble with the same expected value) but risk-seeking for losses (preferring to gamble rather than accept a sure loss). An investor may sell shares that have risen, to lock in the gain, but hold on to shares that have fallen in the hope of getting back to the purchase price, which is a reference point. This tendency is called the disposition effect.

Prospect theory also finds that people overweight small probabilities. This helps explain why the same people may buy lottery tickets (overweighting a tiny chance of a large gain) and insurance against rare events (overweighting a tiny chance of a large loss).

docs.title: 13.4 The endowment effect
docs.text:
Loss aversion predicts that people value a thing more once they own it, because giving it up feels like a loss, while acquiring it would only be a gain. This is the endowment effect. In well-known classroom experiments, half the participants are given a mug and the other half are not; those with mugs are asked the lowest price at which they would sell, and those without are asked the most they would pay. Since the mugs were handed out at random, the two groups should value them similarly on average. In fact, in many such experiments the sellers ask for roughly twice what the buyers offer, and far fewer mugs change hands than the standard theory predicts.

The endowment effect helps explain why people keep things they would never buy at their current price, why "free trial" offers that let customers keep a product for a while are effective, and why workers resist pay cuts much more strongly than they welcome equal pay rises.

docs.title: 13.5 Framing, mental accounting and sunk costs
Framing
docs.text:
In the standard model, the way a choice is described should not matter if the outcomes are the same. In practice, it often does. A framing effect occurs when people choose differently between options with identical outcomes because the options are described differently.

A famous experiment by Tversky and Kahneman asked people to choose between programmes to deal with a disease expected to kill 600 people. Described in terms of lives saved ("programme A saves 200 people for certain; programme B gives a one-third chance of saving all 600 and a two-thirds chance of saving none"), most chose the certain programme A. Described in terms of lives lost ("under programme C, 400 people will die for certain; under programme D, there is a one-third chance that nobody dies and a two-thirds chance that all 600 die"), most chose the risky programme D. Yet A and C are the same, and so are B and D. Framed as gains, people avoided risk; framed as losses, they sought it, as prospect theory predicts.

Framing matters in everyday life too. Meat described as "90 per cent lean" sounds better than meat described as "10 per cent fat". A surcharge for paying by card is resented more than an identical discount for paying in cash.

docs.title: Mental accounting
docs.text:
Money is fungible: a rupee is a rupee, whatever its source or intended use. But people often keep mental accounts, treating money differently depending on where it came from or what it is "for". A family may borrow at a high interest rate while keeping savings earning a low rate in an account labelled "for the children's education". People tend to spend windfalls (a bonus, a tax refund, a lottery win) more freely than regular income. Thaler developed the idea of mental accounting.

A classic illustration: a person who loses a ₹500 note on the way to buy a ₹500 cinema ticket is usually willing to buy the ticket anyway; a person who has bought the ticket and loses it is much less willing to buy another. In both cases the person is ₹500 poorer, but in the second the loss is charged to the "cinema account", making the film seem to cost ₹1,000.

docs.title: The sunk cost fallacy
docs.text: Chapter 1 explained that sunk costs should be ignored. People often do not ignore them. Someone who has paid for a year's gym membership may keep going to "get their money's worth" even when they would rather not; a government may continue a failing project because so much has already been spent on it. This sunk cost fallacy is related to loss aversion: abandoning a project means admitting the money spent was lost.

docs.title: 13.6 Present bias and self-control
docs.text:
Chapter 11 showed how to compare money now with money later by discounting. The standard model assumes that people discount the future consistently: if you prefer ₹100 today to ₹110 in a month, you should also prefer ₹100 in twelve months to ₹110 in thirteen months, since the trade-off is the same one-month delay.

Experiments find otherwise. Many people who choose ₹100 now over ₹110 in a month choose ₹110 in thirteen months over ₹100 in twelve. They are impatient about the immediate present but patient about the distant future. This is present bias.

Example 13.2 A preference reversal

A simple model of present bias says that any benefit not received now is valued at only a fraction \(\beta\) of its amount, with \(\beta = 0.5\) (and, for simplicity, no further discounting for longer delays). Compare the choices (a) ₹100 today or ₹150 in one week, and (b) ₹100 in 52 weeks or ₹150 in 53 weeks.

Solution. (a) Today, ₹100 now is worth 100; ₹150 next week is worth \(0.5 \times 150 = 75\). She takes ₹100 now.

(b) Both payments are in the future, so both are scaled by 0.5: \(0.5 \times 100 = 50\) against \(0.5 \times 150 = 75\). She plans to wait for ₹150.

But when week 52 arrives, choice (b) has become choice (a), and she switches to taking ₹100 immediately. Her plans are time-inconsistent: what she plans for the future is not what she does when the future comes. With consistent (exponential) discounting, the comparison would be the same in both cases and no reversal would occur.

Present bias explains why people plan to start saving, exercising or studying "next month" and then postpone again when next month comes. It helps explain undersaving for old age, procrastination over unpleasant tasks, and the difficulty of giving up smoking.

People who are aware of their present bias may seek commitment devices that restrict their future choices: savings accounts that cannot be drawn on before a certain date, automatic deductions from salary into a pension fund, paying in advance for a course of classes, or simply not keeping sweets in the house. Studies have found that many people choose such commitments when offered, which suggests they recognise their own self-control problems.

docs.title: 13.7 Fairness and social preferences
docs.text:
The standard model usually assumes that people care only about their own consumption. Many experiments suggest that people also care about fairness and about others' well-being.

In the ultimatum game, one player (the proposer) is given a sum of money, say ₹100, and offers some share of it to a second player (the responder). If the responder accepts, the money is divided as proposed; if she rejects, both get nothing. A purely self-interested responder should accept any positive offer, since something is better than nothing, and a self-interested proposer, knowing this, should offer the smallest possible amount. In practice, across many countries, proposers commonly offer a substantial share, often close to half, and responders frequently reject low offers, giving up money to punish what they see as unfair treatment.

In the dictator game, the second player has no choice: the first simply decides how much to give. Many people still give something, though less than in the ultimatum game.

Concern for fairness has economic consequences. Firms often avoid raising prices sharply during shortages (for example, of umbrellas in a sudden storm) because customers regard it as exploitation, even when the higher price would clear the market. Employers may pay more than the market wage because workers who feel fairly treated work harder, an idea related to efficiency wages. People also show reciprocity: they reward kindness and punish unkindness, even at a cost to themselves.

docs.title: 13.8 Nudges and choice architecture
docs.text:
If people's choices are affected by defaults, framing and the way options are presented, then those who design choices (governments, employers, websites, shop owners) inevitably influence them. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, in their book Nudge (2008), called this choice architecture. A nudge is a feature of the way choices are presented that changes behaviour in a predictable way without forbidding any option or significantly changing economic incentives.

Examples include:

  • Defaults. People tend to stick with whatever happens if they do nothing. When employees are enrolled in a pension scheme automatically, with the option to leave, participation is much higher than when they must actively sign up, although the choice open to them is the same. Countries differ in whether people are organ donors unless they opt out, or only if they opt in, and the default affects how many people are registered donors.
  • Simplification. Making a form shorter or a process easier increases take-up of benefits, scholarships and services that people are entitled to.
  • Reminders and timely information. Text messages reminding people of vaccination dates, loan repayments or medicine schedules can raise compliance.
  • Social norms. Telling households how their electricity use compares with that of their neighbours has been found to reduce consumption.
  • Salience and placement. Putting healthy food at eye level in a canteen, or showing the full cost of a loan prominently, changes choices.

Nudges are attractive to governments because they are cheap and preserve freedom of choice. They have also been criticised. Some argue that it is paternalistic for governments to decide what choices are "better" for people; others point out that the same techniques can be used to steer people towards choices that benefit the designer rather than the chooser, as when websites make it easy to subscribe and hard to cancel. And nudges cannot replace taxes, regulation and public provision where the stakes or the market failures are large.

Key idea

Behavioural economics does not throw away the standard model. It keeps the idea that people respond to incentives and adds that they also respond, in predictable ways, to how choices are framed, to reference points, to defaults and to the timing of costs and benefits. Good policy and good business take both into account.

docs.title: 13.9 How much does it matter?
docs.text:
Behavioural findings raise a fair question: if people are so often "irrational", can the theory of the earlier chapters be trusted? Three points suggest that it can, within limits.

  1. Many predictions survive. Demand curves slope down, people respond to prices, and firms enter profitable markets, whatever the psychology of individual buyers.
  2. Markets and learning can reduce some biases. People who make the same choice often, with quick feedback, tend to learn. Professional traders show the endowment effect less than inexperienced people, for example. Biases matter most for choices that are rare, complex and delayed in their consequences: choosing a pension, buying a house, choosing a course of study, or deciding how much to save.
  3. The standard model is a benchmark. Knowing what a fully rational person would do helps to identify where and why real behaviour differs, and what can be done about it.

The most productive view is that the standard model and behavioural economics are complements: the first explains much of what happens in markets, and the second improves predictions and policies where psychology matters most.

docs.title: 13.10 Summary
docs.text:
• The standard model assumes consistent preferences, full rationality, concern with final outcomes, consistent discounting and self-interest. Behavioural economics uses psychology to study systematic departures from these assumptions.
  • Bounded rationality leads people to satisfice and use heuristics, which can cause biases: anchoring, availability, representativeness (including the gambler's fallacy) and overconfidence.
  • Prospect theory: people value gains and losses relative to a reference point; they are loss averse (losses count roughly twice as much as gains in many studies); and sensitivity diminishes with size. They are risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses, and overweight small probabilities.
  • The endowment effect: people value what they own more than identical things they do not own.
  • Framing effects, mental accounting and the sunk cost fallacy show that the description and labelling of choices affect decisions.
  • Present bias causes time-inconsistent choices and procrastination; commitment devices help people stick to their plans.
  • Experiments such as the ultimatum game show concern for fairness and reciprocity.
  • Nudges (defaults, simplification, reminders, social norms) change behaviour without restricting choice; they are cheap but have limits and critics.

docs.title: 13.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Name the bias in each case: (a) after a series of red results at a roulette table, a player bets heavily on black because "black is due"; (b) a shop puts a ₹9,999 watch next to a ₹2,999 one to make the second look cheap; (c) after news of a shark attack, many tourists avoid the sea, while driving to the beach is far more dangerous.

Answer

(a) The gambler's fallacy (representativeness). (b) Anchoring. (c) The availability heuristic.

Exercise 2

With a value function in which losses count 2.5 times as much as gains (\(v = x\) for gains, \(v = 2.5x\) for losses), would a person accept a coin-toss bet to win ₹1,500 or lose ₹1,000? What is the smallest win that would make her accept a bet with a possible loss of ₹1,000?

Answer

Value \(= 0.5 \times 1{,}500 - 0.5 \times 2.5 \times 1{,}000 = 750 - 1{,}250 = -500\), so she refuses, although the expected money value is +₹250. She accepts if \(0.5G \ge 1{,}250\), that is, \(G \ge\) ₹2,500.

Exercise 3

Using the present-bias model of Example 13.2 with \(\beta = 0.6\), does the person choose ₹200 today or ₹300 next week? What does she plan for the choice between ₹200 in 10 weeks and ₹300 in 11 weeks?

Answer

Today: 200 against \(0.6 \times 300 = 180\), so she takes ₹200 today. For the future choice: \(0.6 \times 200 = 120\) against \(0.6 \times 300 = 180\), so she plans to wait for ₹300. When week 10 arrives she will switch, a preference reversal.

Exercise 4

Explain how the endowment effect is related to loss aversion.

Answer

Once a person owns a thing, giving it up is coded as a loss, while acquiring an identical thing would be a gain. With loss aversion, losses weigh more than gains, so the minimum price at which the owner will sell exceeds the maximum price a non-owner will pay.

Exercise 5

A government wants more people to save for retirement. Suggest two nudges and one policy that is not a nudge.

Answer

Nudges: automatic enrolment in a pension scheme with the option to leave; automatic escalation, under which contributions rise with each pay rise unless the worker opts out; simplified forms; reminders. A policy that is not a nudge: a tax incentive for pension contributions, or compulsory contributions, since these change incentives or restrict choice.

Exercise 6

In an ultimatum game over ₹100, what would a purely self-interested responder accept, and what does evidence suggest actually happens?

Answer

A purely self-interested responder would accept any positive offer, even ₹1, since something is better than nothing. In experiments, responders frequently reject low offers, giving up money to punish unfairness, and proposers often offer a substantial share, frequently close to half.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Demand and Supply
docs.text:
How buyers and sellers together set prices and quantities

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the law of demand and the law of supply and explain why each usually holds.
  2. Build a market demand or supply schedule from individual schedules.
  3. Distinguish a movement along a curve from a shift of the curve, and list what shifts each curve.
  4. Find the equilibrium price and quantity of a market from a table, a graph or a pair of equations.
  5. Explain how a surplus or a shortage pushes a market towards equilibrium.
  6. Predict the effect on price and quantity of a change in demand, in supply, or in both.

docs.title: 2.1 Markets and competition
docs.text:
A market is any arrangement through which buyers and sellers of a good or service come into contact and trade. Some markets have a place: a vegetable mandi, a cattle fair, a stock exchange. Many do not: the market for second-hand phones operates through shops, websites and personal contacts across a whole country. What makes it one market is that the buyers and sellers deal in the same good and are aware of one another's prices.

This chapter studies a competitive market, one with so many buyers and so many sellers, each small relative to the market, that no single one of them can influence the price. Each takes the market price as given. A wheat farmer is a good example: whether she sells ten quintals or a hundred, the price in the mandi is the same. The model of demand and supply describes how such a market works. Later chapters (8 to 10) consider markets in which a seller is large enough to set the price.

docs.title: 2.2 Demand
docs.text: The quantity demanded of a good is the amount that buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price, during a given period. "Willing and able" matters: wanting a car is not demand unless you can pay for it. "During a period" matters too: a quantity demanded is a flow, so many kilograms a week or many units a year.

docs.title: The law of demand
docs.text:
Other things being equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls; when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. This inverse relationship is called the law of demand. It holds for almost every good, for two reasons.

  • The substitution effect. When the price of tea rises, tea becomes more expensive relative to coffee, juice and other drinks, so some buyers switch to them.
  • The income effect. When the price of a good rises, a buyer's income buys less than before; the buyer is in effect poorer and, for most goods, buys less.

Chapter 6 makes these two effects precise. A third, simpler reason is diminishing marginal utility (Chapter 5): each extra unit of a good gives a buyer less satisfaction than the one before, so a buyer will take more units only at a lower price.

docs.title: The demand schedule and the demand curve
docs.text: A demand schedule is a table showing the quantity demanded at each price. A demand curve is the same information drawn as a graph, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. Because of the law of demand, the curve slopes downwards.

docs.title: From individual to market demand
docs.text:
The market demand is the total quantity that all buyers together demand at each price. To find it, add the quantities demanded by every buyer at each price. On a graph, this means adding the individual curves horizontally.

Example 2.1 Adding individual demands

A small market for mangoes has two buyers, Anil and Bela. Their weekly demand schedules are below. Find the market demand.

Price (₹ per kg) Anil (kg) Bela (kg) Market (kg) 60 1 2 3 50 2 3 5 40 3 5 8 30 4 7 11 20 5 9 14

Solution. At each price, add the two quantities across the row: at ₹40, \(3 + 5 = 8\) kg. The market demand schedule is the last column. Like the individual schedules, it shows larger quantities at lower prices.

docs.title: A demand curve as an equation
docs.text:
For calculation, a demand curve is often written as an equation. Throughout this chapter we use the market demand

\[ Q_d = 100 - 2P, \]

where \(P\) is the price in rupees and \(Q_d\) the quantity in units per week. Each ₹1 rise in price reduces the quantity demanded by 2 units. At \(P = 0\), buyers would take 100 units; at \(P = 50\) they would take none. Solved for \(P\), the same curve is \(P = 50 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q\), which is the form we draw.

docs.title: 2.3 What shifts demand
docs.text:
The demand curve shows how quantity demanded depends on the price when everything else is held constant. When one of those other things changes, the whole curve shifts. The main ones are these.

  1. Income. For a normal good, a rise in income increases demand: the curve shifts to the right. Most goods are normal: clothes, restaurant meals, air travel. For an inferior good, a rise in income reduces demand, because buyers switch to something they prefer. Coarse grains, the cheapest cuts of cloth, or long-distance travel by the slowest train may be inferior goods for many households: as incomes rise, people buy less of them.
  2. Prices of related goods. Two goods are substitutes if a rise in the price of one increases the demand for the other: tea and coffee, buses and the metro, two brands of soap. They are complements if a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other, because they are used together: cars and petrol, printers and ink cartridges, phones and mobile data.
  3. Tastes and preferences. A health campaign that shows the benefits of millets increases the demand for millets; a fashion moving away from a style reduces the demand for it.
  4. Expectations. If buyers expect the price of a good to rise next month, they buy more now; if they expect their incomes to rise, they may spend more today.
  5. The number and kind of buyers. A growing population, or more tourists in a town, increases the market demand for many goods. A change in the age structure changes the demand for schools, medicines and housing.

docs.title: Movement along the curve versus shift of the curve
docs.text:
This distinction is the most important piece of vocabulary in the chapter.

  • A change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the demand curve. Economists call this a change in the quantity demanded.
  • A change in anything else that affects buyers causes a shift of the demand curve. Economists call this a change in demand.

Common mistake

"The price of petrol rose, so the demand for petrol fell" is wrong in economics vocabulary. A rise in the price of petrol reduces the quantity demanded of petrol: a movement up along the same curve. The demand for petrol (the whole curve) has not changed. But a rise in the price of petrol does reduce the demand for cars, a complement, shifting that curve to the left.

docs.title: 2.4 Supply
docs.text: The quantity supplied is the amount of a good that sellers are willing and able to sell at a given price during a given period.

docs.title: The law of supply
docs.text:
Other things being equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises. The supply curve slopes upwards. The reasons are:

  • a higher price makes producing the good more profitable, so existing producers expand output and new producers may start;
  • producing more usually raises the cost of each extra unit (the marginal cost), because producers must pay overtime, use less suitable land or run machines harder. A producer will offer more only if the price covers this higher marginal cost. Chapter 8 shows that, in a competitive market, the supply curve is the marginal cost curve.

docs.title: Market supply
docs.text:
As with demand, the market supply at each price is the sum of the quantities that all sellers offer at that price: the individual supply curves are added horizontally. In this chapter we use the market supply

\[ Q_s = -20 + 4P, \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad P = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q. \]

At prices of ₹5 or less, nothing is supplied: the price does not cover the cost of even the cheapest unit. Above ₹5, each ₹1 rise in price brings 4 more units.

docs.title: 2.5 What shifts supply
docs.text:
The supply curve is drawn for given conditions of production. When these change, the curve shifts.

  1. Prices of inputs. A rise in wages, in the price of raw materials or in the price of fuel raises the cost of producing each unit, so sellers offer less at each price: the supply curve shifts to the left (upwards). A fall in input prices shifts it to the right.
  2. Technology. An improvement in technology, such as a better seed, a faster machine or a more efficient process, lowers costs and shifts supply to the right.
  3. Prices of other goods the producer could make. A farmer who can grow wheat or mustard will grow less wheat if the price of mustard rises. Wheat and mustard are substitutes in production. Some goods are joint products: a rise in the price of mutton increases the supply of wool and leather.
  4. Expectations. If sellers expect a higher price later, they may hold back supply now.
  5. The number of sellers. More firms entering a market shift market supply to the right.
  6. Natural and other conditions. For agricultural goods, the weather matters a great deal: a good monsoon shifts the supply of many crops to the right; a drought, floods or a pest attack shift it to the left.
  7. Taxes and subsidies. A tax per unit on sellers raises their cost of supplying each unit and shifts supply to the left; a subsidy shifts it to the right. Chapter 4 studies both.

Again: a change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the supply curve (a change in quantity supplied); a change in any of the factors above causes a shift of the curve (a change in supply).

docs.title: 2.6 Market equilibrium
docs.text:
Put the demand and supply curves on the same diagram. The point where they cross is the equilibrium of the market. At the equilibrium price, the quantity that buyers want to buy is exactly equal to the quantity that sellers want to sell. This quantity is the equilibrium quantity.

Price (₹) Quantity demanded, \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\) Quantity supplied, \(Q_s = -20 + 4P\) Situation Pressure on price 10 80 20 shortage of 60 upward 15 70 40 shortage of 30 upward 20 60 60 equilibrium none 25 50 80 surplus of 30 downward 30 40 100 surplus of 60 downward

Table 2.2. Demand and supply schedules of the market in this chapter.

Figure 2.1 Market equilibrium. The market of Table 2.2. Demand and supply cross at E, where the price is ₹20 and 60 units are bought and sold. At ₹25 sellers offer 80 units but buyers take only 50: a surplus of 30. At ₹15 buyers want 70 units but sellers offer only 40: a shortage of 30.

docs.title: How the market reaches equilibrium
docs.text:
Why should the price end up at ₹20? Consider what happens at other prices.

Above equilibrium: a surplus. At ₹25, sellers offer 80 units but buyers want only 50. There is a surplus (or excess supply) of 30 units. Unsold stocks pile up in warehouses and shops. To sell them, sellers cut their prices. As the price falls, the quantity demanded rises and the quantity supplied falls, and the surplus shrinks until it disappears at ₹20.

Below equilibrium: a shortage. At ₹15, buyers want 70 units but sellers offer only 40. There is a shortage (or excess demand) of 30 units. Queues form, shelves empty, and some buyers who cannot get the good offer to pay more. Sellers find they can raise their prices without losing customers. As the price rises, the quantity supplied rises and the quantity demanded falls, until the shortage disappears at ₹20.

Only at the equilibrium price is there no pressure for the price to change. This is why it is called an equilibrium. In many markets the adjustment is fast: prices in a vegetable market change from morning to evening. In others, such as the market for rented housing, prices adjust slowly and shortages or surpluses can persist for some time.

Key idea

In a competitive market the price moves until the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. A surplus pushes the price down; a shortage pushes it up. No one has to plan this: it is the result of buyers and sellers each responding to the price.

docs.title: Finding equilibrium with algebra
docs.text:
At equilibrium \(Q_d = Q_s\). With our equations:

\[ 100 - 2P = -20 + 4P \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 120 = 6P \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P^* = 20. \]

Substituting into either equation gives the quantity: \(Q^* = 100 - 2(20) = 60\), and as a check \(Q^* = -20 + 4(20) = 60\).

In general, for a demand curve \(Q_d = a - bP\) and a supply curve \(Q_s = c + dP\), setting them equal gives

\[ P^* = \frac{a - c}{b + d}, \qquad Q^* = a - bP^*. \]

docs.title: 2.7 How equilibrium changes
docs.text:
The power of the model lies in predicting what happens when conditions change. Use a four-step method.

  1. Decide whether the event shifts the demand curve, the supply curve, or both.
  2. Decide in which direction the curve shifts.
  3. Draw the shift on a diagram.
  4. Compare the new equilibrium with the old one.

docs.title: An increase in demand
docs.text:
Suppose incomes in a town rise and the good is normal. Buyers now want 30 more units than before at every price, so demand becomes

\[ Q_d = 130 - 2P. \]

Supply has not changed. The step-through figure shows what happens.

1The market begins at E1, with a price of ₹20 and 60 units sold.

2Incomes rise and demand shifts right from D1 to D2. At the old price of ₹20, buyers now want 90 units but sellers still offer 60: a shortage of 30.

3The shortage pushes the price up. Sellers move up along the supply curve until the market settles at E2, with a price of ₹25 and 80 units sold.

Figure 2.2 An increase in demand raises both price and quantity. An increase in demand

Algebraically, \(130 - 2P = -20 + 4P\), so \(6P = 150\), \(P^* = 25\) and \(Q^* = 130 - 50 = 80\). An increase in demand raises both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity. Notice that the supply curve did not shift: the rise in quantity supplied, from 60 to 80, is a movement along the supply curve caused by the higher price. A decrease in demand has the opposite effect: price and quantity both fall.

docs.title: A decrease in supply
docs.text:
Suppose instead that the cost of a raw material rises, so that producing each unit costs ₹6 more. Sellers now need ₹6 more than before to offer any given quantity: the supply curve shifts up by ₹6, from \(P = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\) to \(P = 11 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\). Solved for quantity, the new supply is \(Q_s = -44 + 4P\).

Figure 2.3 A decrease in supply. A decrease in supply. The supply curve shifts up from S1 to S2 because each unit costs ₹6 more to produce. The equilibrium moves from E1 (₹20, 60 units) to E2 (₹24, 52 units).

Setting \(100 - 2P = -44 + 4P\) gives \(6P = 144\), \(P^* = 24\) and \(Q^* = 100 - 48 = 52\). A decrease in supply raises the price and reduces the quantity. An increase in supply lowers the price and raises the quantity.

Notice that the price rose by only ₹4, not by the full ₹6 increase in cost. As the price rose, buyers bought less, and the sellers had to absorb part of the cost increase. How the burden is shared depends on how strongly buyers and sellers respond to price, which is the subject of Chapter 3 and, for taxes, of Chapter 4.

Example 2.2 Onion prices after a bad harvest

Heavy unseasonal rain damages a large part of the onion crop in the main growing regions. At the same time, a health report has no effect on the demand for onions. Predict what happens in the onion market.

Solution. The rain affects sellers, not buyers: it shifts supply to the left. Demand is unchanged. The equilibrium moves up along the demand curve: the price rises and the quantity bought and sold falls. Because onions have few close substitutes in cooking, buyers cut their purchases only a little, so the price rise is large. Sharp rises in onion prices after crop damage have been seen in India many times for exactly this reason. Chapter 3 explains why a small fall in supply can cause a large rise in price when demand is inelastic.

docs.title: When both curves shift
docs.text:
When demand and supply shift together, the direction of change of one of the two variables (price or quantity) can be predicted, but the other depends on which shift is larger.

Table 2.3. Effects of shifts in demand and supply on equilibrium.

Take the case of both curves shifting right: demand rises because incomes grow, and supply rises because of a better technology. Both shifts raise quantity, so quantity certainly rises. But the rise in demand pushes the price up and the rise in supply pushes it down; which wins depends on the sizes of the shifts.

Example 2.3 Both curves shift

Starting from \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\) and \(Q_s = -20 + 4P\), demand increases to \(Q_d = 130 - 2P\) and at the same time supply increases to \(Q_s = -2 + 4P\). Find the new equilibrium.

Solution. \(130 - 2P = -2 + 4P\) gives \(6P = 132\), so \(P^* = 22\) and \(Q^* = 130 - 44 = 86\). The price rose from ₹20 to ₹22 and the quantity from 60 to 86. With a larger rise in supply, say to \(Q_s = 16 + 4P\), we would get \(6P = 114\), \(P^* = 19\), \(Q^* = 92\): the quantity still rises but the price now falls. Both outcomes are possible, as Table 2.3 says.

docs.title: 2.8 Checking the arithmetic with a program
docs.text:
The formula for equilibrium is easy to put in a short program. Readers who know a little Python can use it to check answers and try other numbers.

def equilibrium(a, b, c, d):
    """Demand Qd = a - b*P and supply Qs = c + d*P.  Returns (P*, Q*)."""
    p = (a - c) / (b + d)
    q = a - b * p
    return p, q

print(equilibrium(100, 2, -20, 4))   # the market of Table 2.2
print(equilibrium(130, 2, -20, 4))   # after the rise in demand
print(equilibrium(100, 2, -44, 4))   # after the rise in costs
print(equilibrium(130, 2, -2, 4))    # Example 2.3

docs.title: 2.9 Summary
docs.text:
• A market brings buyers and sellers together. In a competitive market no single buyer or seller can influence the price.
  • The law of demand: other things equal, a higher price reduces the quantity demanded. Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands.
  • Demand shifts with income (normal and inferior goods), prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes, expectations and the number of buyers.
  • The law of supply: other things equal, a higher price increases the quantity supplied. Supply shifts with input prices, technology, prices of other goods the producer could make, expectations, the number of sellers, natural conditions and taxes or subsidies.
  • A change in the good's own price causes a movement along a curve; a change in anything else causes a shift of the curve.
  • At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above the equilibrium price there is a surplus, which pushes the price down; below it there is a shortage, which pushes the price up.
  • An increase in demand raises price and quantity; an increase in supply lowers price and raises quantity. When both curves shift, one of the two effects is ambiguous.

docs.title: 2.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

For each event, say whether the demand or the supply of cotton shirts shifts, and in which direction, or whether there is only a movement along a curve. (a) The price of raw cotton rises. (b) Incomes rise. (c) The price of cotton shirts falls. (d) A new loom halves the time needed to weave cloth. (e) Polyester shirts become cheaper.

Answer

(a) Supply shifts left (input cost). (b) Demand shifts right (shirts are a normal good). (c) Movement along the demand curve and along the supply curve; neither shifts. (d) Supply shifts right (technology). (e) Demand for cotton shirts shifts left (a substitute is cheaper).

Exercise 2

The demand for a good is \(Q_d = 120 - 3P\) and the supply is \(Q_s = 2P - 10\). Find the equilibrium price and quantity. What happens at a price of ₹30?

Answer

\(120 - 3P = 2P - 10\) gives \(5P = 130\), so \(P^* = 26\) and \(Q^* = 120 - 78 =\) 42. At ₹30, \(Q_d = 30\) and \(Q_s = 50\): a surplus of 20 units, which will push the price down.

Exercise 3

In the market of Exercise 2, demand increases by 15 units at every price. Find the new equilibrium.

Answer

New demand: \(Q_d = 135 - 3P\). Then \(135 - 3P = 2P - 10\), so \(5P = 145\), \(P^* = 29\), and \(Q^* = 135 - 87 =\) 48. Price and quantity both rise.

Exercise 4

Explain why a fall in the price of petrol might increase the price of second-hand cars.

Answer

Petrol and cars are complements. Cheaper petrol makes owning a car cheaper, so the demand for cars, including second-hand cars, shifts to the right. With supply unchanged, the price of second-hand cars rises.

Exercise 5

A good harvest increases the supply of wheat, and at the same time a rise in incomes reduces the demand for wheat because people switch to other foods. What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity of wheat?

Answer

Both shifts push the price down, so the price certainly falls. The rise in supply increases quantity and the fall in demand reduces it, so the effect on quantity is ambiguous: it depends on which shift is larger. (Note that this wheat is behaving as an inferior good.)

Exercise 6

A student writes: "If demand increases, price rises; but a higher price reduces demand, so demand falls again and the price comes back down." What is wrong with this reasoning?

Answer

It confuses demand with quantity demanded. The increase in demand is a shift of the curve. The resulting rise in price causes a movement along the new demand curve (a fall in quantity demanded from what it would be at the old price), not a shift back. The market settles at a new equilibrium with a higher price and a higher quantity.

Exercise 7

The demand for a good is \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\) and the supply is \(Q_s = -20 + 4P\). Show that a rise of ₹6 per unit in producers' costs raises the equilibrium price by ₹4. How much of the cost increase do the producers bear?

Answer

Section 2.7 shows the new equilibrium is \(P^* = 24\), \(Q^* = 52\), so the price rises by ₹4. Producers now receive ₹24 but their costs per unit have risen by ₹6 relative to the old supply curve; at the new quantity of 52 the old supply curve would have needed only \(5 + 52/4 = 18\) rupees. So producers bear ₹2 per unit of the ₹6 rise, and buyers bear ₹4.

  2. a movement down along the demand curve for tea

Exercise 2

Exercise 3

Answer

20 / ₹20

60 − P = 2P gives 3P = 60.

Exercise 4

In the same market (Qd = 60 − P, Qs = 2P), what is the equilibrium quantity?

Exercise 5

At a price above the equilibrium price there is

  1. a shortage, which pushes the price up
  2. a surplus, which pushes the price down
  3. a surplus, which pushes the price up
  4. no pressure for change

  1. price rises and quantity rises
  2. price falls and quantity rises
  3. price falls and quantity falls
  4. price rises and quantity falls

docs.title: Chapter 3: Elasticity
docs.text:
How strongly buyers and sellers respond to prices and incomes

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define the price elasticity of demand and calculate it by the midpoint method and at a point.
  2. Classify demand as elastic, inelastic or unit elastic, and recognise the extreme cases.
  3. Explain why elasticity changes along a straight-line demand curve.
  4. List the factors that make demand more or less elastic.
  5. Use elasticity to predict how a price change affects total revenue.
  6. Calculate and interpret income elasticity, cross-price elasticity and the price elasticity of supply.

docs.title: 3.1 Why responsiveness matters
docs.text:
The law of demand says that buyers take less when the price rises. It does not say how much less, and the answer matters a great deal. If a bus company raises its fares by 10 per cent, will it lose a few passengers or many? If a bad harvest reduces the supply of a crop, will the price rise a little or a lot? If the government taxes cigarettes, will smoking fall sharply, or will the tax mainly raise revenue? Each of these questions is about the responsiveness of quantity to price, and economists measure it with elasticity.

Elasticity is measured in percentage changes, not in units. This makes it independent of the units chosen: a demand for rice measured in kilograms or in quintals, and a price measured in rupees or in paise, give the same elasticity. It also lets us compare goods as different as salt and air travel.

docs.title: 3.2 The price elasticity of demand
docs.text:
The price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in the quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price:

\[ E_d = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}. \]

Because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, \(E_d\) is negative. Economists often drop the minus sign and speak of the elasticity's absolute value, written \(|E_d|\); "an elasticity of 2" means \(E_d = -2\). In this book we keep the sign in calculations and use the absolute value when comparing.

docs.title: The midpoint method
docs.text:
A percentage change depends on the starting point. If a price rises from ₹20 to ₹25, that is a rise of 25 per cent; if it falls from ₹25 to ₹20, that is a fall of 20 per cent. To get the same elasticity in both directions, economists use the midpoint method, which divides each change by the average of the two values:

\[ E_d = \frac{(Q_2 - Q_1) \big/ \tfrac{1}{2}(Q_1 + Q_2)}{(P_2 - P_1) \big/ \tfrac{1}{2}(P_1 + P_2)}. \]

Example 3.1 Elasticity by the midpoint method

The demand for a good is \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\), the curve of Chapter 2. The price rises from ₹20 to ₹25. Find the price elasticity of demand.

Solution. At ₹20, \(Q = 60\); at ₹25, \(Q = 50\).

\[ \%\Delta Q = \frac{50 - 60}{55} \times 100 = -18.18\%, \qquad \%\Delta P = \frac{25 - 20}{22.5} \times 100 = 22.22\%. \] \[ E_d = \frac{-18.18}{22.22} = -0.82. \]

A 1 per cent rise in price, in this range, reduces the quantity demanded by about 0.82 per cent. If we had used the starting values instead, we would have got \((-10/60)/(5/20) = -0.67\) for the rise and \((10/50)/(-5/25) = -1.00\) for the fall back again: two different answers for the same stretch of the curve. The midpoint method avoids this.

docs.title: Elastic and inelastic demand
docs.text:
Value of \(\lvert E_d \rvert\) Name Meaning greater than 1 elastic quantity changes by a larger percentage than price equal to 1 unit elastic quantity changes by the same percentage as price less than 1 inelastic quantity changes by a smaller percentage than price 0 perfectly inelastic quantity does not change at all; the demand curve is vertical infinite perfectly elastic any rise in price above a certain level reduces quantity to zero; the demand curve is horizontal

Table 3.1. Classes of price elasticity of demand.

The two extremes are limiting cases, useful in theory. A perfectly inelastic demand would describe a patient who needs a fixed dose of a life-saving medicine and will pay almost anything for it. A perfectly elastic demand is what a single wheat farmer faces in a large market: she can sell all she wants at the market price, but nothing at all if she asks even slightly more, because buyers will simply go to another farmer. Chapter 8 builds on this case.

docs.title: 3.3 Elasticity along a straight-line demand curve
docs.text:
It is tempting to think that a steep demand curve is inelastic and a flat one elastic. That is roughly right when comparing two curves through the same point, but it is misleading in general, because elasticity is not the same as slope. Along a straight-line demand curve the slope is constant, but the elasticity changes from point to point.

The point elasticity at a particular price measures the response to a very small change there:

\[ E_d = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P} \times \frac{P}{Q}. \]

For a straight line \(Q_d = a - bP\), the first factor is always \(-b\), so \(E_d = -bP/Q\). For our demand, \(b = 2\) and \(E_d = -2P/Q\). Table 3.2 shows the result.

Price (₹) Quantity Point elasticity \(-2P/Q\) Class Total revenue \(P \times Q\) (₹) 45 10 −9.00 elastic 450 40 20 −4.00 elastic 800 35 30 −2.33 elastic 1,050 30 40 −1.50 elastic 1,200 25 50 −1.00 unit elastic 1,250 20 60 −0.67 inelastic 1,200 15 70 −0.43 inelastic 1,050 10 80 −0.25 inelastic 800 5 90 −0.11 inelastic 450

Table 3.2. Elasticity and total revenue along the demand curve \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\).

The pattern is general. Near the top of a straight-line demand curve the price is high and the quantity small, so a given change in quantity is a large percentage change while a given change in price is a small one: demand is elastic. Near the bottom it is the other way round: demand is inelastic. Exactly half-way down, at the midpoint of the line, the elasticity is −1.

Figure 3.1 Elasticity and revenue along a demand curve. Top: along the straight-line demand curve, demand is elastic above the midpoint (₹25, 50 units), unit elastic at it and inelastic below it. Bottom: total revenue rises as the price falls through the elastic range, reaches its maximum of ₹1,250 at the midpoint, and falls as the price falls through the inelastic range.

Note for readers who know calculus

The point elasticity is \(E_d = \dfrac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\dfrac{P}{Q}\). For \(Q = 100 - 2P\), \(dQ/dP = -2\), which gives the formula used in the table. For a curve of the form \(Q = kP^{-e}\), the elasticity is \(-e\) at every point: such a curve has constant elasticity.

docs.title: 3.4 What makes demand elastic or inelastic
docs.text:
Why is the demand for salt inelastic and the demand for a particular brand of biscuits elastic? Five factors matter.

  1. Availability of close substitutes. This is the most important. The more easily buyers can switch to something else, the more elastic the demand. Salt has no close substitute; one brand of biscuits has many.
  2. Necessities and luxuries. Goods that people regard as necessities (basic food, essential medicines, electricity for lighting) tend to have inelastic demand. Goods that can be postponed or done without (foreign holidays, jewellery) tend to have elastic demand. What counts as a necessity varies between people and over time.
  3. Share of the budget. A good that takes a tiny share of income, such as matches or salt, has inelastic demand: even doubling its price makes little difference to the buyer. A good that takes a large share, such as a car or rent, tends to have more elastic demand.
  4. Time. Demand is usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run. When the price of petrol rises, people can at first do little except drive a bit less. Over several years they can buy more fuel-efficient vehicles, move closer to work, or switch to public transport.
  5. How the market is defined. The demand for "food" is very inelastic; the demand for "vegetables" less so; the demand for "tomatoes" more elastic still; and the demand for "tomatoes from one particular seller" very elastic. The more narrowly a good is defined, the more substitutes it has.

docs.title: 3.5 Elasticity and total revenue
docs.text:
The total revenue of sellers (equal to the total expenditure of buyers) is price times quantity:

\[ TR = P \times Q. \]

When the price falls, two things happen to revenue. Each unit sells for less, which reduces revenue; but more units are sold, which increases it. Which effect wins depends on the elasticity.

  • If demand is elastic, the percentage rise in quantity is larger than the percentage fall in price, so a price cut raises revenue and a price rise reduces it.
  • If demand is inelastic, the percentage rise in quantity is smaller than the percentage fall in price, so a price cut reduces revenue and a price rise increases it.
  • If demand is unit elastic, revenue does not change.

Table 3.2 and Figure 3.1 confirm this. Cutting the price from ₹40 to ₹30 (elastic range) raises revenue from ₹800 to ₹1,200. Cutting it from ₹20 to ₹10 (inelastic range) reduces revenue from ₹1,200 to ₹800. Revenue is greatest, at ₹1,250, at the unit-elastic midpoint.

Key idea

Elastic demand: price and revenue move in opposite directions. Inelastic demand: price and revenue move in the same direction. A seller who faces inelastic demand can raise revenue by raising the price; one who faces elastic demand cannot.

Example 3.2 The paradox of a good harvest

The demand for a staple crop is inelastic. In an ordinary year, 100 lakh quintals are sold at ₹2,000 per quintal. In a year with an excellent harvest, 110 lakh quintals come to market and the price falls to ₹1,500. What happens to farmers' total revenue? What is the elasticity of demand over this range?

Solution. Ordinary year: \(2{,}000 \times 100 = 2{,}00{,}000\) lakh rupees. Good year: \(1{,}500 \times 110 = 1{,}65{,}000\) lakh rupees. Revenue falls by 17.5 per cent even though farmers produced more.

By the midpoint method:

\[ E_d = \frac{10/105}{-500/1{,}750} = \frac{0.0952}{-0.2857} = -0.33. \]

Demand is inelastic, so the large fall in price outweighs the small rise in quantity. This is why a bumper crop can leave farmers worse off as a group, and why governments in many countries, India among them, have used support prices, procurement and storage to steady farm incomes. (Each individual farmer, of course, is better off with a bigger crop than with a smaller one at the same market price; the paradox is about all farmers together.)

The same reasoning explains why a cartel of producers of an inelastic good, such as crude oil in the short run, can raise its revenue by cutting output, and why a tax on a good with inelastic demand raises a lot of revenue without reducing consumption much.

docs.title: 3.6 Income and cross-price elasticities
docs.text: Elasticity can measure the response of demand to any variable. Two others are widely used.

docs.title: Income elasticity of demand
docs.text:
\[ E_Y = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded}}{\%\ \text{change in income}}. \] Value of \(E_Y\) Type of good Example negative inferior coarse grains or the cheapest form of travel, for many households between 0 and 1 normal necessity basic food, electricity greater than 1 normal luxury restaurant meals, air travel, jewellery

Table 3.3. Income elasticity and types of goods.

Income elasticities matter for firms and governments planning ahead. As incomes grow, spending shifts towards goods with high income elasticity. A well-documented regularity, known as Engel's law, is that the share of income spent on food falls as income rises, because food as a whole has an income elasticity below 1.

Example 3.3 Calculating income elasticity

A household's monthly income rises from ₹40,000 to ₹44,000. Its purchases change as follows: restaurant meals from 4 to 5 a month; rice from 20 kg to 21 kg; a coarse grain from 10 kg to 9 kg. Find the income elasticity for each, by the midpoint method.

Solution. The percentage change in income is \(4{,}000 / 42{,}000 = 9.52\%\).

  • Restaurant meals: \(1/4.5 = 22.22\%\), so \(E_Y = 22.22/9.52 = 2.33\): a luxury.
  • Rice: \(1/20.5 = 4.88\%\), so \(E_Y = 4.88/9.52 = 0.51\): a necessity.
  • Coarse grain: \(-1/9.5 = -10.53\%\), so \(E_Y = -10.53/9.52 = -1.11\): an inferior good for this household.

docs.title: Cross-price elasticity of demand
docs.text:
\[ E_{XY} = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity demanded of good X}}{\%\ \text{change in price of good Y}}. \]
  • If \(E_{XY} > 0\), X and Y are substitutes: a rise in the price of Y increases the demand for X.
  • If \(E_{XY} < 0\), they are complements: a rise in the price of Y reduces the demand for X.
  • If \(E_{XY}\) is close to 0, the goods are unrelated.

For example, if the price of coffee rises from ₹100 to ₹120 per packet and a household's purchases of tea rise from 50 to 55 packets a year, the cross-price elasticity is \((5/52.5)/(20/110) = 9.52\%/18.18\% = +0.52\): tea and coffee are substitutes. Competition authorities use cross-price elasticities to decide which products compete in the same market.

docs.title: 3.7 The price elasticity of supply
docs.text:
The price elasticity of supply measures how strongly the quantity supplied responds to price:

\[ E_s = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity supplied}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}. \]

It is positive, because the supply curve slopes upwards. Supply is elastic if \(E_s > 1\) and inelastic if \(E_s < 1\). A vertical supply curve (\(E_s = 0\)) describes a good whose quantity cannot change, such as the number of seats in a stadium on match day or the paintings of an artist who has died. A horizontal supply curve (infinite elasticity) describes a good that sellers will supply in any amount at a given price.

For the supply curve of Chapter 2, \(Q_s = -20 + 4P\), a rise in price from ₹20 to ₹25 raises quantity supplied from 60 to 80. By the midpoint method, \(E_s = (20/70)/(5/22.5) = 28.57\%/22.22\% = 1.29\): supply is elastic over this range.

docs.title: What determines the elasticity of supply
docs.text:
1. Time. This is the most important factor. In the very short run, the quantity of fresh fish on sale in the market this morning is fixed: supply is perfectly inelastic. In the short run, firms can vary output by using their existing plant more intensively. In the long run, they can build new plants and new firms can enter, so supply is much more elastic.
  2. Spare capacity. A firm with idle machines and workers can raise output quickly and cheaply; one working at full capacity cannot.
  3. Ease of storage. Goods that can be stored (grain, cement, garments) can be released from stocks when the price rises, so their supply is more elastic than that of perishable goods.
  4. Mobility of inputs. If workers and machines can easily be moved into the industry from elsewhere, supply is more elastic.

Caution

Do not confuse the elasticity of a curve with its slope, and do not judge elasticity from a diagram whose axes have no numbers. Changing the scale of an axis makes the same curve look steeper or flatter without changing its elasticity at any point.

docs.title: 3.8 Elasticity in a program
docs.text:
The calculations of this chapter are easy to automate. The program below computes midpoint elasticities and the point elasticities of Table 3.2.

def midpoint_elasticity(q1, q2, x1, x2):
    """Percentage change in q over percentage change in x, by the midpoint method."""
    pct_q = (q2 - q1) / ((q1 + q2) / 2)
    pct_x = (x2 - x1) / ((x1 + x2) / 2)
    return pct_q / pct_x

print(round(midpoint_elasticity(60, 50, 20, 25), 2))        # Example 3.1
print(round(midpoint_elasticity(100, 110, 2000, 1500), 2))  # Example 3.2
print(round(midpoint_elasticity(4, 5, 40000, 44000), 2))    # restaurant meals

for p in range(45, 0, -10):
    q = 100 - 2 * p
    print(p, q, round(-2 * p / q, 2), p * q)

-0.33
2.33
45 10 -9.0 450
35 30 -2.33 1050
25 50 -1.0 1250
15 70 -0.43 1050
5 90 -0.11 450

docs.title: 3.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Elasticity measures responsiveness in percentage terms, so it does not depend on units.
  • The price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Use the midpoint method for changes between two points, and \(E_d = (\Delta Q/\Delta P)(P/Q)\) at a point.
  • Demand is elastic if \(|E_d| > 1\), inelastic if \(|E_d| < 1\) and unit elastic if \(|E_d| = 1\).
  • Along a straight-line demand curve, elasticity falls from very elastic at the top to very inelastic at the bottom; it is −1 at the midpoint. Elasticity is not slope.
  • Demand is more elastic when there are close substitutes, when the good is a luxury, when it takes a large share of the budget, over a longer time, and when the market is narrowly defined.
  • With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, in the same direction. Revenue is greatest where demand is unit elastic.
  • Income elasticity separates inferior goods (negative), necessities (0 to 1) and luxuries (above 1). Cross-price elasticity is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.
  • The price elasticity of supply is greater in the long run, with spare capacity, when goods can be stored and when inputs are mobile.

docs.title: 3.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

When the price of a concert ticket rises from ₹400 to ₹600, the number sold falls from 1,100 to 900. Calculate the price elasticity of demand by the midpoint method. Is demand elastic or inelastic? What happens to the organisers' revenue?

Answer

\(\%\Delta Q = -200/1{,}000 = -20\%\); \(\%\Delta P = 200/500 = 40\%\). \(E_d = -20/40 =\) −0.5: inelastic. Revenue rises from \(400 \times 1{,}100 = 4{,}40{,}000\) to \(600 \times 900 = 5{,}40{,}000\) rupees, as expected with inelastic demand.

Exercise 2

The demand for a good is \(Q_d = 200 - 4P\). Find the point elasticity at \(P = 10\), \(P = 25\) and \(P = 40\). At what price is total revenue greatest?

Answer

\(E_d = -4P/Q\). At \(P = 10\): \(Q = 160\), \(E_d = -40/160 = -0.25\). At \(P = 25\): \(Q = 100\), \(E_d = -100/100 = -1\). At \(P = 40\): \(Q = 40\), \(E_d = -160/40 = -4\). Revenue is greatest where demand is unit elastic, at ₹25 (revenue \(25 \times 100 = 2{,}500\) rupees).

Exercise 3

A city bus company is losing money and proposes to raise fares to increase its revenue. Under what condition will this work? Would you expect the condition to hold more in the short run or the long run?

Answer

Revenue rises with a fare increase only if demand is inelastic (\(|E_d| < 1\)). Demand is likely to be more inelastic in the short run: over time passengers can buy two-wheelers, share rides, change jobs or move, so demand becomes more elastic and the fare rise may then reduce revenue.

Exercise 4

When a family's income rises by 10 per cent, its purchases of good A rise by 15 per cent, of good B by 4 per cent, and of good C fall by 3 per cent. Classify each good.

Answer

A: \(E_Y = 1.5\), a luxury. B: \(E_Y = 0.4\), a necessity. C: \(E_Y = -0.3\), an inferior good.

Exercise 5

The price of printers falls by 10 per cent and the quantity of ink cartridges sold rises by 6 per cent. Calculate the cross-price elasticity and say what it shows.

Answer

\(E_{XY} = +6/(-10) =\) −0.6. It is negative, so printers and cartridges are complements.

Exercise 6

Explain why the supply of fresh flowers on the morning of a festival is inelastic, while the supply of plastic buckets is elastic.

Answer

Fresh flowers are perishable and take time to grow: on the morning itself the quantity available is almost fixed, so a higher price brings little extra supply. Plastic buckets can be stored and produced quickly with spare capacity, so producers can respond to a higher price by releasing stocks and running machines longer.

Exercise 7

"The demand curve for petrol is steep, so the demand for petrol is inelastic at every price." Comment.

Answer

The statement confuses slope with elasticity. Elasticity depends on the ratio \(P/Q\) as well as the slope, so it changes along a straight-line curve, and its appearance depends on the scale of the axes. Petrol demand is in fact found to be fairly inelastic in the short run, but that is an empirical finding, not something one can read from the steepness of a drawing.
