docs.title: Chapter 11: Factor Markets: Labour, Capital and Land
docs.text:
How wages, interest and rent are determined

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain why the demand for a factor of production is a derived demand.
  2. Calculate the marginal revenue product of labour and use it to find how many workers a firm hires.
  3. Explain the shape of the labour supply curve, including the possibility that it bends backwards.
  4. Analyse equilibrium in a labour market, the effects of a minimum wage, and the reasons wages differ.
  5. Explain monopsony and why a minimum wage can raise employment in a monopsony.
  6. Use present value to decide whether an investment in capital is worthwhile.
  7. Distinguish economic rent from transfer earnings, and explain why land earns rent.

docs.title: 11.1 Factor markets and derived demand
docs.text:
Chapter 1 introduced the factors of production (labour, capital, land and entrepreneurship) and the incomes they earn: wages, interest, rent and profit. The prices of factors are set in factor markets, and they matter twice over. For firms, factor prices are costs. For households, they are incomes: most people earn most of their income by selling their labour. So the theory of factor markets is also a theory of the distribution of income.

Factor markets differ from markets for goods in one basic way. Households buy goods because the goods themselves give them utility. Firms hire factors not for their own sake but because the factors help produce goods that can be sold. The demand for a factor is therefore a derived demand: it is derived from the demand for the goods the factor helps to produce. The demand for construction workers depends on the demand for buildings; the demand for software engineers on the demand for software. When the demand for a product rises, so does the demand for the factors that make it.

docs.title: 11.2 The demand for labour
docs.text:
How many workers should a firm hire? The answer uses marginal analysis once more: hire another worker as long as the worker adds more to revenue than to cost.

The extra revenue a firm gets from hiring one more worker is the marginal revenue product of labour (MRP). For a firm that sells its output in a competitive market at price \(P\), it equals the worker's marginal product times the price:

\[ MRP_L = MP_L \times P. \]

(For a firm with market power, the price is replaced by marginal revenue: \(MRP_L = MP_L \times MR\).) The extra cost of hiring one more worker, if the firm hires in a competitive labour market, is the wage \(W\).

Example 11.1 How many workers to hire

A workshop making stools has the marginal products of Table 7.1. It sells stools at ₹50 each in a competitive market and can hire as many workers as it wants at ₹400 a day. How many workers should it hire?

Solution.

Workers Marginal product (stools per day) MRP \(= MP \times 50\) (₹) Wage (₹) Hire this worker? 1 10 500 400 yes 2 14 700 400 yes 3 12 600 400 yes 4 8 400 400 yes (just) 5 4 200 400 no 6 0 0 400 no

The workshop hires 4 workers. The fourth adds exactly as much to revenue as to cost; the fifth would add ₹200 to revenue and ₹400 to cost. With 4 workers it produces 44 stools, earning \(44 \times 50 = 2{,}200\) rupees a day, and pays \(4 \times 400 = 1{,}600\) rupees in wages.

Figure 11.1 Marginal revenue product and the hiring decision. The marginal revenue product of each worker in Example 11.1. The firm hires every worker whose MRP is at least the daily wage of ₹400: four workers.

The rule is: hire workers up to the point where the marginal revenue product of labour equals the wage, \(MRP_L = W\). If the wage fell to ₹200, the firm would hire 5 workers; if it rose to ₹600, it would hire 3. Along its falling part, the MRP curve shows how many workers the firm wants at each wage: the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour. It slopes down because of diminishing marginal returns.

docs.title: What shifts the demand for labour
docs.text:
1. The price of the product. A higher price raises MRP at every level of employment, so the firm hires more. This is the derived nature of factor demand.
  2. Productivity and technology. Anything that raises the marginal product of workers (better machines, training, better organisation) raises MRP and the demand for labour. A technology can also replace some kinds of workers while making others more productive, so it may reduce the demand for some skills and increase it for others.
  3. The prices of other factors. If machines become cheaper, a firm may substitute machines for workers (reducing the demand for labour) but may also expand output because its costs have fallen (increasing it). Which effect wins varies.

The market demand for a particular kind of labour is the sum of the demands of all the firms that employ it.

docs.title: 11.3 The supply of labour
docs.text:
Each person has a fixed number of hours in a day and must divide them between work (paid) and leisure (everything else, including rest, study, housework and time with family). The opportunity cost of an hour of leisure is the wage forgone. So the decision of how much to work is a choice between income and leisure, which can be analysed with the tools of Chapter 6.

What happens when the wage rises? Two effects pull in opposite directions.

  • Substitution effect. A higher wage makes leisure more expensive (each hour of leisure now costs more income), so the worker substitutes work for leisure and works more.
  • Income effect. A higher wage makes the worker richer. If leisure is a normal good, a richer person wants more of it, and so works less.

At low wages the substitution effect usually dominates, and a higher wage brings more hours of work. At high wages, the income effect may dominate: a person who already earns a good income may use a pay rise partly to work fewer hours. The individual labour supply curve may therefore bend backwards at high wages. Over the long run, as wages have risen in many economies, average working hours have tended to fall, which is consistent with a strong income effect.

The market supply of a particular kind of labour, however, almost always slopes upwards. A higher wage in one occupation attracts workers from other occupations and draws people into the labour force, and this outweighs any reduction in hours by those already working. The supply of labour to an occupation also depends on the wages in other occupations, the training required, the pleasantness of the work, and the size and skills of the population.

docs.title: 11.4 Wages in a competitive labour market
docs.text: In a competitive labour market, with many employers and many workers, the wage is set where the demand for labour equals the supply, just as the price of a good is set in Chapter 2. Each firm takes this wage as given and hires up to the point where MRP equals it. Changes in demand or supply change the wage: when the demand for software spread across the economy, the demand for software engineers rose and their wages rose; when large numbers of new workers enter an occupation, wages in it tend to fall, other things equal.

docs.title: Why wages differ
docs.text:
If all workers and jobs were alike, competition would bring all wages to the same level. In fact wages differ greatly, for several reasons.

  1. Compensating differentials. Jobs differ in their non-money features. Dangerous, dirty, unpleasant or night-shift jobs must pay more to attract workers; pleasant or secure jobs can pay less.
  2. Human capital. Education and training are investments that raise a worker's productivity and so her MRP. Jobs that require long training (surgeons, engineers, airline pilots) pay more, partly to compensate for the cost of the training, including the earnings forgone while studying (Chapter 1).
  3. Ability and effort. Some people are more able or work harder in a particular job, and are paid more for it.
  4. Superstar effects. In some fields (sport, entertainment, writing) technology lets the best performer reach millions of people, so a small difference in talent can bring a very large difference in pay.
  5. Market power of employers (Section 11.5) or of workers, through trade unions, which bargain for higher wages on behalf of their members.
  6. Discrimination, which is paying people differently, or denying them jobs, because of their sex, caste, religion, race or other characteristics unrelated to their productivity. Discrimination by employers is generally illegal, and competition tends to work against it, since an employer who refuses to hire able workers bears a cost. But it can persist, especially where competition is weak or where customers or co-workers discriminate.

docs.title: The minimum wage
docs.text:
Many countries set a legal minimum wage, a price floor in the labour market (Chapter 4). In a competitive labour market, a minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage raises the pay of those who keep their jobs, but reduces the quantity of labour demanded and increases the quantity supplied, creating unemployment.

Figure 11.2 A minimum wage in a competitive labour market. A competitive labour market with demand W = 200 − L and supply W = 40 + L. The equilibrium is 80 workers at a wage of ₹120. A minimum wage of ₹150 reduces employment to 50 while 110 people want to work at that wage: 60 are unemployed.

In Figure 11.2, the equilibrium wage is ₹120 with 80 workers employed. At a minimum wage of ₹150, employers want only \(200 - 150 = 50\) workers, while \(150 - 40 = 110\) people want jobs. Employment falls by 30, and unemployment of 60 appears.

How large such effects are in practice is one of the most studied and debated questions in economics. The answer depends on how high the minimum wage is relative to typical wages, on the elasticity of labour demand, and on whether employers have market power. Much research has found that moderate minimum wages have small effects on employment, while very high ones reduce it. The next section explains one reason why.

docs.title: 11.5 Monopsony
docs.text:
A monopsony is a market with a single buyer. In a labour market, it is a single employer, or one so dominant that it can influence the wage: a large factory in a small town, a mine in a remote area, or the main hospital employing nurses in a region. Where a competitive employer can hire as many workers as it wants at the market wage, a monopsonist faces the upward-sloping market supply curve of labour: to hire more workers, it must raise the wage, and (if it cannot pay different workers different wages) it must raise it for all its workers.

So the cost of hiring one more worker, the marginal cost of labour, is greater than the wage: it is the new worker's wage plus the increase paid to everyone already employed.

Example 11.2 A monopsony employer

A factory is the only employer in a town. The labour supply is \(W = 20 + L\), and the factory's marginal revenue product of labour is \(MRP = 200 - 2L\) (wages in rupees per hour, \(L\) in workers). Compare the monopsony outcome with the competitive one.

Solution. The total wage bill is \(W \times L = 20L + L^2\), so the marginal cost of labour is \(MCL = 20 + 2L\), rising twice as fast as the wage.

Monopsony. The factory hires where \(MCL = MRP\): \(20 + 2L = 200 - 2L\), so \(L = 45\). It pays the lowest wage at which 45 people will work, from the supply curve: \(W = 20 + 45 = 65\).

Competition. If many employers competed for these workers, the wage would be set where supply meets demand (MRP): \(20 + L = 200 - 2L\), so \(L = 60\) and \(W = 80\).

The monopsonist employs fewer workers (45 instead of 60) and pays a lower wage (₹65 instead of ₹80). Each worker's MRP at 45 workers is \(200 - 90 = 110\) rupees, well above the wage.

Now suppose a minimum wage of ₹80 is imposed on the monopsonist. It can no longer pay less than ₹80, and at that wage it can hire up to 60 workers without raising pay further, so its marginal cost of labour is ₹80 for each of the first 60 workers. It hires up to where \(MRP = 80\): \(200 - 2L = 80\), so \(L = 60\). The minimum wage raises both the wage and employment. This is why the effects of minimum wages are an empirical question: in labour markets where employers have market power, a well-chosen minimum wage need not reduce employment, and may increase it.

docs.title: 11.6 Capital and the rate of interest
docs.text: Capital (machines, buildings, vehicles, computers) is a durable factor: it is bought once and yields services over many years. A firm's decision to buy capital is an investment decision, and to make it the firm must compare money spent today with money received in the future.

docs.title: Present value
docs.text:
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year, because a rupee today can be lent at interest. If the interest rate is \(r\) per year, ₹100 lent today becomes \(100(1 + r)\) next year. Turning this round, a sum \(X\) received one year from now is worth \(X/(1 + r)\) today, and a sum received in \(t\) years is worth

\[ PV = \frac{X}{(1 + r)^t}. \]

This is the present value of the future sum, and the process of finding it is called discounting. At an interest rate of 10 per cent, ₹110 a year from now has a present value of ₹100, and ₹121 two years from now also has a present value of ₹100.

docs.title: The investment decision
docs.text:
A firm should buy a piece of capital if the present value of the extra net revenue it will produce is greater than its cost. Equivalently, the net present value (present value of returns minus cost) should be positive.

Example 11.3 Is the machine worth buying?

A machine costs ₹1,000. It will add ₹600 to the firm's net revenue at the end of each of the next two years and then be worthless. Should the firm buy it if the interest rate is 10 per cent? If it is 15 per cent?

Solution. At 10 per cent:

\[ PV = \frac{600}{1.10} + \frac{600}{1.10^2} = 545.45 + 495.87 = 1{,}041.32. \]

The present value exceeds the cost, so the machine is worth buying: its net present value is ₹41.32.

At 15 per cent:

\[ PV = \frac{600}{1.15} + \frac{600}{1.15^2} = 521.74 + 453.69 = 975.43. \]

The present value is now less than the cost, so the machine is not worth buying.

The example shows why investment falls when the interest rate rises: higher interest rates reduce the present value of future returns, so fewer investment projects are worthwhile. The interest rate is the price that balances the demand for funds to invest with the supply of funds from savers. It is also why central banks, by influencing interest rates, can influence the amount firms invest, a subject for macroeconomics.

def present_value(flows, r):
    """Present value of the amounts in flows, received at the end of years 1, 2, ..."""
    return sum(x / (1 + r) ** t for t, x in enumerate(flows, start=1))

for r in (0.10, 0.15):
    pv = present_value([600, 600], r)
    print(f"r = {r:.0%}: PV = {pv:.2f}, NPV = {pv - 1000:.2f}")

r = 10%: PV = 1041.32, NPV = 41.32
r = 15%: PV = 975.43, NPV = -24.57

The same reasoning applies to human capital. A student deciding whether to take a degree compares the present value of the extra earnings it will bring with its cost, including forgone earnings. Lower interest rates, and longer working lives over which to earn the return, make such investments more attractive.

docs.title: 11.7 Land and economic rent
docs.text:
In economics, land means all natural resources, and the payment for its use is rent. What makes land special is that its total quantity is fixed: the area of a country, or of a particular city centre, cannot be increased (apart from small amounts of reclamation). Its supply curve is vertical.

Figure 11.3 Rent on land in fixed supply. The supply of land is fixed, so its supply curve is vertical. A rise in demand from D1 to D2 raises the rent from R1 to R2 without changing the quantity of land.

With a vertical supply curve, the rent is determined entirely by demand. When the demand for land in a growing city rises, the quantity of land cannot rise, so the whole effect falls on the rent. This is why land in the centres of growing cities becomes extremely expensive. David Ricardo, in the early nineteenth century, argued that rent on farmland is high because the price of corn is high, not the other way round: the rent is a result of the demand for what the land produces.

docs.title: Economic rent and transfer earnings
docs.text:
The idea can be generalised to any factor. A factor's transfer earnings are the minimum payment needed to keep it in its present use: what it could earn in its next best use. Anything it is paid above this is economic rent:

\[ \text{economic rent} = \text{actual earnings} - \text{transfer earnings}. \]

Land in fixed supply with no other use earns only economic rent, since it would be there whatever it was paid. A famous cricketer who earns ₹5 crore a year and whose best alternative would be a job paying ₹10 lakh earns transfer earnings of ₹10 lakh and economic rent of ₹4.9 crore. The rent arises because his particular talent is scarce and cannot be supplied by anyone else.

Economic rent has an important property: a tax on it does not change the quantity supplied. Taxing part of the economic rent of a fixed factor leaves it in its present use, since it still earns more there than anywhere else. This is why some economists, notably Henry George in the nineteenth century, argued for taxing land values: such a tax raises revenue without the deadweight loss of most taxes (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 11.8 The distribution of income
docs.text:
The theory of this chapter explains the incomes earned by factors: each factor tends to be paid according to its marginal revenue product, adjusted for market power on either side. This is the functional distribution of income, between wages, interest, rent and profit.

How income is shared among people (the personal distribution) depends also on how much of each factor each person owns. A person who owns land and capital as well as labour receives rent and interest as well as wages. Differences in skills, education, inherited wealth, health and opportunity all shape the personal distribution, and inequalities in these tend to pass from one generation to the next. Governments influence the distribution through taxes, transfers, public education and health care, and laws on wages and working conditions. How much inequality a society should accept is a normative question (Chapter 1); positive economics can describe the trade-offs involved in reducing it.

docs.title: 11.9 Summary
docs.text:
• The demand for a factor is a derived demand, depending on the demand for the goods it helps to produce.
  • A firm hires labour up to the point where the marginal revenue product equals the wage: \(MP_L \times P = W\). The MRP curve is the firm's labour demand curve.
  • A higher wage has a substitution effect (work more) and an income effect (work less); individual labour supply may bend backwards, but market supply to an occupation slopes upwards.
  • In a competitive labour market, the wage is set by demand and supply. Wages differ because of compensating differentials, human capital, ability, superstar effects, market power and discrimination.
  • A minimum wage above the competitive wage reduces employment in a competitive market. In a monopsony, where the marginal cost of labour exceeds the wage, the employer hires fewer workers at a lower wage, and a minimum wage can raise both wages and employment.
  • Investment in capital is worthwhile if the present value of its returns exceeds its cost. Higher interest rates reduce present values and investment.
  • Land is in fixed supply, so its rent is determined by demand. Economic rent is the payment above transfer earnings; taxing it does not change the quantity supplied.

docs.title: 11.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A firm sells its product at ₹20 in a competitive market. The marginal products of the 1st to 5th workers are 30, 25, 20, 15 and 10 units a day. How many workers will it hire at a daily wage of ₹350? At ₹250?

Answer

MRPs: ₹600, ₹500, ₹400, ₹300, ₹200. At ₹350 it hires 3 workers (the 4th's MRP of ₹300 is below the wage). At ₹250 it hires 4 workers.

Exercise 2

Explain why a fall in the price of tea leaves would reduce the wages of tea pickers, other things equal.

Answer

The demand for tea pickers is derived from the demand for tea. A lower price of tea reduces the marginal revenue product of each picker (\(MP \times P\)), so the demand curve for pickers shifts left. With the supply of pickers unchanged, their wage and employment fall.

Exercise 3

A consultant's hourly fee rises from ₹2,000 to ₹3,000 and she decides to work fewer hours. Explain this using income and substitution effects.

Answer

The substitution effect of the higher fee makes leisure more costly and on its own would lead her to work more. The income effect makes her richer, and with leisure a normal good, leads her to want more leisure. Since she works fewer hours, the income effect is larger: she is on the backward-bending part of her labour supply curve.

Exercise 4

In the labour market of Figure 11.2 (\(W = 200 - L\) for demand, \(W = 40 + L\) for supply), what happens if the minimum wage is set at ₹100?

Answer

₹100 is below the equilibrium wage of ₹120, so the minimum wage is not binding. The market stays at 80 workers and ₹120.

Exercise 5

A monopsonist faces labour supply \(W = 10 + 2L\) and has \(MRP = 130 - 2L\). Find the employment and wage it chooses, and compare with a competitive market.

Answer

Wage bill \(= 10L + 2L^2\), so \(MCL = 10 + 4L\). Monopsony: \(10 + 4L = 130 - 2L\) gives \(L = 20\), wage \(= 10 + 40 =\) ₹50. Competitive: \(10 + 2L = 130 - 2L\) gives \(L = 30\), wage \(= 10 + 60 =\) ₹70. The monopsonist hires fewer workers at a lower wage.

Exercise 6

A project costs ₹5,000 today and will return ₹3,000 at the end of each of the next two years. Is it worth undertaking at an interest rate of 8 per cent?

Answer

\(PV = 3{,}000/1.08 + 3{,}000/1.08^2 = 2{,}777.78 + 2{,}572.02 = 5{,}349.79\) rupees. This exceeds the cost of ₹5,000, so yes: the net present value is about ₹349.79.

Exercise 7

A singer earns ₹80 lakh a year. Her best alternative is teaching music for ₹6 lakh a year. Find her transfer earnings and economic rent. What would happen if a tax took ₹20 lakh of her earnings?

Answer

Transfer earnings ₹6 lakh; economic rent \(80 - 6 =\) ₹74 lakh. A tax of ₹20 lakh leaves her earning ₹60 lakh after tax, still far more than ₹6 lakh, so she would continue singing: a tax that falls on economic rent does not change the quantity supplied.

docs.title: 11.11 Quiz
docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 11

Exercise 1

The demand for labour is called a derived demand because

  1. it is derived from the supply of labour
  2. it depends on the demand for the goods that labour produces
  3. it is set by the government
  4. workers derive utility from work
Answer

it depends on the demand for the goods that labour produces

Exercise 2

A worker's marginal product is 12 units a day and the product sells for ₹40 in a competitive market. What is her marginal revenue product, in rupees per day?

Answer

480 / ₹480

Exercise 3

A competitive firm hires workers up to the point where

  1. the wage equals the price of the product
  2. marginal revenue product equals the wage
  3. marginal product is at its maximum
  4. average product equals the wage
Answer

marginal revenue product equals the wage

Exercise 4

The labour supply curve of an individual bends backwards when, at high wages,

  1. the substitution effect outweighs the income effect
  2. the income effect outweighs the substitution effect
  3. leisure is an inferior good
  4. the demand for labour falls
Answer

the income effect outweighs the substitution effect

Exercise 5

In a monopsony labour market, compared with a competitive one, the employer

  1. hires more workers at a higher wage
  2. hires fewer workers at a lower wage
  3. hires the same number at a lower wage
  4. pays the marginal revenue product
Answer

hires fewer workers at a lower wage

Exercise 6

At an interest rate of 10 per cent, what is the present value of ₹550 received one year from now, in rupees?

Answer

500 / ₹500

Exercise 7

Economic rent is

  1. the payment for using land only
  2. earnings above what is needed to keep a factor in its present use
  3. the rent paid for a flat
  4. the same as transfer earnings
Answer

earnings above what is needed to keep a factor in its present use

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Standard textbooks and classic works for going further

docs.title: Introductory textbooks
docs.text:
The following are widely used textbooks that cover the ground of this book, often in more depth and with many more exercises. Editions are revised regularly; any recent edition will serve.

  1. N. Gregory Mankiw, Principles of Microeconomics, Cengage Learning. A clear and widely used first course, with an emphasis on applications and policy.
  2. Paul Krugman and Robin Wells, Microeconomics, Worth Publishers. An introductory text with many examples from current events.
  3. Robert S. Pindyck and Daniel L. Rubinfeld, Microeconomics, Pearson. A step up from a first course, with fuller treatment of consumer theory, market structure and information.
  4. Hal R. Varian, Intermediate Microeconomics: A Modern Approach, W. W. Norton. The standard next step for readers comfortable with some mathematics.
  5. The CORE Project, The Economy, available free online. An introductory course built around real problems, with good coverage of behavioural economics, game theory and inequality.
  6. OpenStax, Principles of Microeconomics, Rice University. A free, openly licensed introductory textbook.
  7. National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT), Introductory Microeconomics (Class XII), New Delhi. A freely available school textbook covering consumer behaviour, production, costs and market forms.

docs.title: Game theory and behavioural economics
docs.text:
1. Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff, Thinking Strategically, W. W. Norton. A non-technical introduction to game theory and its uses.
  2. Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011. An account of research on judgement and choice, including prospect theory, written for a general reader.
  3. Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein, Nudge, Yale University Press, 2008. The book that introduced choice architecture and nudges to a wide audience.
  4. Richard H. Thaler, Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics, W. W. Norton, 2015. A history of behavioural economics by one of its founders.

docs.title: Classic works
docs.text:
1. Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 1776. The source of the division of labour, the pin factory and the "invisible hand".
  2. David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, 1817. The original statement of comparative advantage and of the theory of rent.
  3. Alfred Marshall, Principles of Economics, 1890. The work that established demand and supply analysis, elasticity and consumer surplus in their modern form.
  4. Ronald H. Coase, "The Problem of Social Cost", Journal of Law and Economics, 1960. The article behind the Coase theorem.
  5. George A. Akerlof, "The Market for 'Lemons': Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism", Quarterly Journal of Economics, 1970. The classic analysis of adverse selection.
  6. Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons, Cambridge University Press, 1990. A study of how communities manage common resources.

docs.title: How to use these sources
docs.text: For more practice with the tools of this book, Mankiw, Krugman and Wells, or the OpenStax text are the most useful next steps. For a more rigorous treatment using calculus, go on to Varian or Pindyck and Rubinfeld. For behavioural economics and game theory written for the general reader, start with Kahneman and with Dixit and Nalebuff. The classic works repay reading in extracts: the opening chapters of Smith and the seventh chapter of Ricardo, on foreign trade, are good places to begin.

(Chapter 7) Diminishing marginal utility The fall in the extra satisfaction from each additional unit of a good consumed within a period. (Chapter 12) Factors of production The inputs used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. docs.title: Chapter 6: Indifference Curves and Budget Constraints
docs.text:
The modern theory of consumer choice, and the income and substitution effects

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Draw indifference curves and explain their four properties.
  2. Define and calculate the marginal rate of substitution, and explain why it usually diminishes.
  3. Draw a budget line, find its intercepts and slope, and show how it moves when income or prices change.
  4. Find the consumer's best bundle as the tangency of an indifference curve and the budget line, both graphically and with a simple utility function.
  5. Derive an Engel curve and a demand curve from changes in income and price.
  6. Split the effect of a price change into a substitution effect and an income effect, and use them to distinguish normal, inferior and Giffen goods.

docs.title: 6.1 Indifference curves
docs.text:
Chapter 5 ended with the observation that consumer choice needs only a ranking of bundles. This chapter builds the theory on that basis. We keep to two goods, X and Y, so that everything can be drawn; the conclusions extend to any number of goods.

An indifference curve joins all the bundles of X and Y that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. She is indifferent between any two points on the same curve. Table 6.1 lists some bundles between which a consumer, Nisha, is indifferent.

Bundle Good X Good Y A 5 30 B 10 15 C 15 10 D 25 6 E 30 5

Table 6.1. Bundles that Nisha likes equally well.

Plotted with X on the horizontal axis and Y on the vertical axis, these points lie on one indifference curve. A collection of indifference curves, one for each level of satisfaction, is called an indifference map.

docs.title: Properties of indifference curves
docs.text:
Given the assumptions about preferences in Chapter 5, indifference curves have four properties.

  1. They slope downwards. Because more is better, if a bundle has more X it must have less Y to leave the consumer equally well off. A curve sloping upwards would join a bundle to another with more of both goods, which she would prefer.
  2. Curves further from the origin represent higher satisfaction. A curve further out contains bundles with more of both goods than some bundles on a curve further in.
  3. They do not cross. Suppose two curves crossed at a bundle A. Take a bundle B on one curve and C on the other, with C containing more of both goods than B. The consumer is indifferent between A and B (same curve) and between A and C (same curve), so by transitivity between B and C. But C has more of both goods, so she must prefer C. This contradiction shows the curves cannot cross.
  4. They are usually convex to the origin (bowed inwards). This reflects a diminishing marginal rate of substitution, explained next.

docs.title: 6.2 The marginal rate of substitution
docs.text:
The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) of X for Y is the amount of Y that the consumer is willing to give up to get one more unit of X, while staying equally well off. It is the absolute value of the slope of the indifference curve:

\[ MRS_{XY} = -\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta X} \quad \text{(along an indifference curve)}. \]

From Table 6.1:

Move Change in X Change in Y MRS (Y given up per unit of X) A to B +5 −15 3.0 B to C +5 −5 1.0 C to D +10 −4 0.4 D to E +5 −1 0.2

Table 6.2. Nisha's marginal rate of substitution falls as she has more X.

When Nisha has little X and much Y (bundle A), she would give up 3 units of Y for one more X. When she has much X and little Y (bundle D), she would give up only 0.2 units of Y. This is the diminishing marginal rate of substitution: the more of a good a consumer has, the less of the other good she will give up to get still more of it. It is why indifference curves are bowed towards the origin: steep where X is scarce, flat where X is plentiful. Consumers generally prefer balanced bundles to extreme ones.

docs.title: MRS and marginal utilities
docs.text:
If we do use utility numbers, the MRS has a simple meaning. Moving along an indifference curve, the utility lost by giving up \(\Delta Y\) must equal the utility gained from \(\Delta X\): \(MU_Y \times |\Delta Y| = MU_X \times \Delta X\). Rearranging,

\[ MRS_{XY} = \frac{MU_X}{MU_Y}. \]

The bundles of Table 6.1 all give \(X \times Y = 150\). They lie on an indifference curve of the utility function \(U = XY\), for which \(MU_X = Y\) and \(MU_Y = X\), so \(MRS = Y/X\). At bundle C, \(MRS = 10/15 = 0.67\): in this small neighbourhood Nisha would give up about two-thirds of a unit of Y for one more X. (The figures in Table 6.2 are averages over larger steps.)

docs.title: Two special cases
docs.text:
• Perfect substitutes. If two goods are interchangeable at a fixed rate, such as two brands of identical bottled water, the MRS is constant and indifference curves are straight lines.
  • Perfect complements. If two goods are only useful together in fixed proportions, such as left and right shoes, an extra unit of one without the other adds nothing. Indifference curves are L-shaped, with the corner where the goods are in the right proportion.

Most pairs of goods lie between these extremes, with smoothly curved indifference curves.

docs.title: 6.3 The budget constraint
docs.text:
Preferences say what the consumer would like; the budget constraint says what she can afford. With income \(M\) and prices \(P_X\) and \(P_Y\), she can buy any bundle with

\[ P_X X + P_Y Y \le M. \]

The bundles that use the whole income lie on the budget line \(P_X X + P_Y Y = M\).

Suppose Nisha has ₹120 to spend, X costs ₹4 and Y costs ₹6. Her budget line is \(4X + 6Y = 120\).

  • If she spends everything on X, she gets \(120/4 = 30\) units: the horizontal intercept is \(M/P_X = 30\).
  • If she spends everything on Y, she gets \(120/6 = 20\) units: the vertical intercept is \(M/P_Y = 20\).
  • The slope of the line is \(-P_X/P_Y = -4/6 = -2/3\). To get one more unit of X she must give up two-thirds of a unit of Y. The ratio \(P_X/P_Y\) is the relative price of X: the rate at which the market lets her exchange Y for X.

Bundles on or inside the line are affordable; bundles outside are not.

docs.title: Changes in income and prices
docs.text:
• A rise in income shifts the budget line outwards, parallel to itself. Both intercepts rise in proportion and the slope (relative price) is unchanged. With \(M = 180\), the intercepts become 45 and 30.
  • A fall in the price of X makes the line pivot outwards around the vertical intercept. The consumer can buy more X with all her income, but no more Y. If \(P_X\) falls to ₹3, the horizontal intercept rises to 40, the vertical intercept stays at 20, and the slope becomes \(-3/6 = -1/2\).
  • Doubling all prices and income together leaves the budget line exactly where it was. Only relative prices and real income matter.

docs.title: 6.4 The consumer's optimum
docs.text:
Put the indifference map and the budget line together. The consumer wants to reach the highest indifference curve she can, given her budget line. The best bundle is the point where the budget line just touches an indifference curve without crossing it: a point of tangency.

Figure 6.1 The consumer's optimum. Nisha's indifference curves for U = 96, 150 and 216 and her budget line 4X + 6Y = 120. The highest curve she can reach is U = 150, which touches the budget line at E: 15 units of X and 10 of Y.

In Figure 6.1, the curve \(U = 96\) cuts the budget line in two places: Nisha can afford bundles on it, but she can do better by moving along the line towards E. The curve \(U = 216\) lies wholly outside the budget line: she cannot afford any bundle on it. The curve \(U = 150\) touches the line at E, so E is the best affordable bundle.

At the tangency, the slope of the indifference curve equals the slope of the budget line:

\[ MRS_{XY} = \frac{P_X}{P_Y}. \]

The left side is the rate at which Nisha is willing to exchange Y for X; the right side is the rate at which the market allows her to. If they differ, she can gain by trading. Suppose \(MRS = 2\) while \(P_X/P_Y = 2/3\): she would give up 2 units of Y for one more X, but the market asks only two-thirds of a unit. She should buy more X and less Y, moving down the budget line, until the MRS has fallen to equal the price ratio.

Since \(MRS = MU_X/MU_Y\), the tangency condition can be written

\[ \frac{MU_X}{MU_Y} = \frac{P_X}{P_Y} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{MU_X}{P_X} = \frac{MU_Y}{P_Y}, \]

which is exactly the equimarginal principle of Chapter 5. The two approaches agree, but the indifference-curve approach needs only the ranking of bundles.

Example 6.1 Finding the optimum with a utility function

Nisha's preferences can be represented by \(U = XY\). Her income is ₹120, \(P_X = 4\) and \(P_Y = 6\). Find her best bundle.

Solution. For \(U = XY\), \(MRS = Y/X\). The tangency condition is

\[ \frac{Y}{X} = \frac{4}{6} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y = \tfrac{2}{3}X. \]

Substitute into the budget line: \(4X + 6\left(\tfrac{2}{3}X\right) = 120\), so \(8X = 120\) and \(X = 15\). Then \(Y = 10\). She spends \(4 \times 15 = 60\) rupees on X and \(6 \times 10 = 60\) rupees on Y, and reaches \(U = 150\), as in Figure 6.1.

Notice that she spends exactly half her income on each good. This is a property of \(U = XY\): for any income and prices, \(X = M/(2P_X)\) and \(Y = M/(2P_Y)\).

Corner solutions

Sometimes the best bundle contains none of one good: the highest indifference curve the consumer can reach touches the budget line at an intercept. A person who does not drink coffee buys none, whatever its price. The tangency condition then does not hold with equality; instead, at the corner, the MRS is less than the price ratio, so even the first unit of the good is not worth its price to her.

docs.title: 6.5 How the optimum responds to income
docs.text:
If income rises and prices stay the same, the budget line shifts out in parallel and the consumer moves to a new tangency on a higher indifference curve. Joining the optimal bundles for different incomes gives the income-consumption curve.

With \(U = XY\) and \(P_X = 4\), \(P_Y = 6\):

Income (₹) X bought Y bought 60 7.5 5 120 15 10 180 22.5 15 240 30 20

Table 6.3. Nisha's purchases at different incomes.

The relationship between income and the quantity bought of a good, at fixed prices, is called an Engel curve (after the statistician Ernst Engel). Here both goods are normal: more income, more of each. For an inferior good, the income-consumption curve bends back, and a rise in income leads the consumer to buy less of it.

docs.title: 6.6 How the optimum responds to price: the demand curve
docs.text:
If the price of X changes while income and the price of Y stay the same, the budget line pivots and the consumer moves to a new tangency. The curve joining these optimal bundles is the price-consumption curve, and the relationship between the price of X and the quantity of X bought is the consumer's demand curve for X.

With \(U = XY\) and \(M = 120\), the demand for X is \(X = 60/P_X\):

Price of X (₹) 6 4 3 2 Quantity of X 10 15 20 30

Table 6.4. Nisha's demand for X, derived from her indifference curves.

The demand curve slopes down, as the law of demand says. But indifference curves can tell us more: they can show why, by splitting the effect of the price change into two parts.

docs.title: 6.7 Income and substitution effects
docs.text:
When the price of X falls from ₹4 to ₹3, Nisha's purchases of X rise from 15 to 20. Two things have happened at once.

  • X has become cheaper relative to Y. Even if she were no better off, she would substitute X for Y. This is the substitution effect.
  • Her income buys more than before: her real income, or purchasing power, has risen. With more real income she changes her purchases, as in Section 6.5. This is the income effect.

To separate them, imagine that at the same time as the price falls, we take away just enough income to leave Nisha on her original indifference curve. The change in her purchases in this imaginary situation is the pure substitution effect; giving the income back produces the income effect. This way of dividing the change is due to John Hicks.

Example 6.2 Measuring the two effects

Nisha has \(U = XY\), \(M = 120\) and \(P_Y = 6\). The price of X falls from ₹4 to ₹3. Find the substitution and income effects on her purchases of X.

Solution.

Original bundle A. From Example 6.1, \(X = 15\), \(Y = 10\), \(U = 150\).

Final bundle C. At \(P_X = 3\): \(X = 120/(2 \times 3) = 20\) and \(Y = 120/(2 \times 6) = 10\), giving \(U = 200\).

Compensated bundle B. Find the cheapest way to reach \(U = 150\) at the new prices. Tangency requires \(Y/X = 3/6\), so \(Y = X/2\). On the original indifference curve, \(XY = 150\), so \(X \cdot X/2 = 150\), \(X^2 = 300\) and \(X = 17.32\), \(Y = 8.66\). This bundle costs \(3(17.32) + 6(8.66) = 103.92\) rupees; taking away \(120 - 103.92 = 16.08\) rupees of income would keep Nisha exactly as well off as before.

Effect Move Change in X Substitution effect A (15) to B (17.32) +2.32 Income effect B (17.32) to C (20) +2.68 Total effect A (15) to C (20) +5.00 Figure 6.2 Substitution and income effects of a fall in price. The fall in the price of X pivots the budget line from intercept 30 to intercept 40. The dashed compensated budget line, parallel to the new one, touches the original indifference curve at B. The move from A to B is the substitution effect; the move from B to C, on the higher curve U = 200, is the income effect.

docs.title: Normal, inferior and Giffen goods
docs.text:
The substitution effect of a price fall is always to buy more of the good that has become cheaper. Along a convex indifference curve, a flatter budget line always touches it further to the right. This is the solid foundation of the law of demand.

The income effect depends on the kind of good.

  • For a normal good, the income effect works in the same direction as the substitution effect: a price fall raises real income, and more income means more of the good. Both effects increase the quantity demanded, so the demand curve certainly slopes down. Nisha's X is normal.
  • For an inferior good, the income effect works against the substitution effect: the rise in real income leads her to buy less. Usually the substitution effect is the larger, so the quantity demanded still rises when the price falls, and the demand curve still slopes down, though less steeply than it otherwise would.
  • In principle, for a strongly inferior good that takes a large part of the budget, the income effect could outweigh the substitution effect. Then a fall in price would reduce the quantity demanded, and the demand curve would slope upwards. Such a good is called a Giffen good. The classic story is of very poor households for whom a cheap staple food takes most of their income: when its price rises, they can no longer afford the small amounts of better food they used to buy, and they buy more of the staple to fill the gap. Giffen goods are a theoretical possibility that is very rare in practice; some careful studies of very poor households have found evidence of it for staple foods.
Type of good Substitution effect of a price fall Income effect of a price fall Demand curve Normal buy more buy more slopes down Inferior (ordinary) buy more buy less, but smaller slopes down Giffen buy more buy less, and larger slopes up

Table 6.5. Income and substitution effects for three types of good.

Common mistake

Every Giffen good is inferior, but very few inferior goods are Giffen goods. Do not call a good "Giffen" just because demand for it falls when income rises; that only makes it inferior.

Key idea

A price change has two effects. The substitution effect always moves the consumer towards the good that has become relatively cheaper. The income effect moves her towards more of normal goods and less of inferior goods as her real income rises. The law of demand holds for all normal goods and almost all inferior goods.

docs.title: 6.8 Summary
docs.text:
• An indifference curve joins bundles that give equal satisfaction. Indifference curves slope down, do not cross, represent more satisfaction further from the origin, and are usually convex.
  • The marginal rate of substitution is the amount of Y the consumer will give up for one more X; it equals \(MU_X/MU_Y\) and usually diminishes along a curve.
  • The budget line \(P_X X + P_Y Y = M\) has intercepts \(M/P_X\) and \(M/P_Y\) and slope \(-P_X/P_Y\). Income changes shift it in parallel; price changes pivot it.
  • The consumer's optimum is the tangency of the budget line and the highest attainable indifference curve, where \(MRS = P_X/P_Y\), equivalent to \(MU_X/P_X = MU_Y/P_Y\).
  • Changing income traces the income-consumption curve and the Engel curve; changing a price traces the price-consumption curve and the demand curve.
  • A price change has a substitution effect (always towards the cheaper good) and an income effect (depending on whether the good is normal or inferior). A Giffen good is an inferior good whose income effect outweighs its substitution effect, so its demand curve slopes upwards.

docs.title: 6.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A consumer has ₹300 to spend on X at ₹10 each and Y at ₹15 each. Write her budget line, find its intercepts and slope, and say whether the bundle (15, 12) is affordable.

Answer

Budget line: \(10X + 15Y = 300\). Intercepts: \(X = 30\), \(Y = 20\). Slope: \(-10/15 = -2/3\). The bundle (15, 12) costs \(150 + 180 = 330\) rupees, more than ₹300, so it is not affordable.

Exercise 2

In Exercise 1, the price of Y falls to ₹10. Describe how the budget line moves.

Answer

It pivots outwards around the X-intercept, which stays at 30. The Y-intercept rises from 20 to 30, and the slope becomes \(-10/10 = -1\).

Exercise 3

A consumer with \(U = XY\) has an income of ₹200, \(P_X = 5\) and \(P_Y = 10\). Find her best bundle and her utility.

Answer

She spends half her income on each good: \(X = 100/5 =\) 20, \(Y = 100/10 =\) 10. Check: \(MRS = Y/X = 0.5 = P_X/P_Y\). Utility \(= 200\).

Exercise 4

Explain why two indifference curves of the same consumer cannot cross.

Answer

If they crossed at bundle A, the consumer would be indifferent between A and every bundle on both curves, and so, by transitivity, between a bundle B on one curve and a bundle C on the other that contains more of both goods than B. But more is better implies she prefers C to B. The contradiction shows the curves cannot cross.

Exercise 5

At a consumer's current bundle, her MRS is 3 and the price ratio \(P_X/P_Y\) is 2. Is she at her optimum? Which way should she move along her budget line?

Answer

No. She values one more X at 3 units of Y, but the market charges only 2. She should buy more X and less Y. As she does, her MRS falls until it equals 2.

Exercise 6

The price of a good falls. The substitution effect raises the quantity demanded by 8 units and the income effect reduces it by 3 units. Is the good normal, inferior or Giffen? What is the total effect?

Answer

The income effect works against the substitution effect, so the good is inferior. The substitution effect is larger, so it is not Giffen. Total effect: \(8 - 3 =\) +5 units.

Exercise 7

Draw the indifference curves of a person who always takes exactly two spoons of sugar with each cup of tea. Where will she choose to be on any budget line?

Answer

Tea and sugar are perfect complements for her: indifference curves are L-shaped, with corners on the ray where sugar = 2 × tea. Extra tea without sugar, or extra sugar without tea, adds nothing. On any budget line she chooses the bundle where the line crosses that ray, so that she buys sugar and tea in the ratio 2 : 1.

Exercise 5

docs.title: Chapter 14: International Trade
docs.text:
Comparative advantage, the gains from trade, and the effects of tariffs

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage and identify each from a table of costs.
  2. Show with numbers that specialisation according to comparative advantage lets both countries consume more.
  3. Find the range of terms of trade at which both countries gain.
  4. Explain the main sources of comparative advantage.
  5. Use demand and supply to show who gains and who loses when a country imports or exports a good.
  6. Analyse the effects of a tariff and of an import quota on prices, quantities and welfare.
  7. Evaluate the common arguments for restricting trade.

docs.title: 14.1 Why trade?
docs.text:
Nobody produces everything they consume. A farmer sells grain and buys cloth, medicine and a phone; a teacher sells teaching and buys food. Each specialises in what she does well and trades for the rest, and both sides of each trade gain, or they would not trade. International trade is the same principle extended across borders. A country that sells software services and buys oil, or sells textiles and buys aircraft, is specialising and trading just as individuals do.

The fact that the trade crosses a border changes some practical details (currencies differ, governments can tax imports, workers and capital move less freely between countries than within them), but not the basic logic. This chapter explains that logic, which was set out by David Ricardo in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) and remains one of the most important and least obvious ideas in economics.

docs.title: 14.2 Absolute and comparative advantage
docs.text:
Imagine two countries, Northland and Southland, each with 120 hours of labour a day, producing two goods, cloth and wheat. The hours needed to produce one unit of each are shown in Table 14.1.

Hours per unit of cloth Hours per unit of wheat Northland 1 2 Southland 6 3

Table 14.1. Labour needed to produce one unit of each good.

A country has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce it with fewer resources than the other country. Northland needs fewer hours for both goods, so it has an absolute advantage in both. It might seem that Northland has nothing to gain from trading with Southland. Ricardo's insight is that this is wrong, because what matters is not absolute but comparative advantage.

A country has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than the other country. Opportunity cost is measured in units of the other good given up.

Opportunity cost of 1 cloth Opportunity cost of 1 wheat Northland \(1/2 = 0.5\) wheat \(2/1 = 2\) cloth Southland \(6/3 = 2\) wheat \(3/6 = 0.5\) cloth

Table 14.2. Opportunity costs in the two countries.

In Northland, an hour spent making one unit of cloth could have made half a unit of wheat, so one cloth costs 0.5 wheat. In Southland, the six hours needed for one cloth could have made two units of wheat, so one cloth costs 2 wheat.

  • Northland has the lower opportunity cost of cloth (0.5 wheat against 2): its comparative advantage is in cloth.
  • Southland has the lower opportunity cost of wheat (0.5 cloth against 2): its comparative advantage is in wheat.

Notice that every country has a comparative advantage in something, even if it has an absolute advantage in nothing. If one country's opportunity cost of cloth is lower, its opportunity cost of wheat (the reciprocal) must be higher. Southland is less productive at everything, but it is relatively less bad at wheat.

Key idea

Comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, determines the pattern of trade. A country gains by specialising in the goods it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and trading for the others, even if another country is more productive at everything.

docs.title: Without trade
docs.text:
Without trade (in autarky), each country must produce everything it consumes. With 120 hours and constant costs, Northland can produce up to 120 cloth or 60 wheat, or any combination on the straight line between; Southland up to 20 cloth or 40 wheat. These are their production possibility frontiers (Chapter 1), straight lines because opportunity costs are constant.

Suppose each country divides its labour equally between the two goods.

Cloth Wheat Northland: 60 hours on each 60 30 Southland: 60 hours on each 10 20 Total 70 50

Table 14.3. Production and consumption without trade.

docs.title: With specialisation
docs.text:
Now let each country specialise according to its comparative advantage. Southland puts all 120 hours into wheat and produces 40. Northland produces mostly cloth but, so that the world still has enough wheat, spends 28 hours on wheat (14 units) and 92 hours on cloth (92 units).

Cloth Wheat Northland: 92 hours cloth, 28 hours wheat 92 14 Southland: 120 hours wheat 0 40 Total 92 54

Table 14.4. Production with specialisation.

With the same labour, world output has risen from 70 to 92 units of cloth and from 50 to 54 units of wheat. More of both goods. The extra output exists because each good is now produced where its opportunity cost is lowest.

docs.title: Trading the gains
docs.text:
To share the gains, the countries trade. Suppose they agree on terms of trade of 1 cloth for 1 wheat, and Southland exports 18 wheat to Northland in return for 18 cloth.

Northland Southland Production 92 cloth, 14 wheat 0 cloth, 40 wheat Trade exports 18 cloth, imports 18 wheat imports 18 cloth, exports 18 wheat Consumption with trade 74 cloth, 32 wheat 18 cloth, 22 wheat Consumption without trade 60 cloth, 30 wheat 10 cloth, 20 wheat Gain +14 cloth, +2 wheat +8 cloth, +2 wheat

Table 14.5. Both countries consume more with trade.

Both countries consume more of both goods than they could without trade. In particular, both end up at points outside their own production possibility frontiers, which no country could reach on its own.

Figure 14.1 Specialisation and trade let both countries consume beyond their frontiers. (a) Northland's production possibility frontier runs from 120 cloth to 60 wheat; without trade it consumes at (60, 30). With trade it produces at (92, 14) and consumes at (74, 32), outside its frontier. (b) Southland's frontier runs from 20 cloth to 40 wheat; without trade it consumes at (10, 20). With trade it produces only wheat (0, 40) and consumes at (18, 22), far outside its frontier.

docs.title: The terms of trade
docs.text:
Would any terms of trade do? No. Northland can make wheat itself at a cost of 2 cloth per wheat, so it will not pay more than 2 cloth for a unit of wheat. Southland can make cloth itself at a cost of 2 wheat per cloth, so it will not pay more than that. Put in terms of cloth:

\[ 0.5 \text{ wheat} < \text{price of 1 cloth} < 2 \text{ wheat}. \]

At any terms of trade in this range, both countries gain. Where the terms of trade settle within the range depends on demand in the two countries, and it decides how the gains are shared: the closer the price of cloth is to 2 wheat, the more Northland gains; the closer to 0.5, the more Southland gains.

Common mistake

"A rich, productive country cannot gain from trading with a poor, less productive one" and "a poor country cannot compete with a rich one" are both wrong. Trade depends on comparative advantage, and every country has one. The poor country's lower productivity shows up in lower wages, not in an inability to trade; and the rich country gains by leaving to others the goods in which its advantage is smallest.

docs.title: 14.4 Where comparative advantage comes from
docs.text:
Ricardo's example traced comparative advantage to differences in labour productivity, that is, in technology. Several sources are recognised today.

  1. Technology and productivity, as in Ricardo's model.
  2. Factor endowments. The theory associated with Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin holds that countries tend to export goods that use intensively the factors they have in abundance. A country with much labour relative to capital tends to export labour-intensive goods (garments, assembly); a country with much capital relative to labour, capital-intensive goods (machinery, chemicals); a country with much fertile land, agricultural goods.
  3. Climate and natural resources. Tea grows well in some climates and not others; oil, coal and minerals are found only in some places.
  4. Economies of scale and specialisation. Much trade, especially between rich countries, is in similar goods: countries both export and import cars, machinery and electronics. Such intra-industry trade arises because economies of scale (Chapter 7) make it efficient for each firm to produce a limited range of varieties for a large world market, while consumers value variety (Chapter 10).
  5. Skills and human capital, built up through education and experience. Comparative advantage can change over time as countries invest in skills, infrastructure and technology.

docs.title: 14.5 Winners and losers within a country
docs.text: Trade raises the total income of each country, but it does not benefit everyone in it. To see who gains and who loses, return to the market of Chapters 2 and 4 and suppose it is the domestic market for a good in a small country, which can trade at the world price without affecting it. Domestic demand is \(Q_d = 100 - 2P\) and domestic supply is \(Q_s = -20 + 4P\). Without trade the price is ₹20, and 60 units are produced and consumed.

docs.title: When the country imports
docs.text:
Suppose the world price is ₹15, below the domestic price. Once trade is allowed, no buyer will pay more than ₹15, so the domestic price falls to the world price.

  • Domestic consumption rises to \(100 - 30 = 70\).
  • Domestic production falls to \(-20 + 60 = 40\).
  • The difference, \(70 - 40 = 30\) units, is imported.
Without trade (₹) With imports at ₹15 (₹) Change (₹) Consumer surplus \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 30 = 900\) \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 70 \times 35 = 1{,}225\) +325 Producer surplus \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 15 = 450\) \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 10 = 200\) −250 Total surplus 1,350 1,425 +75

Table 14.6. Welfare effects of opening to imports.

Domestic consumers gain and domestic producers lose, but the gains of consumers exceed the losses of producers, so the country as a whole gains ₹75. (This gain is the triangle between demand and supply from 40 to 70 units, below the old price: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 5 = 75\).)

docs.title: When the country exports
docs.text:
If instead the world price is ₹25, above the domestic price, domestic producers can sell abroad at ₹25 and the domestic price rises to ₹25. Production rises to 80, consumption falls to 50, and 30 units are exported. Producer surplus rises from ₹450 to \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 20 = 800\) (a gain of ₹350); consumer surplus falls from ₹900 to \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 25 = 625\) (a loss of ₹275). Again the country gains, by ₹75, but now producers gain and consumers lose.

The general lesson: opening to trade raises total surplus in each country, but it creates losers as well as winners. In an importing industry, domestic producers and their workers lose; in an exporting industry, domestic consumers of the good lose. Because the gains exceed the losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and everyone could be better off. Whether such compensation happens (through retraining, support for affected regions, social insurance) is a matter of policy, and when it does not, opposition to trade is understandable.

docs.title: Tariffs
docs.text:
A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Suppose the importing country of Section 14.5 imposes a tariff of ₹3 per unit. Imported goods now cost ₹15 + ₹3 = ₹18, and domestic producers can also charge ₹18.

  • Domestic consumption falls from 70 to \(100 - 36 = 64\).
  • Domestic production rises from 40 to \(-20 + 72 = 52\).
  • Imports fall from 30 to \(64 - 52 = 12\).
  • Tariff revenue is \(3 \times 12 = 36\) rupees.
Figure 14.2 The effects of a tariff. A tariff of ₹3 raises the domestic price from the world price of ₹15 to ₹18. Domestic production rises from 40 to 52 units, consumption falls from 70 to 64, and imports fall from 30 to 12. The green rectangle is the tariff revenue; the two orange triangles are deadweight losses. Effect of the tariff Amount (₹) Working Loss of consumer surplus −201 \(3 \times (70 + 64)/2\) Gain of producer surplus +138 \(3 \times (40 + 52)/2\) Tariff revenue +36 \(3 \times 12\) Net loss to the country −27

Table 14.7. Welfare effects of a tariff of ₹3.

The net loss of ₹27 consists of two deadweight losses, the triangles in Figure 14.2:

  • a production loss of \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (52 - 40) = 18\): the extra 12 units are produced at home at a cost above the world price at which they could have been imported;
  • a consumption loss of \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (70 - 64) = 9\): 6 units that buyers valued above the world price are no longer bought.

So a tariff, like the tax of Chapter 4, transfers surplus (from consumers to producers and the government) and destroys some (the deadweight loss). Domestic producers gain from protection, but consumers lose more.

docs.title: Import quotas
docs.text: An import quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported. A quota of 12 units would have the same effect on the domestic price (₹18), domestic production and consumption as the tariff of ₹3. The difference is who gets the ₹36 that the tariff gave the government. Under a quota, the right to import is valuable: whoever holds an import licence can buy at ₹15 abroad and sell at ₹18 at home. If the government gives licences away, the ₹36 goes to the licence holders, and the country's loss is larger than under the tariff. If it auctions the licences, it can collect the revenue itself. Quotas also have the disadvantage that, when domestic demand rises, the price rises further instead of more being imported.

docs.title: 14.7 Arguments for restricting trade
docs.text:
If free trade raises total surplus, why do countries restrict it? Several arguments are made. Some are stronger than others.

  1. Protecting jobs. Imports reduce employment in competing industries. This is true and the loss can be painful, especially when it is concentrated in particular regions. But trade also creates jobs in export industries and in industries that use cheaper imported inputs, and protecting jobs by tariffs usually costs consumers much more than the wages saved. Support for retraining and moving to new jobs is generally a cheaper way to help.
  2. Infant industries. A new industry may need temporary protection until it grows large enough to benefit from economies of scale and experience. The argument is respectable in principle, but in practice it is hard to pick industries that will eventually succeed, and "temporary" protection often becomes permanent.
  3. National security. A country may not want to depend on imports of goods vital in war, such as weapons or some critical materials. This can justify some protection, though the argument is easily stretched to cover industries with little connection to security.
  4. Unfair competition and dumping. Dumping means selling exports below cost, or below the price in the home market. International rules allow countries to impose anti-dumping duties in such cases. But low prices that reflect a genuine comparative advantage are not unfair, and consumers in the importing country benefit from them.
  5. Retaliation and bargaining. A threat of tariffs may be used to persuade other countries to reduce their own barriers. If the threat fails and tariffs are imposed, both sides lose.
  6. Revenue. Tariffs are easy to collect, which made them an important source of government revenue historically, and they still are in some low-income countries.

Over the decades since the Second World War, many countries have reduced their trade barriers through negotiation, first under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (1947) and, since 1995, through the World Trade Organization, and through regional agreements. India, for example, lowered many tariffs substantially as part of the economic reforms that began in 1991. The question of how open economies should be, and how to share the gains and help those who lose, remains one of the central debates of economic policy.

docs.title: 14.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Countries, like people, gain by specialising and trading.
  • Absolute advantage is producing with fewer resources; comparative advantage is producing at a lower opportunity cost. Every country has a comparative advantage in something, and comparative advantage determines the pattern of trade.
  • Specialisation according to comparative advantage raises world output of all goods, and trade at terms of trade between the two countries' opportunity costs lets both consume beyond their own production possibility frontiers.
  • Comparative advantage comes from differences in technology, factor endowments, climate and resources, economies of scale and skills.
  • Opening to trade raises total surplus. In an importing industry, consumers gain and producers lose; in an exporting industry, producers gain and consumers lose. Gains exceed losses.
  • A tariff raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, reduces consumption and imports, raises revenue, and causes deadweight losses. An import quota has similar effects, but the revenue may go to licence holders.
  • Arguments for protection include jobs, infant industries, national security, dumping, retaliation and revenue; most are weaker than they appear, though some have merit in particular cases.

docs.title: 14.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

In one day, a worker in country A can make 8 shirts or 4 radios; a worker in country B can make 6 shirts or 1 radio. Which country has an absolute advantage in each good? Which has a comparative advantage in each?

Answer

A has an absolute advantage in both (8 > 6 shirts, 4 > 1 radio). Opportunity cost of 1 radio: in A, 2 shirts; in B, 6 shirts. So A has a comparative advantage in radios. Opportunity cost of 1 shirt: in A, 0.5 radio; in B, 1/6 radio. So B has a comparative advantage in shirts.

Exercise 2

In Exercise 1, within what range must the price of a radio, in shirts, lie for both countries to gain from trade?

Answer

A will sell radios only for more than its opportunity cost of 2 shirts; B will buy them only for less than its own cost of 6 shirts. So between 2 and 6 shirts per radio.

Exercise 3

Using Table 14.1, suppose Southland and Northland trade at terms of 1 cloth for 1.5 wheat instead of 1 for 1, with Northland exporting 12 cloth in return for 18 wheat and producing as in Table 14.4. Find each country's consumption and check that both still gain.

Answer

Northland: \(92 - 12 = 80\) cloth and \(14 + 18 = 32\) wheat, against 60 and 30 without trade: gains. Southland: 12 cloth and \(40 - 18 = 22\) wheat, against 10 and 20: gains. The terms are more favourable to Northland than 1 for 1, so it now gets a larger share of the gains.

Exercise 4

A small country's domestic demand for a good is \(Q_d = 200 - 4P\) and its supply is \(Q_s = 6P - 50\). Find the price without trade. If the world price is ₹20, how much does the country import, and what is the gain in total surplus?

Answer

Without trade: \(200 - 4P = 6P - 50\), so \(P = 25\), \(Q = 100\). At ₹20: \(Q_d = 120\), \(Q_s = 70\), so imports = 50. Gain \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times (25 - 20) =\) ₹125.

Exercise 5

In Exercise 4, a tariff of ₹2 per unit is imposed. Find the new imports, the tariff revenue and the deadweight loss.

Answer

Domestic price ₹22: \(Q_d = 112\), \(Q_s = 82\), so imports = 30. Revenue \(= 2 \times 30 =\) ₹60. Deadweight loss \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (82 - 70) + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (120 - 112) = 12 + 8 =\) ₹20.

Exercise 6

Why might a government prefer a tariff to an import quota that restricts imports by the same amount?

Answer

A tariff raises revenue for the government, while a quota gives the equivalent sum to whoever holds import licences (unless they are auctioned). A tariff also lets imports increase if domestic demand rises, whereas a fixed quota causes the domestic price to rise further instead. Quotas may also invite favouritism in the allocation of licences.

docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 14

Exercise 1

  1. with fewer resources than another country
  2. at a lower opportunity cost than another country
  3. at a higher price
  4. only for export
Answer

Exercise 2

Exercise 3

0.025 / 1/40

Exercise 4

  2. consumers gain, producers lose, and total surplus rises
  3. consumers lose, producers gain, and total surplus falls
  4. nothing changes

Exercise 5

  2. raises domestic production and reduces imports

Exercise 7

  2. who receives the difference between the world and domestic prices on imports

  4. the effect on domestic production
