who receives the difference between the world and domestic prices on imports

docs.title: Chapter 12: Market Failure
docs.text:
Externalities, public goods, common resources and asymmetric information

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Explain what market failure is and name its main sources.
  2. Distinguish private and social costs and benefits, and show the deadweight loss of a negative or positive externality.
  3. Compare corrective taxes and subsidies, regulation, tradable permits and private bargaining as remedies for externalities, and state the Coase theorem.
  4. Classify goods by rivalry and excludability, and explain the free-rider problem and the efficient quantity of a public good.
  5. Explain the tragedy of the commons and ways of avoiding it.
  6. Explain adverse selection, moral hazard, signalling and screening.

docs.title: 12.1 When markets fail
docs.text:
Chapter 4 showed that a competitive market, left to itself, produces the quantity at which total surplus is as large as possible. Chapter 8 showed that competition leads firms to produce at the lowest cost and to price at marginal cost. These are powerful results, but they rest on assumptions. When the assumptions fail, the market outcome may be inefficient: too much of some goods, too little of others. Economists call this market failure.

Market power, studied in Chapters 9 and 10, is one source of market failure. This chapter studies four others.

  1. Externalities: costs or benefits that fall on people outside the transaction.
  2. Public goods: goods that cannot easily be sold to individuals, because people cannot be excluded from using them.
  3. Common resources: resources that anyone can use but whose use by one person reduces what is left for others.
  4. Asymmetric information: one side of a transaction knows more than the other.

Market failure is a reason why governments may improve on the market. It is not a guarantee that they will: Section 12.8 discusses government failure.

docs.title: 12.2 Negative externalities
docs.text:
An externality is a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people who are not party to the transaction and is not reflected in the price. A factory that discharges waste into a river imposes costs on fishermen and on villages downstream that use the water. A driver adds to congestion and air pollution in a city. Someone who plays loud music late at night disturbs the neighbours. These are negative externalities (or external costs).

The key distinction is between private and social cost.

  • Marginal private cost (MPC) is the cost borne by the producer of one more unit: labour, materials, energy.
  • Marginal external cost (MEC) is the cost of one more unit imposed on others.
  • Marginal social cost (MSC) is the full cost to society: \(MSC = MPC + MEC\).

Producers base their decisions on private costs, so the market supply curve is the MPC curve. When there is a negative externality, the market ignores part of the cost and produces too much.

Example 12.1 A polluting industry

The demand for a chemical is \(P = 100 - Q\), which also measures its marginal social benefit, since there are no external benefits. The industry's supply (marginal private cost) is \(P = 20 + Q\). Each unit produced causes pollution damage of ₹20 to people living nearby. Find the market outcome, the efficient outcome and the deadweight loss.

Solution. Market. \(100 - Q = 20 + Q\) gives \(Q = 40\) and \(P = 60\).

Efficient. The marginal social cost is \(MSC = 20 + Q + 20 = 40 + Q\). Setting \(MSB = MSC\): \(100 - Q = 40 + Q\) gives \(Q = 30\) and \(P = 70\).

Deadweight loss. For each unit from 30 to 40, the cost to society (MSC) exceeds the benefit (MSB). The loss is the triangle between MSC and demand from 30 to 40: at \(Q = 40\), \(MSC = 80\) and \(MSB = 60\), so

\[ DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (40 - 30) \times (80 - 60) = 100. \] Figure 12.1 A negative externality. A negative externality. The market produces where demand meets marginal private cost (40 units at ₹60). The efficient output, where demand meets marginal social cost, is 30 units at ₹70. The orange triangle is the deadweight loss of ₹100 from overproduction.

docs.title: 12.3 Positive externalities
docs.text:
A positive externality (or external benefit) is a benefit that falls on others. When a person is vaccinated against an infectious disease, she protects not only herself but also those she might otherwise have infected. Education benefits the student, but also the society that gains from an informed citizen and from ideas she may produce. A homeowner who keeps an attractive garden pleases the neighbours. Research by one firm often spreads to others.

  • Marginal private benefit (MPB) is the benefit to the buyer, which is what the demand curve measures.
  • Marginal external benefit (MEB) is the benefit to others.
  • Marginal social benefit (MSB) \(= MPB + MEB\).

Buyers base their decisions on private benefits, so the market produces too little of a good with external benefits.

Example 12.2 Vaccination

The private demand for a vaccine is \(P = 80 - Q\) and its marginal cost of supply is \(P = 20 + Q\) (no external costs). Each vaccination gives others an external benefit of ₹20. Find the market and efficient quantities, the deadweight loss, and a subsidy that would correct the problem.

Solution. Market. \(80 - Q = 20 + Q\) gives \(Q = 30\), \(P = 50\).

Efficient. \(MSB = 100 - Q\). Setting \(MSB = MC\): \(100 - Q = 20 + Q\) gives \(Q = 40\).

Deadweight loss. Units 30 to 40 are worth more to society than they cost but are not produced: \(DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (70 - 50) = 100\), where 70 and 50 are MSB and MC at \(Q = 30\).

Subsidy. A subsidy of ₹20 per vaccination, equal to the external benefit, raises buyers' effective willingness to pay to \(100 - Q\). Output rises to 40; sellers receive ₹60 and buyers pay \(60 - 20 = 40\) rupees.

Figure 12.2 A positive externality. A positive externality. Buyers consider only their private benefit (MPB), so the market produces 30 units. The marginal social benefit (MSB) includes the benefit to others, and the efficient output is 40. The orange triangle is the deadweight loss of ₹100 from underproduction.

This is why governments subsidise or provide vaccinations, primary education and basic research, and why some (such as childhood vaccinations or schooling up to a certain age) are made compulsory or free.

docs.title: 12.4 Remedies for externalities
docs.text: The problem with an externality is that the decision-maker does not bear the full cost or receive the full benefit of her actions. The remedies all aim to make her take the externality into account: to internalise it.

docs.title: Corrective taxes and subsidies
docs.text:
The economist Arthur Pigou proposed in the 1920s that a negative externality be corrected by a tax equal to the marginal external cost, now called a Pigouvian tax. In Example 12.1, a tax of ₹20 per unit shifts the supply curve up to \(P = 40 + Q\), which is the MSC curve, and the market produces the efficient 30 units. Unlike the taxes of Chapter 4, which caused a deadweight loss, a correctly set Pigouvian tax removes a deadweight loss, and raises revenue as well. Taxes on fuel, on tobacco and on carbon emissions are partly justified in this way. Similarly, a Pigouvian subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit corrects a positive externality, as in Example 12.2.

The difficulty is that the government must estimate the external cost or benefit, which is often hard to measure.

docs.title: Regulation
docs.text: The government can instead regulate the activity directly: set limits on emissions, require certain technologies (such as catalytic converters in cars or filters in factory chimneys), ban particular substances, or restrict activities to certain places and times. Regulation is simple to understand and enforce in some cases, and appropriate where the damage is very large or where a substance is so dangerous that it should not be used at all. But a uniform rule that requires every firm to cut pollution by the same amount ignores the fact that some firms can cut pollution much more cheaply than others.

docs.title: Tradable permits
docs.text:
A tradable permit system (also called cap and trade) combines the certainty of regulation with the efficiency of prices. The government sets a total limit (the cap) on emissions, issues permits adding up to that limit, and allows firms to buy and sell them. Firms that can cut pollution cheaply do so and sell their spare permits; firms for which cutting is expensive buy permits instead.

Example 12.3 Permits versus a uniform standard

Two factories each emit 100 tonnes of a pollutant a year. The government wants total emissions cut by 100 tonnes. Factory A can cut emissions at a cost of ₹20 per tonne; factory B at ₹50 per tonne. Compare (a) a rule that each must cut 50 tonnes with (b) giving each permits for 50 tonnes and allowing trade.

Solution. (a) Each cuts 50 tonnes. Cost \(= 50 \times 20 + 50 \times 50 = 1{,}000 + 2{,}500 = 3{,}500\) rupees.

(b) B would rather pay anything less than ₹50 a tonne than cut its own emissions; A would sell a permit for anything more than ₹20, since it can cut a tonne for ₹20. So B buys A's 50 permits at a price between ₹20 and ₹50, and A cuts 100 tonnes while B cuts none. Total cost of cutting \(= 100 \times 20 = 2{,}000\) rupees.

Both systems achieve the same cut of 100 tonnes, but permits do it at ₹1,500 less, because the cutting is done by the firm that can do it most cheaply. The payment for permits is a transfer from B to A; it is not a cost to society.

Systems of this kind have been used, for example, for sulphur dioxide emissions in the United States and for carbon emissions in the European Union.

docs.title: Private bargaining and the Coase theorem
docs.text:
Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that externalities need not always require government action. Suppose a factory's smoke damages a neighbouring laundry by ₹5 lakh a year, and a filter that would stop the smoke costs ₹3 lakh a year.

  • If the laundry has the right to clean air, the factory must either install the filter (cost ₹3 lakh) or compensate the laundry (₹5 lakh). It installs the filter.
  • If the factory has the right to pollute, the laundry can offer to pay the factory to install the filter. It would pay up to ₹5 lakh to avoid ₹5 lakh of damage, and the factory would accept anything over ₹3 lakh. They agree, and the filter is installed.

Either way, the efficient outcome (the filter) is reached; only the distribution of the cost differs. If the filter cost ₹7 lakh instead, it would not be installed under either assignment of rights, which is also efficient, since the filter would cost more than the damage it prevents.

This is the Coase theorem: if property rights are clearly defined and the parties can bargain at low cost, they will reach the efficient outcome, whoever holds the rights. Its practical lesson is that clear property rights and low transaction costs can solve some externality problems privately. Its limitation is equally important: when many people are affected (a whole city breathing polluted air), bargaining is too costly to organise, and government action is needed.

docs.title: 12.5 Public goods
docs.text:
Goods can be classified by two properties.

  • A good is excludable if people who do not pay can be prevented from using it. A shirt is excludable; a fireworks display seen from the street is not.
  • A good is rival in consumption if one person's use reduces the amount available to others. A plate of food is rival; a radio broadcast is not, since one more listener does not reduce what others hear.
Rival Non-rival Excludable Private goods: food, clothes, phones, a ride in a taxi Club goods: cable television, a toll road that is not congested, software Non-excludable Common resources: fish in the sea, groundwater, a crowded free road Public goods: national defence, street lighting, flood control, basic scientific knowledge

Table 12.1. Four types of goods.

A public good is both non-rival and non-excludable. National defence protects everyone in a country; protecting one more person costs nothing extra, and no one can be excluded from protection. A lighthouse guides every ship that passes. Street lighting helps everyone who walks down the street.

docs.title: The free-rider problem
docs.text: Because no one can be excluded from a public good, each person has an incentive to let others pay for it and enjoy it for free. Such a person is a free rider. If everyone reasons this way, a private firm cannot sell the good, since few will pay for something they get anyway. So the market provides too little of a public good, or none at all, even when its benefits to society far exceed its cost. This is why public goods are usually provided by governments and paid for by taxes.

docs.title: How much of a public good?
docs.text:
Since a public good is non-rival, every person consumes the same quantity of it. The marginal social benefit of one more unit is therefore the sum of the marginal benefits to all the people who enjoy it. (For a private good, by contrast, we add quantities at each price, Chapter 2.) The efficient quantity is where this sum equals the marginal cost.

Example 12.4 Street lamps

Three households share a lane. The marginal benefit of the \(n\)-th street lamp is \(50 - 5n\) rupees a month to household A, \(40 - 5n\) to household B and \(30 - 5n\) to household C. Each lamp costs ₹60 a month to run. How many lamps should there be?

Solution. The marginal social benefit of the \(n\)-th lamp is the sum:

\[ MSB = (50 - 5n) + (40 - 5n) + (30 - 5n) = 120 - 15n. \]

Set \(MSB = MC\): \(120 - 15n = 60\), so \(n = 4\). At \(n = 4\), the three households value the fourth lamp at ₹30, ₹20 and ₹10, which together just cover its cost of ₹60.

No household would pay for even one lamp on its own: household A, which values lamps most, values the first at only ₹45, less than its cost. Without some way to share the cost, the lane would stay dark, although four lamps are worth more than they cost.

docs.title: 12.6 Common resources and the tragedy of the commons
docs.text:
Common resources are rival but non-excludable. Anyone can fish in the open sea, pump groundwater from beneath their land, graze animals on a village common or drive on a free public road; but each fish caught, each litre pumped and each car on the road leaves less for everyone else. Each user bears only part of the cost of her use; the rest falls on other users. The result is overuse: fish stocks collapse, water tables fall, pastures are overgrazed and roads become congested. The biologist Garrett Hardin called this the tragedy of the commons in 1968. It is a negative externality, and also a prisoner's dilemma (Chapter 10): each user is better off taking more, whatever the others do, but all are worse off if everyone does.

Remedies include:

  • regulation: fishing seasons and quotas, limits on the number of boats, licences for tube wells;
  • pricing: charges for road use in congested city centres, or for water;
  • property rights: dividing the resource, or giving individuals transferable quotas, so that users bear the cost of overuse themselves;
  • community management: the political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who shared the Nobel prize in economics in 2009, documented many communities around the world (forest users, irrigation groups, fishing villages) that have managed common resources successfully for long periods through rules they made and enforced themselves.

docs.title: 12.7 Asymmetric information
docs.text: Markets work well when buyers and sellers are well informed. Often one side knows more than the other: the seller of a used car knows whether it has hidden faults; a person buying health insurance knows more about her health than the insurer; a worker knows how hard she is working, and her employer may not. This is asymmetric information, and it causes two main problems.

docs.title: Adverse selection
docs.text:
Adverse selection arises when one side cannot observe the quality or type of what is being traded before the transaction. George Akerlof's famous article "The Market for 'Lemons'" (1970) used used cars to explain it.

Example 12.5 The market for lemons

Half the used cars of a certain model are good and half are "lemons" with hidden faults. Owners know which they have; buyers cannot tell. A good car is worth ₹4 lakh to a buyer and ₹3.5 lakh to its owner; a lemon is worth ₹2 lakh to a buyer and ₹1.5 lakh to its owner. What happens?

Solution. With full information, every car would be sold, since each is worth more to a buyer than to its owner: good cars at a price between ₹3.5 and ₹4 lakh, lemons between ₹1.5 and ₹2 lakh.

Without information, a buyer knows only that a car is equally likely to be good or bad, so she will pay at most the average value, \(\tfrac{1}{2}(4) + \tfrac{1}{2}(2) = 3\) lakh rupees. But owners of good cars will not sell for ₹3 lakh, since they value their cars at ₹3.5 lakh. They withdraw. Buyers realise that only lemons are left and offer at most ₹2 lakh. Only lemons are traded.

The good cars, each worth ₹0.5 lakh more to a buyer than to its owner, are never sold. Bad quality drives good quality out of the market.

The same problem affects insurance. If an insurer charges a premium based on the average risk, people with low risk find it too expensive and do not buy, while those with high risk do. The insurer's customers are riskier than average, so it must raise the premium, which drives out more of the low-risk customers. In the extreme the market can disappear. This is one reason why health insurance is often provided through employers (so that the insured are a broad group, not self-selected) or made compulsory.

Markets and institutions have developed ways of reducing adverse selection.

  • Signalling: the informed side takes a costly action that the uninformed side can observe and that only a high-quality type would find worthwhile. A warranty on a used car signals that the seller believes it is good, since offering a warranty on a lemon would be expensive. Michael Spence argued that education can act partly as a signal of ability to employers.
  • Screening: the uninformed side designs choices that make the informed side reveal its type. Insurers offer a choice between a low premium with a large deductible (attractive to low-risk customers) and a high premium with full cover (attractive to high-risk ones).
  • Reputation and certification: brands, seller ratings on online platforms, independent inspections, and licences for doctors and lawyers give buyers information about quality.

docs.title: Moral hazard
docs.text:
Moral hazard arises when one side cannot observe the actions of the other after the transaction, and the other side has less incentive to act carefully because it does not bear the full consequences. A person with full insurance against theft may be less careful about locking the door. A borrower who can walk away from a loan may take bigger risks with the money. A manager paid a fixed salary may work less hard than the owners would like.

The general situation, in which one party (the principal) wants another (the agent) to act in the principal's interest but cannot fully observe the agent's actions, is called the principal-agent problem. Remedies try to align the agent's incentives with the principal's:

  • insurance with deductibles and co-payments, so that the insured bears part of any loss;
  • collateral for loans, so that the borrower has something to lose;
  • pay linked to performance, such as commissions, bonuses or shares in the firm;
  • monitoring, such as inspections and audits.

Common mistake

Keep the two problems apart by asking when the information is missing. Adverse selection is about hidden characteristics before the deal (who chooses to buy insurance). Moral hazard is about hidden actions after the deal (how the insured behave once insured).

docs.title: 12.8 Government failure
docs.text:
Market failure shows that the market outcome may be inefficient. It does not show that government action will make things better. Governments can fail too, for several reasons.

  • Limited information. To set the right Pigouvian tax or provide the right quantity of a public good, the government must know costs and benefits that are hard to measure.
  • Incentives of politicians and officials. Decisions may be shaped by elections, lobbying by organised groups, or the interests of the officials themselves, rather than by efficiency.
  • Unintended consequences. As with price controls (Chapter 4), well-meant policies can change behaviour in ways that were not foreseen.
  • Costs of administration and enforcement, which can exceed the benefits of a small correction.

The practical question is therefore not "market or government?" but which combination of markets, regulation, taxes, property rights and community action gives the best result in each case, given the imperfections of all of them.

docs.title: 12.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Market failure occurs when a market allocates resources inefficiently. Sources include market power, externalities, public goods, common resources and asymmetric information.
  • A negative externality makes marginal social cost exceed marginal private cost; the market overproduces. A positive externality makes marginal social benefit exceed marginal private benefit; the market underproduces. Either causes a deadweight loss.
  • Remedies: Pigouvian taxes and subsidies equal to the external cost or benefit; regulation; tradable permits, which achieve a given cut in pollution at the lowest cost; and private bargaining, which by the Coase theorem reaches efficiency when property rights are clear and transaction costs are low.
  • Public goods are non-rival and non-excludable. The free-rider problem means the market provides too little. The efficient quantity is where the sum of individual marginal benefits equals marginal cost.
  • Common resources are rival but non-excludable and tend to be overused: the tragedy of the commons.
  • Asymmetric information leads to adverse selection (hidden characteristics, as in the market for lemons) and moral hazard (hidden actions). Signalling, screening, reputation, deductibles and incentive pay are responses.
  • Governments can also fail; good policy weighs the imperfections of markets against those of government.

docs.title: 12.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each as a negative or positive externality, and say whether the market produces too much or too little of the activity: (a) a neighbour's dog barking at night; (b) a farmer keeping bees that pollinate nearby orchards; (c) burning crop stubble; (d) a person getting a flu vaccination.

Answer

(a) Negative; too much barking (dog-keeping without control). (b) Positive; too little beekeeping. (c) Negative (smoke harms others' health); too much burning. (d) Positive; too few vaccinations.

Exercise 2

The demand for a good is \(P = 120 - 2Q\) and its marginal private cost is \(P = 30 + Q\). Production causes an external cost of ₹15 per unit. Find the market quantity, the efficient quantity, the deadweight loss and the Pigouvian tax.

Answer

Market: \(120 - 2Q = 30 + Q\) gives \(Q = 30\). Efficient: \(120 - 2Q = 45 + Q\) gives \(Q = 25\). At \(Q = 30\): \(MSC = 75\), \(MSB = 60\). \(DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 15 =\) ₹37.50. Pigouvian tax ₹15 per unit.

Exercise 3

Two firms must together cut emissions by 60 tonnes. Firm X can cut at ₹10 per tonne (up to 60 tonnes) and firm Y at ₹40 per tonne. Find the cost if each must cut 30 tonnes, and the cost under tradable permits.

Answer

Uniform rule: \(30 \times 10 + 30 \times 40 =\) ₹1,500. Permits: X does all the cutting, \(60 \times 10 =\) ₹600, and Y buys permits from X at a price between ₹10 and ₹40. Permits save ₹900.

Exercise 4

Classify each good as private, public, club or common resource: (a) a cup of tea; (b) a public park that is rarely crowded; (c) fish in a river open to all; (d) a subscription video service; (e) a flood embankment protecting a town.

Answer

(a) Private (rival and excludable). (b) Close to a public good (non-rival when uncrowded, and hard to exclude), though it becomes a common resource when crowded. (c) Common resource. (d) Club good (excludable, non-rival). (e) Public good.

Exercise 5

Two residents value a neighbourhood security guard. The marginal benefit of the \(h\)-th hour of patrol per night is \(100 - 10h\) to resident 1 and \(80 - 10h\) to resident 2. An hour of patrol costs ₹60. Find the efficient number of hours. Would either resident hire a guard alone for that many hours?

Answer

\(MSB = 180 - 20h = 60\) gives \(h = 6\) hours. Alone, resident 1 would hire up to where \(100 - 10h = 60\), i.e. 4 hours, and resident 2 up to \(80 - 10h = 60\), i.e. 2 hours. Neither would hire 6 hours alone, and each has an incentive to free ride on the other.

Exercise 6

Is each an example of adverse selection or moral hazard? (a) After buying full car insurance, a driver parks in unsafe places. (b) People who know they are likely to need expensive dental work are the most eager to buy dental insurance. (c) A salesperson on a fixed salary makes few calls when not supervised.

Answer

(a) Moral hazard (hidden action after the deal). (b) Adverse selection (hidden characteristic before the deal). (c) Moral hazard (a principal-agent problem).

docs.title: Chapter 4: Markets, Welfare and Government Intervention
docs.text:
Consumer and producer surplus, and what taxes, subsidies and price controls do

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define willingness to pay and consumer surplus, and measure consumer surplus on a demand curve.
  2. Define producer surplus and measure it on a supply curve.
  3. Explain why a competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus, and state the limits of that result.
  4. Analyse a price ceiling and a price floor: shortages, surpluses and deadweight loss.
  5. Find the effect of a per-unit tax on prices, quantity, tax revenue and welfare, and explain who bears the tax.
  6. Analyse a per-unit subsidy in the same way.
  7. Explain how deadweight loss depends on elasticities and on the size of a tax.

docs.title: 4.1 Willingness to pay and consumer surplus
docs.text:
Chapter 2 explained how a market reaches equilibrium. This chapter asks a different question: how well off are buyers and sellers in that equilibrium, and how does government intervention change their well-being? The branch of economics that studies how the allocation of resources affects well-being is called welfare economics. Its basic tools are consumer and producer surplus.

A buyer's willingness to pay for a good is the most she would pay for it: the price at which she would be just indifferent between buying and not buying. If she pays less than her willingness to pay, she gains. Her consumer surplus is the difference:

\[ \text{consumer surplus} = \text{willingness to pay} - \text{price actually paid}. \]

Example 4.1 Consumer surplus of four buyers

Four students want a second-hand bicycle. Their willingness to pay is: Asha ₹5,000, Bilal ₹4,000, Chitra ₹3,500, Dev ₹2,500. Bicycles of the same kind are on sale at ₹3,000. Who buys, and what is the total consumer surplus?

Solution. Asha, Bilal and Chitra are willing to pay more than ₹3,000, so they buy. Dev is not. Their surpluses are \(5{,}000 - 3{,}000 = 2{,}000\), \(4{,}000 - 3{,}000 = 1{,}000\) and \(3{,}500 - 3{,}000 = 500\) rupees. Total consumer surplus is ₹3,500. If the price fell to ₹2,000, all four would buy and the total would rise to \(3{,}000 + 2{,}000 + 1{,}500 + 500 = 7{,}000\) rupees.

The willingness to pay of the buyers, arranged from highest to lowest, is the demand curve: at any quantity, the height of the demand curve shows the willingness to pay of the marginal buyer, the one who would just stop buying if the price rose a little. So consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity bought.

For the market of Chapters 2 and 3, demand is \(P = 50 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q\) and the equilibrium is \(P^* = 20\), \(Q^* = 60\). The area below demand and above the price is a triangle with base 60 and height \(50 - 20 = 30\):

\[ CS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 30 = 900 \text{ rupees}. \]

docs.title: 4.2 Cost and producer surplus
docs.text:
On the other side of the market, each seller has a cost: the lowest price at which she would be willing to sell, which covers the value of everything she gives up to produce the unit. If she sells for more than this, she gains. Her producer surplus is

\[ \text{producer surplus} = \text{price received} - \text{cost}. \]

The supply curve shows the cost of the marginal seller at each quantity, so producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price. With supply \(P = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\), it is a triangle with base 60 and height \(20 - 5 = 15\):

\[ PS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 15 = 450 \text{ rupees}. \] Figure 4.1 Consumer and producer surplus. Consumer surplus (the blue triangle between the demand curve and the price of ₹20) is ₹900. Producer surplus (the red triangle between the price and the supply curve) is ₹450.

docs.title: 4.3 Market efficiency
docs.text:
Total surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus. It equals the total value that buyers place on the goods minus the total cost of producing them: the net gain to society from the trade. In our market it is \(900 + 450 = 1{,}350\) rupees.

An allocation of resources is efficient if it maximises total surplus. The competitive equilibrium is efficient in this sense, for three reasons.

  1. The goods go to the buyers who value them most. Everyone who buys has a willingness to pay of at least ₹20; everyone who does not, less than ₹20.
  2. The goods are produced by the sellers with the lowest costs. Everyone who sells has a cost of at most ₹20.
  3. The quantity is right. For each unit up to 60, the value to the buyer (the height of the demand curve) exceeds the cost to the seller (the height of the supply curve), so producing it adds to total surplus. For each unit beyond 60, the cost exceeds the value, so producing it would reduce total surplus.

This is the precise meaning of Adam Smith's "invisible hand": buyers and sellers, each pursuing their own interest and guided only by the price, reach the allocation that makes total surplus as large as possible.

The limits of this result

Efficiency is not everything. First, it says nothing about equity: a market can be efficient while some people are very poor, because willingness to pay depends on ability to pay. Second, the result assumes that markets are competitive and that there are no market failures: no pollution or other effects on third parties, no goods that cannot be sold to individuals, and no important differences in information between buyers and sellers. Chapters 9 to 12 study what happens when these assumptions fail. Governments intervene in markets for both reasons, efficiency and equity.

docs.title: Deadweight loss
docs.text: When an intervention moves the quantity away from the efficient level, some total surplus is lost: trades that would have benefited both a buyer and a seller do not happen. The lost surplus, which nobody gains, is called deadweight loss. The rest of this chapter uses it to measure the cost of price controls, taxes and subsidies.

docs.title: 4.4 Price ceilings
docs.text:
A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. Governments impose ceilings to make goods affordable: controls on the rents of flats, on the prices of essential medicines, on the prices of food grains or fuel at times of scarcity. A ceiling set above the equilibrium price has no effect, because the market price is already lower. A ceiling set below the equilibrium price is binding.

Suppose the government fixes a ceiling of ₹15 in our market, where the equilibrium price is ₹20.

  • Quantity demanded at ₹15: \(100 - 2(15) = 70\).
  • Quantity supplied at ₹15: \(-20 + 4(15) = 40\).
  • There is a shortage of \(70 - 40 = 30\) units.

Only 40 units are now produced, and at that quantity buyers would be willing to pay \(50 - \tfrac{1}{2}(40) = 30\) rupees for the last unit.

Figure 4.2 A binding price ceiling. A price ceiling of ₹15 below the equilibrium price of ₹20. Sellers supply only 40 units while buyers want 70, a shortage of 30. The orange triangle is the deadweight loss of ₹150.

docs.title: Who gains and who loses
docs.text:
Assume for the moment that the 40 units go to the buyers who value them most.

  • Consumer surplus becomes the area below demand and above ₹15, up to 40 units: a triangle \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times (50 - 30) = 400\) plus a rectangle \(40 \times (30 - 15) = 600\), a total of ₹1,000. Buyers who still get the good gain from the lower price; buyers who no longer get it lose.
  • Producer surplus becomes the triangle above supply and below ₹15: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times (15 - 5) =\) ₹200, down from ₹450.
  • Total surplus falls from ₹1,350 to ₹1,200. The deadweight loss is ₹150, the triangle between demand and supply from 40 to 60 units: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (30 - 15) = 150\).

So in this example consumers as a group gain ₹100, producers lose ₹250, and ₹150 is lost altogether.

docs.title: The hidden costs of a ceiling
docs.text:
The calculation above is the best case, because it assumes the scarce goods go to those who value them most. In practice, with a shortage, something other than price must decide who gets the good:

  • queues, in which buyers waste time, so that part of the gain from the low price is used up in waiting;
  • rationing by the government, with ration cards or quotas, which may give the good to buyers who value it less than others who go without;
  • favouritism and bribery, as sellers choose their buyers;
  • black markets, in which the good is resold illegally at a higher price;
  • falling quality, as sellers save costs in ways the law does not control. A landlord whose rent is controlled has little reason to repair the building.

In the long run supply is usually more elastic than in the short run (Chapter 3), so the shortage caused by a ceiling grows over time. This is why economists often argue that rent control, while it helps sitting tenants, reduces the quantity and quality of rented housing. A government that wants to help poor buyers can often do so at lower cost through direct transfers of income or vouchers, which do not create shortages.

docs.title: 4.5 Price floors
docs.text:
A price floor is a legal minimum price. It is binding if it is set above the equilibrium price. Examples include minimum wages (Chapter 11) and guaranteed minimum prices for farm products.

Suppose a floor of ₹25 is set in our market.

  • Quantity demanded at ₹25: \(100 - 50 = 50\).
  • Quantity supplied at ₹25: \(-20 + 100 = 80\).
  • There is a surplus of \(80 - 50 = 30\) units.

If nothing else is done, only 50 units are sold (buyers cannot be made to buy more), and sellers are left with unsold goods. If the 50 units are produced by the lowest-cost sellers, total surplus falls by a deadweight loss of \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times (60 - 50) \times (25 - 17.5) = 37.5\) rupees, where ₹17.5 is the supply price of the 50th unit, \(5 + 50/4\). In practice the loss is larger, because sellers produce the extra 30 units in the hope of selling them, and their cost is wasted.

Often the government supports the floor by buying the surplus. At ₹25, buying 30 units costs the government \(30 \times 25 = 750\) rupees. The goods must then be stored, given away, sold abroad or destroyed, each of which has further costs. Schemes that guarantee a minimum price to farmers and procure grain at that price, such as those used in India for some crops, raise farmers' incomes and support food distribution, but they also face these trade-offs: large stocks, storage costs, and an incentive to grow the supported crops rather than others.

Key idea

A binding ceiling (below equilibrium) causes a shortage; a binding floor (above equilibrium) causes a surplus. Both reduce the quantity traded below the efficient level and create a deadweight loss. Both transfer surplus between buyers and sellers, which is usually their purpose.

docs.title: 4.6 Taxes
docs.text: Governments tax goods to raise revenue and sometimes to discourage consumption (of tobacco, for example). Here we study a per-unit tax (also called a specific tax): a fixed number of rupees for each unit sold.

docs.title: A tax on sellers
docs.text:
Suppose the government levies a tax of ₹6 on each unit, collected from sellers. A seller who needed ₹20 to supply a unit before the tax now needs ₹26, because ₹6 goes to the government. So the supply curve, as buyers see it, shifts up by the amount of the tax: from \(P = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\) to \(P = 11 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\). This is exactly the shift we met in Chapter 2.

The new equilibrium is where demand meets the shifted supply:

\[ 50 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q = 11 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 39 = \tfrac{3}{4}Q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = 52. \]
  • Price paid by buyers: \(P_b = 50 - \tfrac{1}{2}(52) = 24\).
  • Price kept by sellers: \(P_s = P_b - 6 = 18\). (Check on the original supply curve: \(5 + 52/4 = 18\).)
  • Quantity falls from 60 to 52.
  • Tax revenue is \(6 \times 52 = 312\) rupees.
Figure 4.3 A per-unit tax. A tax of ₹6 per unit drives a wedge between the price buyers pay (₹24) and the price sellers keep (₹18). The quantity falls from 60 to 52. The green rectangle is the tax revenue of ₹312; the orange triangle is the deadweight loss of ₹24.

docs.title: Welfare effects of the tax
docs.text:
Before the tax (₹) After the tax (₹) Change (₹) Consumer surplus \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 30 = 900\) \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 52 \times 26 = 676\) −224 Producer surplus \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 15 = 450\) \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 52 \times 13 = 338\) −112 Tax revenue 0 312 +312 Total surplus 1,350 1,326 −24

Table 4.1. Who gains and who loses from a tax of ₹6 per unit.

Buyers and sellers together lose \(224 + 112 = 336\) rupees; the government gains ₹312. The difference, ₹24, is the deadweight loss: the triangle between demand and supply from 52 to 60 units, \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (60 - 52) = 24\). It represents the 8 units that would have been traded without the tax, each worth more to a buyer than it cost a seller to produce, which the tax prevents.

docs.title: Who really pays the tax?
docs.text:
The law said the sellers must pay the tax. But the buyers' price rose from ₹20 to ₹24, so buyers bear ₹4 of each ₹6; the sellers' price fell from ₹20 to ₹18, so sellers bear ₹2. The division of a tax burden is called its incidence, and the lesson is that the incidence of a tax does not depend on who is legally required to pay it.

To see this, suppose instead the tax were collected from buyers. Each buyer would now be willing to pay the seller ₹6 less than before, so the demand curve, as sellers see it, shifts down by ₹6, to \(P = 44 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q\). Setting \(44 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\) gives \(Q = 52\) again; sellers receive \(5 + 13 = 18\) and buyers pay \(18 + 6 = 24\). Exactly the same outcome.

What does decide the incidence is the elasticities of demand and supply. The side of the market that is less elastic bears more of the tax, because it is less able to escape it by changing its behaviour. At the original equilibrium the price elasticity of demand is \(-2 \times 20/60 = -0.67\) and the price elasticity of supply is \(4 \times 20/60 = 1.33\). A useful approximation is

\[ \text{share of the tax borne by buyers} = \frac{E_s}{E_s + |E_d|} = \frac{1.33}{1.33 + 0.67} = \frac{2}{3}, \]

which is exactly the ₹4 out of ₹6 we found. (The formula is exact for straight-line curves, as here.)

Example 4.2 A tax on a good with inelastic demand

The demand for cigarettes in a town is \(Q_d = 100 - P\) and the supply is \(Q_s = 4P - 100\), with prices in rupees per packet and quantities in hundreds of packets a week. A tax of ₹10 per packet is imposed on sellers. Find the prices paid and received, the tax revenue and the deadweight loss. Who bears most of the tax?

Solution. Before the tax: \(100 - P = 4P - 100\) gives \(P = 40\), \(Q = 60\).

With the tax, sellers need ₹10 more for each quantity, so supply becomes \(Q_s = 4(P - 10) - 100 = 4P - 140\). Setting \(100 - P = 4P - 140\) gives \(5P = 240\), so buyers pay \(P_b = 48\) and \(Q = 52\). Sellers keep \(48 - 10 = 38\).

Revenue is \(10 \times 52 = 520\) (hundred rupees). Deadweight loss is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (60 - 52) = 40\).

Buyers bear ₹8 of the ₹10 and sellers ₹2. At the old equilibrium \(E_d = -1 \times 40/60 = -0.67\) and \(E_s = 4 \times 40/60 = 2.67\), so buyers bear \(2.67/(2.67 + 0.67) = 0.8\) of the tax. Because demand is the less elastic side, buyers bear most of it.

docs.title: 4.7 Subsidies
docs.text:
A per-unit subsidy is a negative tax: the government pays a fixed sum for each unit sold. Governments subsidise goods such as fertiliser, cooking gas, public transport and renewable energy, to make them cheaper or to encourage their use.

A subsidy of ₹3 per unit paid to sellers shifts the supply curve down by ₹3, from \(P = 5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\) to \(P = 2 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\):

\[ 50 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q = 2 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = 64. \]

Buyers pay \(50 - 32 = 18\) rupees, and sellers receive \(18 + 3 = 21\) rupees (check: \(5 + 64/4 = 21\)). The government pays \(3 \times 64 = 192\) rupees.

  • Consumer surplus rises from ₹900 to \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 64 \times 32 = 1{,}024\), a gain of ₹124.
  • Producer surplus rises from ₹450 to \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 64 \times 16 = 512\), a gain of ₹62.
  • The subsidy costs the government ₹192, more than the combined gain of ₹186.

The difference, ₹6, is the deadweight loss of the subsidy: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (64 - 60) = 6\). It arises because the subsidy encourages 4 units to be produced whose cost to society (the height of the supply curve) is greater than their value to buyers (the height of the demand curve). As with a tax, the benefit of the subsidy is shared between buyers and sellers according to elasticities: here buyers get ₹2 of each ₹3 (their price falls from ₹20 to ₹18) and sellers ₹1.

Note: when subsidies and taxes improve efficiency

The deadweight losses in this chapter arise because the market, left alone, was already efficient. When a market fails, for instance because production causes pollution or because a good such as vaccination benefits people other than the buyer, a well-designed tax or subsidy can increase total surplus. Chapter 12 shows how.

docs.title: 4.8 How big is the deadweight loss?
docs.text:
The deadweight loss of a tax depends on two things.

Elasticities. The deadweight loss arises because the tax changes behaviour: it reduces the quantity traded. If demand or supply is very inelastic, the quantity hardly changes and the deadweight loss is small. If both are elastic, the quantity falls a lot and the loss is large. This is one reason governments tax goods with inelastic demand, such as fuel, tobacco and alcohol: they raise much revenue with little distortion. (Whether such taxes are fair is a separate question, since many of these goods take a larger share of the budgets of poorer households.)

The size of the tax. For straight-line curves, the deadweight loss is a triangle whose base (the fall in quantity) and height (the tax) both grow in proportion to the tax. So doubling a tax roughly quadruples its deadweight loss. In our market, a tax of ₹12 would reduce the quantity to 44 (buyers pay ₹28, sellers keep ₹16), raise revenue of \(12 \times 44 = 528\) rupees, and cause a deadweight loss of \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 16 = 96\) rupees, four times the loss from a tax of ₹6.

Tax per unit (₹) Quantity Revenue (₹) Deadweight loss (₹) 0 60 0 0 6 52 312 24 12 44 528 96 18 36 648 216 24 28 672 384 30 20 600 600

Table 4.2. Revenue and deadweight loss for taxes of different sizes in the market of this chapter.

Table 4.2 also shows that revenue first rises with the tax and then falls: a very high tax shrinks the market so much that it raises less money. Revenue is greatest at a tax of ₹22.50 in this market, where the quantity is 30 and revenue is \(22.5 \times 30 = 675\) rupees. This is why economists generally prefer taxes with a broad base and low rates to taxes with a narrow base and high rates.

docs.title: 4.9 Summary
docs.text:
• Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus price: the area below the demand curve and above the price. Producer surplus is price minus cost: the area above the supply curve and below the price.
  • Total surplus is maximised at the competitive equilibrium, provided markets are competitive and there are no market failures. Efficiency says nothing about equity.
  • Deadweight loss is the fall in total surplus when the quantity traded moves away from the efficient level.
  • A binding price ceiling creates a shortage and a deadweight loss, and leads to queues, rationing, black markets and lower quality. A binding price floor creates a surplus and a deadweight loss, and often requires the government to buy the surplus.
  • A per-unit tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, reduces the quantity, raises revenue, and causes a deadweight loss.
  • The incidence of a tax does not depend on who legally pays it. The less elastic side of the market bears more of it.
  • A per-unit subsidy lowers the price buyers pay and raises the price sellers receive; it costs the government more than the gain to buyers and sellers.
  • Deadweight loss is larger when demand and supply are more elastic, and grows roughly with the square of the tax.

docs.title: 4.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Demand is \(P = 80 - Q\) and supply is \(P = 20 + Q\). Find the equilibrium, the consumer surplus, the producer surplus and the total surplus.

Answer

\(80 - Q = 20 + Q\) gives \(Q^* = 30\) and \(P^* = 50\). \(CS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times (80 - 50) =\) 450. \(PS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times (50 - 20) =\) 450. Total surplus = 900.

Exercise 2

In the market of Exercise 1, a price ceiling of ₹40 is imposed. Find the shortage and the deadweight loss.

Answer

At ₹40: \(Q_d = 80 - 40 = 40\), \(Q_s = 40 - 20 = 20\). Shortage = 20 units. Only 20 are traded; the demand price at \(Q = 20\) is \(80 - 20 = 60\). Deadweight loss \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times (30 - 20) \times (60 - 40) =\) 100.

Exercise 3

In the market of Exercise 1, a tax of ₹10 per unit is imposed on sellers. Find the price buyers pay, the price sellers keep, the tax revenue and the deadweight loss. How is the tax shared?

Answer

Supply becomes \(P = 30 + Q\). \(80 - Q = 30 + Q\) gives \(Q = 25\), \(P_b = 55\), \(P_s = 45\). Revenue \(= 10 \times 25 =\) 250. Deadweight loss \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 5 =\) 25. Buyers bear ₹5 and sellers ₹5: the curves have slopes of equal size, so the burden is shared equally.

Exercise 4

Explain why the incidence of a tax on a life-saving medicine with very inelastic demand falls mainly on patients, whatever the law says about who pays it.

Answer

Patients cannot easily reduce the quantity they buy when the price rises, so sellers can pass the tax on in a higher price without losing many sales. The less elastic side of a market bears more of a tax, and here that is the buyers. Writing the law so that sellers pay it does not change this, because the price adjusts.

Exercise 5

A government sets a minimum price of ₹30 for a crop whose market has demand \(Q_d = 120 - 2P\) and supply \(Q_s = 3P - 30\). Find the equilibrium without the floor, the surplus at the floor, and the cost to the government of buying the surplus.

Answer

Without the floor: \(120 - 2P = 3P - 30\), so \(P = 30\) and \(Q = 60\). The floor of ₹30 equals the equilibrium price, so it is not binding: there is no surplus and no cost. (A floor of, say, ₹35 would give \(Q_d = 50\), \(Q_s = 75\), a surplus of 25 costing \(25 \times 35 = 875\) rupees.)

Exercise 6

Using the market of this chapter, show that a subsidy of ₹6 per unit causes a deadweight loss four times as large as a subsidy of ₹3.

Answer

With a ₹6 subsidy, supply becomes \(P = -1 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\). \(50 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q = -1 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q\) gives \(Q = 68\). The deadweight loss is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (68 - 60) =\) 24, which is four times the ₹6 loss from the ₹3 subsidy.

Exercise 7

Why might rent control cause a larger shortage after ten years than after one year?

Answer

Both demand and supply become more elastic over time. In one year the stock of flats is nearly fixed, so the quantity supplied falls little. Over ten years, landlords convert flats to other uses, fail to maintain them, and build fewer new ones, while more people seek flats at the low controlled rent. The gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the ceiling therefore widens.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Monopolistic Competition and Oligopoly
docs.text:
Markets between the extremes, and the game theory that explains rivalry

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Place a market on the spectrum from perfect competition to monopoly, using the number of firms, product differentiation and barriers to entry.
  2. Explain the short-run and long-run equilibrium of a monopolistically competitive firm, and the idea of excess capacity.
  3. Describe oligopoly and explain why the decisions of oligopolists are interdependent.
  4. Represent a game in a payoff matrix and find dominant strategies and Nash equilibria.
  5. Explain the prisoner's dilemma and use it to show why cartels are unstable.
  6. Find the Cournot equilibrium of a simple duopoly and compare it with monopoly and competition.

docs.title: 10.1 Between competition and monopoly
docs.text:
Perfect competition and monopoly are the two ends of a spectrum. Most real markets lie in between: there are several or many sellers, but each has some power over its price, because its product differs from its rivals' or because there are few rivals. Economists distinguish two intermediate structures.

Perfect competition Monopolistic competition Oligopoly Monopoly Number of sellers very many many a few one Product identical differentiated identical or differentiated unique Entry and exit free free difficult blocked Control over price none some considerable, but depends on rivals considerable Examples many farm products restaurants, salons, clothing brands telecom services, cement, aircraft a local water supplier

Table 10.1. Four market structures.

One simple measure of how many firms really compete is the concentration ratio: the share of industry sales of the largest few firms (often four). A four-firm concentration ratio close to 100 per cent indicates oligopoly; a low ratio indicates a competitive or monopolistically competitive industry.

docs.title: 10.2 Monopolistic competition
docs.text:
The term was introduced in the 1930s by Edward Chamberlin; Joan Robinson developed a similar theory of "imperfect competition" at the same time. A market is monopolistically competitive when:

  1. there are many sellers;
  2. each sells a differentiated product: similar to its rivals' but not identical, so that some buyers prefer it;
  3. there is free entry and exit in the long run.

Restaurants in a city are a good example. Each offers a somewhat different menu, location, atmosphere and service, so each has some loyal customers and can raise its price a little without losing them all. But there are many close substitutes, and anyone can open a new restaurant. The same is true of hair salons, clothing brands, bakeries, coaching classes and many small retail shops.

Products can be differentiated by physical features (taste, design, quality), location (the nearest shop is more convenient), service (speed, friendliness, after-sales support) and image, which advertising and branding help to create.

docs.title: The short run
docs.text: Because its product is differentiated, a monopolistically competitive firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, though a fairly elastic one, since close substitutes exist. In the short run it behaves exactly like a monopolist: it produces where \(MR = MC\) and charges the price on its demand curve. If demand is strong it earns an economic profit; if weak, a loss.

docs.title: The long run
docs.text:
The difference from monopoly appears in the long run. If firms earn profits, new firms enter with their own varieties. Each existing firm loses some customers to the newcomers, so its demand curve shifts left (and becomes more elastic). Entry continues until economic profit is zero. If firms make losses, some exit, and the demand curves of those remaining shift right. In long-run equilibrium:

  • each firm produces where \(MR = MC\) (it maximises profit), and
  • price equals average total cost (profit is zero), so the demand curve is tangent to the ATC curve.

Example 10.1 Long-run equilibrium

A restaurant's average total cost is \(ATC = 64/Q + 4 + Q/4\) (in hundreds of rupees per meal, with \(Q\) in meals per hour), so its marginal cost is \(MC = 4 + Q/2\). After entry has run its course, its demand is \(P = 20 - 0.75Q\). Show that it is in long-run equilibrium at \(Q = 8\).

Solution. Marginal revenue is \(MR = 20 - 1.5Q\). At \(Q = 8\): \(MR = 20 - 12 = 8\) and \(MC = 4 + 4 = 8\), so \(MR = MC\): the restaurant maximises profit. The price is \(P = 20 - 6 = 14\), and \(ATC = 64/8 + 4 + 8/4 = 8 + 4 + 2 = 14\). Price equals average cost, so economic profit is zero. Both conditions hold.

The lowest point of ATC is at \(Q = 16\), where \(ATC = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12\). The restaurant produces only 8 meals an hour, half its efficient scale, at a cost of 14 instead of 12.

Figure 10.1 Long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition. Long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition. The demand curve D is tangent to ATC at 8 units, where MR = MC. Price equals ATC (14), so profit is zero, but the firm produces less than the output (16) at which ATC is lowest: it has excess capacity.

docs.title: Is monopolistic competition efficient?
docs.text:
Compared with perfect competition, two differences stand out.

  • Excess capacity. Because the demand curve slopes down, it can touch the U-shaped ATC curve only on its falling part, to the left of the minimum. Each firm produces less than the output that minimises average cost; productive efficiency fails. This is why many restaurants are half-empty at most hours and many petrol pumps or shops could serve more customers at little extra cost.
  • Markup over marginal cost. Price is above marginal cost (14 against 8 in the example), so allocative efficiency fails too, and there is a deadweight loss.

But there is a benefit that the model of perfect competition leaves out: variety. Consumers value having many kinds of restaurants, clothes and books to choose from, and excess capacity is in part the cost of that variety. Economists do not agree on whether monopolistically competitive markets provide too much variety or too little, and in practice governments rarely regulate them.

docs.title: Advertising
docs.text: Firms in monopolistic competition (and in oligopoly) spend heavily on advertising and branding. Critics argue that much advertising tries to create differences in buyers' minds between essentially similar products, raising prices and costs. Defenders argue that advertising informs buyers about prices, new products and the location of shops, which makes markets more competitive, and that a costly advertising campaign is a signal of quality: a firm would not spend heavily to attract buyers to a product they would not buy again. Both effects are found in practice.

docs.title: 10.3 Oligopoly
docs.text:
An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms. Entry is difficult, usually because of economies of scale, high fixed costs, control of key inputs, patents or licences. The product may be identical (cement, steel) or differentiated (cars, smartphones, airline services). A market with exactly two firms is a duopoly.

The defining feature of oligopoly is interdependence. Because there are few firms, each one's decisions noticeably affect the others. When one airline cuts fares on a route, its rivals lose passengers and must decide whether to respond. So each firm, in choosing its price, output or advertising, must think about how its rivals will react. A competitive firm or a monopolist need not do this; an oligopolist must.

This makes oligopoly harder to analyse than the other structures. There is no single model of oligopoly; the outcome depends on whether firms compete on price or quantity, whether they choose at the same time or in turn, and whether they can cooperate. The tool for thinking about all of these is game theory.

docs.title: 10.4 Game theory
docs.text:
Game theory studies strategic situations: situations in which the outcome for each participant depends on the choices of others. It was developed by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in the 1940s; John Nash, in the early 1950s, introduced the idea of equilibrium that bears his name. A game has three elements:

  • players: the decision-makers (here, firms);
  • strategies: the options open to each player;
  • payoffs: what each player gets for each combination of strategies (here, profits).

A game in which the players choose at the same time can be written as a payoff matrix.

docs.title: A pricing game
docs.text:
Two firms, Alpha and Beta, are the only sellers of a product. Each can set a high price or a low price. Their monthly profits, in lakh rupees, are shown below; the first number in each cell is Alpha's profit, the second Beta's.

Beta: high price Beta: low price Alpha: high price 10, 10 4, 14 Alpha: low price 14, 4 6, 6

Table 10.2. A pricing game (profits in lakh rupees: Alpha, Beta).

If both charge high prices, they share the market at a good margin and earn 10 each. If one charges low while the other charges high, the low-price firm wins most customers and earns 14, while the high-price firm earns only 4. If both charge low prices, they share the market at a thin margin and earn 6 each.

docs.title: Dominant strategies
docs.text:
A dominant strategy is a strategy that gives a player a higher payoff whatever the other player does. Consider Alpha's reasoning.

  • If Beta charges high, Alpha earns 10 with high and 14 with low: low is better.
  • If Beta charges low, Alpha earns 4 with high and 6 with low: low is better.

So charging a low price is Alpha's dominant strategy. The game is symmetric, so low is Beta's dominant strategy too. Both charge low prices and each earns 6.

docs.title: Nash equilibrium
docs.text:
A Nash equilibrium is a combination of strategies in which each player's strategy is the best response to the strategies of the others, so that no player can gain by changing its own strategy alone. In the pricing game, (low, low) is a Nash equilibrium: if Beta charges low, Alpha's best response is low, and vice versa. (High, high) is not: if Beta charges high, Alpha would gain by switching to low.

Not every game has dominant strategies, but many games without them still have Nash equilibria, sometimes more than one. Consider two firms choosing a technical standard for a new device, where each gains only if they choose the same standard:

Firm 2: standard A Firm 2: standard B Firm 1: standard A 5, 5 0, 0 Firm 1: standard B 0, 0 3, 3

Table 10.3. A coordination game.

Neither firm has a dominant strategy: the best choice depends on what the other does. Both (A, A) and (B, B) are Nash equilibria. Which one occurs depends on history, expectations or communication; the firms might even get stuck on the worse standard B if each expects the other to choose it.

Key idea

A dominant strategy is best whatever others do. A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies in which each is the best response to the others. If every player has a dominant strategy, playing them is a Nash equilibrium; but a Nash equilibrium does not require dominant strategies.

docs.title: 10.5 The prisoner's dilemma and cartels
docs.text:
The pricing game has a striking feature. Each firm, acting in its own interest, charges a low price, and each ends up with 6. If both had charged high prices, each would have had 10. Individually rational choices lead to an outcome that is worse for both. A game with this structure is called a prisoner's dilemma, after the story usually told to illustrate it.

Two suspects are arrested and questioned separately. If both stay silent, the police can convict each only of a minor offence: 1 year in prison each. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the one who confesses goes free and the silent one gets 10 years. If both confess, each gets 5 years. Whatever the other does, confessing reduces one's own sentence (0 instead of 1, or 5 instead of 10), so both confess and each serves 5 years, although both staying silent would have given each only 1.

The prisoner's dilemma appears wherever individual incentives work against a shared interest: firms competing in advertising, countries in arms races, fishing fleets over-fishing a common sea (Chapter 12), and nations deciding whether to cut pollution.

docs.title: Collusion and cartels
docs.text:
The firms in the pricing game would like to escape the dilemma by agreeing to charge high prices. An agreement among firms to restrict output or fix prices is called collusion, and a formal group of colluding firms is a cartel. A successful cartel acts like a single monopolist and shares the monopoly profit among its members. The best-known international example is the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), whose members have at times agreed on limits to their oil output.

But the prisoner's dilemma shows why cartels are unstable. Once the others are charging a high price, each member gains by secretly undercutting it or producing more than its quota. If all members reason this way, the cartel collapses. Cartels have historically found it hard to hold together, especially when they have many members, when cheating is hard to detect, and when demand is falling.

Collusion is also, in most countries, illegal. Competition laws (Chapter 9) prohibit agreements to fix prices, limit output or divide markets, and competition authorities impose heavy penalties on firms caught in such agreements.

docs.title: Repeated games
docs.text: The pricing game above is played once. Real firms meet again and again, month after month. In a repeated game, cooperation can be sustained more easily, because a firm that cheats today can be punished tomorrow. A simple strategy called tit-for-tat (cooperate in the first round, then do whatever the rival did in the previous round) rewards cooperation and punishes cheating. When firms expect to interact for a long time and can observe each other's prices, high prices may persist without any explicit agreement. This is called tacit collusion, and it is one reason oligopoly prices are often stable.

docs.title: 10.6 The Cournot model of duopoly
docs.text:
Game theory can also be applied when firms choose quantities from a continuous range. The oldest model of this kind is due to Augustin Cournot (1838). Two firms produce an identical good. Each chooses its output, taking the rival's output as given, and the market price is set by total output.

Let market demand be \(P = 120 - Q\), where \(Q = q_1 + q_2\), and let each firm have a constant marginal cost of ₹30 and no fixed cost.

Firm 1's best response. Given \(q_2\), firm 1 faces the "residual" demand \(P = (120 - q_2) - q_1\). Its marginal revenue is \(MR_1 = 120 - q_2 - 2q_1\). Setting \(MR_1 = MC\):

\[ 120 - q_2 - 2q_1 = 30 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_1 = \frac{90 - q_2}{2}. \]

This is firm 1's best-response function (or reaction function): the more firm 2 produces, the less firm 1 wants to produce. By symmetry, \(q_2 = (90 - q_1)/2\).

The Nash equilibrium is where each firm is on its best-response function, so that neither wants to change. With symmetry, \(q_1 = q_2 = q\) and \(q = (90 - q)/2\), which gives \(q = 30\). Total output is 60, the price is \(120 - 60 = 60\), and each firm's profit is \((60 - 30) \times 30 = 900\) rupees.

Figure 10.2 Cournot equilibrium. Best-response functions of the two firms in the Cournot duopoly. Each firm's best output falls as its rival produces more. They cross at the Nash equilibrium, where each firm produces 30 units. Total output Price (₹) Total profit (₹) Perfect competition (\(P = MC\)) 90 30 0 Cournot duopoly 60 60 1,800 Monopoly or perfect cartel (\(MR = MC\)) 45 75 2,025

Table 10.4. Duopoly lies between competition and monopoly.

The duopoly outcome lies between competition and monopoly. Economists have shown that as the number of Cournot firms grows, the outcome moves closer to the competitive one.

Example 10.2 The temptation to cheat

In the duopoly above, the two firms form a cartel and agree to produce the monopoly output, 45, splitting it equally: 22.5 each. Show that each firm has an incentive to cheat.

Solution. Under the agreement, the price is \(120 - 45 = 75\) and each firm earns \((75 - 30) \times 22.5 = 1{,}012.50\) rupees.

Suppose firm 2 keeps to its quota of 22.5. Firm 1's best response is \(q_1 = (90 - 22.5)/2 = 33.75\). Total output is \(56.25\) and the price falls to \(120 - 56.25 = 63.75\). Firm 1 earns \((63.75 - 30) \times 33.75 = 1{,}139.06\) rupees, more than its ₹1,012.50 under the agreement, while firm 2's profit falls to \((63.75 - 30) \times 22.5 = 759.38\) rupees. Cheating pays, which is the prisoner's dilemma again.

docs.title: Other models of oligopoly
docs.text:
• Price competition with identical products (Bertrand). If two firms sell an identical product and compete by setting prices, each can take the whole market by undercutting the other slightly. Undercutting continues until the price equals marginal cost: just two firms can produce the competitive outcome. In practice firms avoid this by differentiating their products or building up capacity limits.
  • Leaders and followers. If one firm chooses its output first and the other responds, the leader can gain by committing to a large output (a model due to Heinrich von Stackelberg).
  • The kinked demand curve. One explanation of why oligopoly prices are stable assumes that rivals will match a price cut (so a cut gains few customers) but will not match a price rise (so a rise loses many). The firm's demand curve then has a kink at the current price, and the firm has little reason to change the price even when its costs change somewhat.

docs.title: 10.7 Game theory in a program
docs.text:
The search for pure-strategy Nash equilibria in a small game, and the Cournot best responses, are easy to program.

def pure_nash(payoffs, rows, cols):
    """payoffs[(r, c)] = (payoff to the row player, payoff to the column player)."""
    found = []
    for r in rows:
        for c in cols:
            a, b = payoffs[(r, c)]
            best_for_row = all(a >= payoffs[(r2, c)][0] for r2 in rows)
            best_for_col = all(b >= payoffs[(r, c2)][1] for c2 in cols)
            if best_for_row and best_for_col:
                found.append((r, c))
    return found

pricing = {("High", "High"): (10, 10), ("High", "Low"): (4, 14),
           ("Low", "High"): (14, 4), ("Low", "Low"): (6, 6)}
print(pure_nash(pricing, ["High", "Low"], ["High", "Low"]))

standards = {("A", "A"): (5, 5), ("A", "B"): (0, 0),
             ("B", "A"): (0, 0), ("B", "B"): (3, 3)}
print(pure_nash(standards, ["A", "B"], ["A", "B"]))

# Cournot: P = 120 - Q, MC = 30.  Each firm in turn plays its best response.
q1 = q2 = 0.0
for _ in range(40):
    q1 = (90 - q2) / 2
    q2 = (90 - q1) / 2
print(round(q1, 2), round(q2, 2), round(120 - q1 - q2, 2))

[('Low', 'Low')]
[('A', 'A'), ('B', 'B')]
30.0 30.0 60.0

The last part shows that if each firm repeatedly adjusts its output to the rival's last output, the two outputs converge to the Nash equilibrium of 30 each.

docs.title: 10.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, free entry. In the short run a firm behaves like a monopolist; in the long run entry drives profit to zero and the demand curve is tangent to ATC. Firms have excess capacity and price above marginal cost, but consumers gain variety.
  • Oligopoly: a few firms, barriers to entry, and interdependence: each firm must consider its rivals' reactions.
  • Game theory describes strategic situations by players, strategies and payoffs. A dominant strategy is best whatever others do; a Nash equilibrium is a set of mutual best responses.
  • In a prisoner's dilemma, each player's dominant strategy leads to an outcome worse for all than cooperation. It explains why cartels are unstable, although repeated interaction can support cooperation.
  • In the Cournot duopoly each firm chooses output as a best response to the other's; the equilibrium output and price lie between competition and monopoly.
  • Collusion to fix prices or restrict output is generally prohibited by competition law.

docs.title: 10.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each market as perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly or monopoly, and give a reason: (a) beauty parlours in a large town; (b) the manufacture of large passenger aircraft; (c) a crop sold by thousands of farmers at a regulated market; (d) the only electricity distributor in a city.

Answer

(a) Monopolistic competition: many sellers, differentiated services, easy entry. (b) Oligopoly: very few firms, huge economies of scale and high barriers. (c) Close to perfect competition: many sellers of a standard product, each a price taker. (d) Monopoly, probably a natural monopoly regulated by the government.

Exercise 2

Why does a monopolistically competitive firm earn zero economic profit in the long run, even though it faces a downward-sloping demand curve?

Answer

Because entry is free. Profits attract new firms with similar products, which take customers away and shift each existing firm's demand curve to the left until it is just tangent to ATC. At that point price equals average cost and economic profit is zero, although the firm still has some control over its price.

Exercise 3

Find any dominant strategies and all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of this advertising game (profits in lakh rupees: Firm A, Firm B).

B advertises B does not advertise A advertises 3, 3 8, 1 A does not advertise 1, 8 6, 6 Answer

For A: if B advertises, 3 > 1; if B does not, 8 > 6. Advertising is A's dominant strategy, and by symmetry B's. The only Nash equilibrium is (advertise, advertise), with 3 each, although both would earn 6 if neither advertised. It is a prisoner's dilemma.

Exercise 4

In this game, find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria (payoffs: Row, Column).

Left Right Up 4, 2 1, 3 Down 2, 1 3, 4 Answer

Check each cell. (Up, Left): Column would switch to Right (3 > 2), so no. (Up, Right): Row would switch to Down (3 > 1), so no. (Down, Left): Row would switch to Up (4 > 2), so no. (Down, Right): Row gets 3 versus 1 from Up; Column gets 4 versus 1 from Left; neither wants to switch. The only Nash equilibrium is (Down, Right). Note that Row has no dominant strategy; Column's dominant strategy is Right (3 > 2 and 4 > 1).

Exercise 5

Two Cournot duopolists face demand \(P = 100 - Q\) and each has a marginal cost of ₹10. Find each firm's best-response function, the equilibrium outputs, the price and each firm's profit.

Answer

\(MR_1 = 100 - q_2 - 2q_1 = 10\) gives \(q_1 = (90 - q_2)/2\), and symmetrically for firm 2. In equilibrium \(q = (90 - q)/2\), so \(q_1 = q_2 = 30\). Total output 60, price ₹40. Profit of each \(= (40 - 10) \times 30 =\) ₹900.

Exercise 6

Give two reasons why cartels tend to break down.

Answer

(1) Each member has an incentive to cheat: with the others restricting output, it can raise its own profit by selling more or undercutting the agreed price (the prisoner's dilemma). (2) Cartels are illegal in most countries, so agreements cannot be enforced in court and members risk penalties. Other reasons: cheating is hard to detect when there are many members; falling demand increases the temptation to cut prices; and high prices attract new entrants.
