docs.title: Chapter 9: Monopoly
docs.text:
A single seller, its pricing, its costs to society, and how governments respond

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Define monopoly and explain the barriers to entry that create and protect it.
  2. Explain why a monopolist's marginal revenue is below its price, and relate marginal revenue to elasticity.
  3. Find a monopolist's profit-maximising output, price and profit.
  4. Measure the deadweight loss of monopoly and compare monopoly with perfect competition.
  5. Explain price discrimination, its conditions and its effects, and calculate prices in two separate markets.
  6. Explain natural monopoly and compare the main ways of regulating it.

docs.title: 9.1 What is a monopoly?
docs.text:
A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a good that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers that prevent other firms from entering. Where a competitive firm is a price taker, a monopolist is a price maker: since it is the only seller, the market demand curve is its own demand curve, and it can choose the price (or the quantity) along it.

Pure monopoly, like perfect competition, is a limiting case. A local water supplier, the only railway in a region, or the holder of a patent on a new medicine comes close. Many firms have some degree of market power, the ability to raise the price above marginal cost without losing all their customers; the analysis of this chapter applies to them too, in diluted form.

docs.title: Barriers to entry
docs.text:
A monopoly lasts only if other firms cannot enter and compete away its profit. The main barriers are these.

  1. Control of a key resource. A firm that owns the only source of a raw material, or the only suitable site, can keep others out.
  2. Legal barriers. Governments create monopolies deliberately. A patent gives an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention for a limited period, commonly twenty years; a copyright does the same for books, music and software. Governments also grant exclusive licences, for example to run a public service.
  3. Economies of scale. If average cost falls over the whole range of output the market demands, one firm can supply the market more cheaply than two or more. This is natural monopoly, discussed in Section 9.6.
  4. Network effects. For some goods, each user gains when others use the same product: a telephone network, a social media platform, a payment system. A firm that gets ahead may become dominant because new users join the network that already has the most users.
  5. Strategic behaviour. An existing firm may deter entry by threatening price wars, tying up distributors, or building more capacity than it needs. Competition law tries to prevent the abusive forms of such behaviour.

docs.title: 9.2 Demand and marginal revenue
docs.text:
Because the monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, it can sell more only by lowering its price, and (unless it can charge different prices to different buyers) the lower price applies to all units, not just the extra one. So the extra revenue from one more unit is less than its price.

Consider a monopolist facing the demand curve \(P = 100 - 2Q\).

Quantity (Q) Price (P = AR, ₹) Total revenue (₹) Marginal revenue per unit over the step (₹) 0 100 0 5 90 450 90 10 80 800 70 15 70 1,050 50 20 60 1,200 30 25 50 1,250 10 30 40 1,200 −10

Table 9.1. Revenue of a monopolist facing \(P = 100 - 2Q\).

Moving from 15 to 20 units, the monopolist gains revenue from the 5 extra units sold at ₹60 (₹300) but loses ₹10 on each of the 15 units it was already selling at ₹70 (₹150). Net extra revenue is ₹150, or ₹30 per unit, well below the price of ₹60.

For a straight-line demand curve \(P = a - bQ\), total revenue is \(aQ - bQ^2\) and marginal revenue is

\[ MR = a - 2bQ. \]

The marginal revenue curve starts at the same point as the demand curve but falls twice as steeply. Here \(MR = 100 - 4Q\): it is zero at \(Q = 25\), where total revenue is greatest, and negative beyond.

docs.title: Marginal revenue and elasticity
docs.text:
Chapter 3 showed that total revenue rises with output where demand is elastic and falls where it is inelastic. So marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic and negative where demand is inelastic. The exact relationship is

\[ MR = P\left(1 - \frac{1}{\lvert E_d \rvert}\right). \]

A profit-maximising monopolist never produces where marginal revenue is negative, since cutting output would then raise revenue and lower cost. A monopolist always operates on the elastic part of its demand curve.

docs.title: 9.3 Choosing output and price
docs.text:
The monopolist maximises profit by the same rule as every firm: produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Then it charges the highest price buyers will pay for that quantity, read from the demand curve.

Suppose the monopolist has a constant marginal cost of ₹20 per unit and no fixed cost, so that its average cost is also ₹20.

  1. Quantity. Set \(MR = MC\): \(100 - 4Q = 20\), so \(Q = 20\).
  2. Price. From the demand curve, \(P = 100 - 2(20) = 60\).
  3. Profit. \((P - AC) \times Q = (60 - 20) \times 20 = 800\) rupees.
Figure 9.1 Monopoly output, price and deadweight loss. A monopolist with demand D, marginal revenue MR and constant marginal and average cost of ₹20. It produces 20 units, where MR = MC, and charges ₹60 (point M). Its profit is the green rectangle (₹800). A competitive industry with the same costs would produce 40 units at ₹20; the orange triangle is the deadweight loss of monopoly (₹400).

At this price, the elasticity of demand is \((\Delta Q/\Delta P)(P/Q) = (-\tfrac{1}{2})(60/20) = -1.5\), and the formula above gives \(MR = 60(1 - 1/1.5) = 20\), equal to marginal cost, as it should be.

docs.title: The monopolist's markup
docs.text:
Rearranging \(MR = MC\) with the elasticity formula gives a useful rule for the monopolist's price:

\[ \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{1}{\lvert E_d \rvert}. \]

The left side, the markup as a share of the price, is called the Lerner index of market power. Here it is \((60 - 20)/60 = 2/3 = 1/1.5\). The less elastic the demand, the higher the markup a monopolist can charge. A monopolist whose product has close substitutes faces elastic demand and has little power to raise prices.

Common mistakes

  1. A monopolist does not charge "the highest possible price". At a very high price it would sell almost nothing. It chooses the price that maximises profit, given the demand curve.
  2. A monopolist is not guaranteed a profit. If demand is weak relative to costs, the best it can do may still be a loss, and in the long run it will leave the market.
  3. A monopolist has no supply curve. A supply curve shows how much a price taker supplies at each given price, but the monopolist sets the price itself. Its output depends on the whole shape of demand, through MR.

docs.title: 9.4 The social cost of monopoly
docs.text:
Compare the monopoly with a perfectly competitive industry that has the same costs. Competition would drive the price down to marginal cost, ₹20, and output would be where demand meets MC: \(100 - 2Q = 20\), so \(Q = 40\).

Perfect competition Monopoly Price ₹20 ₹60 Quantity 40 20 Consumer surplus \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 80 = 1{,}600\) \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 40 = 400\) Producer surplus (profit) 0 \(40 \times 20 = 800\) Total surplus 1,600 1,200 Deadweight loss 0 \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 40 = 400\)

Table 9.2. Monopoly compared with competition at the same costs (all amounts in ₹).

Two different things happen.

  • A transfer. ₹800 of what was consumer surplus becomes profit for the monopolist: buyers who still buy pay ₹40 more per unit. Whether this is good or bad is a question of equity, not efficiency; a rupee is a rupee whoever has it.
  • A deadweight loss. Units 21 to 40 are not produced, although each would be worth more to some buyer (between ₹60 and ₹20) than it costs to produce (₹20). The lost surplus, ₹400, goes to nobody. This is the inefficiency of monopoly.

The source of the inefficiency is that the monopolist sets price above marginal cost: at the monopoly output, \(P = 60 > MC = 20\). Allocative efficiency (Chapter 8) fails. The monopolist restricts output to keep the price high.

Other costs and possible benefits of monopoly

Economists point to further costs. A monopolist protected from competition may have less pressure to keep costs down, and may spend resources on lobbying to keep its position (sometimes called rent seeking). On the other side, the prospect of monopoly profit is what rewards innovation: patents deliberately grant temporary monopolies so that firms will invest in developing new medicines, technologies and products. The economist Joseph Schumpeter argued that large firms with market power may be the main source of innovation. Policy has to balance these considerations.

docs.title: 9.5 Price discrimination
docs.text:
So far the monopolist has charged every buyer the same price. Price discrimination means selling the same good to different buyers at different prices for reasons not related to differences in cost. Examples are everywhere: lower cinema and museum prices for students, cheaper off-peak electricity or travel, airline fares that depend on how early one books, and software sold at lower prices in poorer countries.

Price discrimination is possible only under three conditions.

  1. The firm must have market power: a price taker cannot set prices at all.
  2. The firm must be able to identify groups of buyers with different willingness to pay (or different elasticities), for example by age, student status, location or time of purchase.
  3. Resale must be prevented: otherwise buyers who pay the low price would resell to those charged the high price. Services (haircuts, travel, medical care) are hard to resell, which is why discrimination is common in them.

docs.title: Types of price discrimination
docs.text:
• First-degree (perfect) price discrimination: each buyer is charged exactly her willingness to pay. The firm captures all consumer surplus as profit. Output is the same as under competition (the firm sells to everyone who values the good at more than its marginal cost), so there is no deadweight loss, but consumers get no surplus. It is rare in its pure form, but bargaining over the price of a car or a carpet comes close.
  • Second-degree price discrimination: prices vary with the quantity bought, as with bulk discounts or tariffs where the first units of electricity or data cost more than later ones. Buyers sort themselves by choosing how much to buy.
  • Third-degree price discrimination: the firm divides buyers into groups and charges each group a single price, as with student and adult tickets.

docs.title: Third-degree discrimination worked out
docs.text:
Example 9.1 Student and adult prices

A cinema has a marginal cost of ₹20 per ticket. It faces two groups: students, with demand \(P_1 = 60 - Q_1\), and other adults, with demand \(P_2 = 100 - Q_2\). Find its prices and profit if it charges each group separately, and compare with a single price for everyone.

Solution. Separate prices. In each market, set \(MR = MC\).

  • Students: \(MR_1 = 60 - 2Q_1 = 20\) gives \(Q_1 = 20\) and \(P_1 = 40\).
  • Adults: \(MR_2 = 100 - 2Q_2 = 20\) gives \(Q_2 = 40\) and \(P_2 = 60\).

Profit \(= (40 - 20) \times 20 + (60 - 20) \times 40 = 400 + 1{,}600 = 2{,}000\) rupees.

Single price. At prices up to ₹60 both groups buy, and total demand is \(Q = (60 - P) + (100 - P) = 160 - 2P\), or \(P = 80 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q\). Then \(MR = 80 - Q = 20\) gives \(Q = 60\) and \(P = 50\). Students buy 10 and adults 50. Profit \(= (50 - 20) \times 60 = 1{,}800\) rupees.

Discrimination raises profit from ₹1,800 to ₹2,000. Students pay less (₹40 instead of ₹50) and adults pay more (₹60 instead of ₹50).

The pattern is general: the lower price goes to the group with the more elastic demand. At their prices, the students' elasticity is \(-1 \times 40/20 = -2\) and the adults' is \(-1 \times 60/40 = -1.5\). Students have more alternatives and less income, so they are more sensitive to price.

Is third-degree discrimination good or bad for society? It depends. It raises profit and harms the group charged more, but it can increase total output by opening the market to buyers who would be priced out at a single price. When discrimination lets a firm serve a group that would otherwise not be served at all (a medicine sold cheaply in poor countries, for instance), it can make both that group and the firm better off.

docs.title: 9.6 Natural monopoly and regulation
docs.text:
A natural monopoly arises when a single firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms could, because average cost falls over the whole relevant range of output. This happens when there is a large fixed cost and a low marginal cost: water and sewerage pipes, electricity transmission and distribution lines, railway tracks, gas pipelines. Building two sets of water pipes along every street would double the fixed cost for no benefit.

Example 9.2 A natural monopoly

A water company has a fixed cost of ₹8,000 a month and a marginal cost of ₹10 per unit, so \(ATC = 10 + 8{,}000/Q\). Monthly demand is \(P = 100 - Q/10\). Compare (a) one firm producing 800 units with two firms producing 400 each; (b) the unregulated monopoly; (c) marginal cost pricing; (d) average cost pricing.

Solution.

(a) One firm producing 800 units has \(ATC = 10 + 8{,}000/800 = 20\) rupees. Two firms producing 400 each have \(ATC = 10 + 8{,}000/400 = 30\) rupees each. One firm is cheaper: the market is a natural monopoly.

(b) Unregulated monopoly. \(MR = 100 - Q/5 = 10\) gives \(Q = 450\) and \(P = 100 - 45 = 55\). Profit \(= (55 - 10) \times 450 - 8{,}000 = 20{,}250 - 8{,}000 = 12{,}250\) rupees. Price is far above marginal cost, and there is a deadweight loss.

(c) Marginal cost pricing. If a regulator sets \(P = MC = 10\), then \(Q = 900\), which is allocatively efficient. But ATC at 900 units is \(10 + 8{,}000/900 = 18.89\), so the firm loses \((18.89 - 10) \times 900 = 8{,}000\) rupees, its whole fixed cost. It would need a subsidy to stay in business.

(d) Average cost pricing. If the regulator sets the price equal to average cost, the firm just breaks even. Solving \(100 - Q/10 = 10 + 8{,}000/Q\) gives \(Q = 800\) and \(P = 20\) (check: \(ATC = 20\)). Output is much larger than under monopoly and the firm needs no subsidy, but price is still above marginal cost, so a small deadweight loss remains.

Governments respond to natural monopoly in several ways.

  1. Regulation of prices, by marginal cost pricing with a subsidy, or average cost pricing, or a price cap that falls over time to encourage cost-cutting. Regulators find it hard to know the firm's true costs, and a firm allowed to cover its costs has little reason to reduce them.
  2. Public ownership, common for water supply, railways and postal services in many countries. A public enterprise can be told to price at marginal or average cost, but it may lack the incentive to be efficient.
  3. Competition for the market. Where competition in the market is impossible, the right to be the sole supplier for a period can be auctioned to the firm offering the lowest price.
  4. Separating the network from the service. Often only part of an industry is a natural monopoly (the tracks, the wires, the pipes). The network can be regulated while competition is allowed in the parts that can support it, such as generating electricity or running trains.

docs.title: Competition policy
docs.text: For monopolies that are not natural, governments rely on competition law (called antitrust law in the United States). Such laws typically prohibit agreements among firms to fix prices or share markets, prohibit the abuse of a dominant position (for example, by predatory pricing to drive out rivals), and allow the authorities to review and block mergers that would substantially reduce competition. In the United States the Sherman Act of 1890 was an early example; in India, the Competition Act, 2002, is enforced by the Competition Commission of India.

docs.title: 9.8 Summary
docs.text:
• A monopoly is a single seller of a good without close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry: control of resources, patents and licences, economies of scale, network effects and strategic behaviour.
  • A monopolist must lower its price to sell more, so MR < P. For a straight-line demand curve, MR falls twice as steeply. \(MR = P(1 - 1/|E_d|)\), so a monopolist operates on the elastic part of demand.
  • A monopolist produces where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that output. The markup satisfies \((P - MC)/P = 1/|E_d|\).
  • Compared with competition, monopoly charges a higher price and produces less. It transfers surplus from consumers to the firm and causes a deadweight loss, because \(P > MC\).
  • Price discrimination requires market power, a way to separate buyers, and no resale. The lower price goes to the more elastic group.
  • A natural monopoly has falling average cost over the relevant range. It may be regulated (marginal cost pricing with a subsidy, average cost pricing, price caps) or publicly owned. Other monopolies are addressed by competition law.

docs.title: 9.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A monopolist faces demand \(P = 120 - 3Q\) and has a constant marginal and average cost of ₹30. Find its output, price and profit, and the deadweight loss.

Answer

\(MR = 120 - 6Q = 30\) gives \(Q = 15\), \(P = 120 - 45 = 75\). Profit \(= (75 - 30) \times 15 =\) ₹675. Under competition, \(120 - 3Q = 30\) gives \(Q = 30\). Deadweight loss \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times (30 - 15) \times (75 - 30) =\) ₹337.50.

Exercise 2

At a monopolist's current output, the price is ₹50 and the price elasticity of demand is −0.8. Explain why it is not maximising profit.

Answer

With \(|E_d| = 0.8 < 1\), demand is inelastic, so \(MR = 50(1 - 1/0.8) = -12.5\): marginal revenue is negative. Cutting output would raise revenue and also lower cost, so profit would rise. A profit-maximising monopolist always produces where demand is elastic.

Exercise 3

The price elasticity of demand for a monopolist's product is −4 at its profit-maximising output, and its marginal cost is ₹30. What price does it charge?

Answer

\((P - 30)/P = 1/4\), so \(P - 30 = P/4\), \(\tfrac{3}{4}P = 30\), \(P = 40\) rupees.

Exercise 4

A theatre has a marginal cost of ₹10 per seat. Senior citizens have demand \(P = 50 - Q\) and others \(P = 90 - Q\). Find the profit-maximising price for each group.

Answer

Seniors: \(50 - 2Q = 10\) gives \(Q = 20\), \(P = 30\). Others: \(90 - 2Q = 10\) gives \(Q = 40\), \(P = 50\). The group with more elastic demand (seniors, elasticity \(-30/20 = -1.5\), against \(-50/40 = -1.25\)) pays less.

Exercise 5

Why do airlines charge very different fares for seats on the same flight? Which conditions for price discrimination do they meet?

Answer

Airlines have market power on many routes. They separate buyers by when they book, whether they can change the ticket, and whether they stay over a weekend: business travellers who book late and need flexibility have less elastic demand and pay more. Resale is prevented because tickets are issued in the traveller's name. So all three conditions hold.

Exercise 6

Explain why marginal cost pricing of a natural monopoly leads to a loss.

Answer

For a natural monopoly, average cost falls over the whole relevant range of output, so marginal cost is below average cost (a falling average means the marginal is below it). If price is set equal to marginal cost, price is below average cost, and the firm loses money on every unit; the total loss in the simple case of constant MC equals the fixed cost.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Perfect Competition
docs.text:
How price-taking firms decide output, and why competition drives profit to zero

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. State the conditions of perfect competition and explain why a competitive firm is a price taker.
  2. Show that for a competitive firm marginal revenue equals price.
  3. Find the profit-maximising output using the rule MR = MC, from a table or a diagram.
  4. Decide whether a firm making a loss should keep producing or shut down in the short run.
  5. Derive the firm's and the market's short-run supply curves from marginal cost.
  6. Explain how entry and exit drive economic profit to zero in the long run.
  7. Explain in what sense perfect competition is efficient.

docs.title: 8.1 What makes a market perfectly competitive
docs.text:
Chapter 2 described a competitive market loosely, as one with many buyers and sellers. Economists define perfect competition more precisely, by four conditions.

  1. Many buyers and many sellers, each so small relative to the market that its own decisions have no noticeable effect on the price.
  2. A homogeneous product. The goods of all sellers are the same, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller over another. Wheat of a given grade is wheat, whoever grew it.
  3. Free entry and exit. In the long run, new firms can enter the industry and existing firms can leave without special barriers or costs.
  4. Perfect information. Buyers and sellers know the prices and the quality of the goods.

Few markets meet these conditions exactly. Markets for many farm products, for standard raw materials, and for some financial assets come close. The model is important less because it describes particular markets perfectly than because it is a benchmark: it shows how markets work when competition is as strong as possible, so that we can see what changes when it is weaker.

docs.title: The firm as a price taker
docs.text:
Under these conditions, each firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it wants at the market price, but nothing at a higher price, because buyers would simply go to another seller of the identical good. Nor would it want to charge less, since it can already sell all it wants at the market price.

So although the market demand curve slopes down, the demand curve facing an individual firm is horizontal at the market price: perfectly elastic (Chapter 3). The market price is set by market demand and supply; each firm takes it as given and chooses only how much to produce.

docs.title: 8.2 Revenue of a competitive firm
docs.text:
For a firm selling \(Q\) units at price \(P\):

  • Total revenue \(TR = P \times Q\).
  • Average revenue \(AR = TR/Q = P\). Average revenue is always the price, for any firm.
  • Marginal revenue \(MR = \Delta TR/\Delta Q\): the extra revenue from selling one more unit.

For a price taker, each extra unit sells at the same price, so marginal revenue equals price:

\[ MR = AR = P. \]

If the market price is ₹40, every extra unit brings in exactly ₹40. The firm's demand curve, its average revenue curve and its marginal revenue curve are all the same horizontal line at ₹40.

docs.title: 8.3 Choosing output to maximise profit
docs.text:
We use the cost table of Chapter 7, for a firm with a fixed cost of ₹60, and suppose the market price is ₹40.

Q TR (₹) TC (₹) Profit (₹) MR (₹) MC (₹) 0 0 60 −60 1 40 90 −50 40 30 2 80 110 −30 40 20 3 120 126 −6 40 16 4 160 140 20 40 14 5 200 160 40 40 20 6 240 186 54 40 26 7 280 220 60 40 34 8 320 268 52 40 48

Table 8.1. Revenue, cost and profit of a competitive firm at a price of ₹40.

Profit is greatest, at ₹60, when the firm produces 7 units. Notice how this relates to the last two columns. Each of the first 7 units adds more to revenue (₹40) than to cost (MC from ₹14 to ₹34), so each raises profit. The 8th unit adds ₹40 to revenue but ₹48 to cost, so it reduces profit by ₹8.

docs.title: The rule MR = MC
docs.text:
This is marginal analysis (Chapter 1) applied to the firm:

  • if MR > MC for the next unit, producing it raises profit, so the firm should expand output;
  • if MR < MC, producing it lowers profit, so the firm should cut output;
  • profit is maximised where MR = MC (with whole units, at the largest output for which MR is still at least MC).

The rule holds for every firm, competitive or not. For a competitive firm, since \(MR = P\), it becomes:

\[ \textbf{produce where } P = MC \text{ (on the rising part of the MC curve).} \]

The qualification matters. In Table 8.1 marginal cost also passes through ₹40 on its way down (if we imagine a smooth curve), at an output below one unit. That point is a profit minimum: beyond it, MC is below the price and output should be expanded. The profit-maximising output is where MC crosses the price from below.

docs.title: Measuring profit on a diagram
docs.text:
At the chosen output, profit can be written as

\[ \text{profit} = TR - TC = (P - ATC) \times Q. \]

At 7 units, ATC is \(220/7 = 31.43\) rupees, so profit is \((40 - 31.43) \times 7 = 60\) rupees, as in the table. On a diagram, profit is the rectangle whose height is the gap between price and ATC and whose width is the quantity.

Figure 8.1 A competitive firm earning a profit. (a) The market price is set by market demand and supply. (b) The firm takes this price as its marginal revenue, produces the output q* at which price equals marginal cost, and earns the profit shown by the green rectangle between price and average total cost.

docs.title: 8.4 Losses and the shutdown decision
docs.text:
Suppose the market price falls to ₹30. Applying the rule, the firm produces up to the last unit whose MC is no more than ₹30: the 6th unit (MC ₹26); the 7th (MC ₹34) would not pay. At 6 units,

\[ TR = 30 \times 6 = 180, \qquad TC = 186, \qquad \text{profit} = -6. \]

The firm makes a loss of ₹6. Should it close down?

In the short run, the fixed cost of ₹60 must be paid whether the firm produces or not: the rent is due, the machines are already bought. If the firm shuts down (produces nothing), its loss is the whole fixed cost, ₹60. If it produces 6 units, its loss is only ₹6. So it should keep producing. Its revenue of ₹180 more than covers its variable cost of ₹126, and the extra ₹54 goes towards paying the fixed cost.

Now suppose the price falls to ₹18. The lowest AVC in Table 7.2 is ₹20. At any output, revenue falls short of even the variable cost. For example, at 4 units, \(TR = 72\) while \(VC = 80\), so producing loses \(60 + 8 = 68\) rupees, more than the ₹60 lost by shutting down. The firm should shut down.

Key idea: the shutdown rule

In the short run, a firm should keep producing as long as the price covers average variable cost, even if it does not cover average total cost. It should shut down if the price falls below the minimum of average variable cost. Fixed costs are irrelevant to the decision, because they are paid either way.

Three ranges of price summarise the firm's position.

Price compared with costs Firm's position Short-run decision \(P >\) minimum ATC (₹31) economic profit produce where \(P = MC\) minimum AVC (₹20) \(\le P <\) minimum ATC loss smaller than fixed cost produce where \(P = MC\) \(P <\) minimum AVC (₹20) producing would lose more than fixed cost shut down

Table 8.2. The firm's short-run decision at different prices.

At a price equal to minimum ATC (₹31), the firm produces 6 units and just breaks even: \(31 \times 6 = 186 = TC\). This is the break-even point. At a price equal to minimum AVC (₹20), it is indifferent between producing 5 units (loss \(160 - 100 = 60\)) and shutting down (loss ₹60). This is the shutdown point.

Shutting down is not the same as leaving

A firm that shuts down in the short run still has its fixed costs: it pays the rent and keeps its machines, hoping prices will recover. Exit means leaving the industry altogether, which is a long-run decision: the firm sells its equipment and ends its lease, so that it no longer has any costs. A seasonal hotel that closes in the off-season has shut down; one that sells its building has exited.

docs.title: 8.5 The firm's short-run supply curve
docs.text:
The firm produces where price equals marginal cost, as long as the price is at least the minimum of AVC. So the firm's short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost. Below that price, it supplies nothing.

From Table 7.2 the firm's supply schedule is:

Price (₹) below 20 20 to under 26 26 to under 34 34 to under 48 48 and above Quantity supplied 0 5 6 7 8

Table 8.3. The firm's short-run supply schedule, read from its marginal cost.

Figure 8.2 The firm's short-run supply curve. The firm's short-run supply curve (thick red) is the part of its marginal cost curve above the shutdown point, the minimum of average variable cost. At prices below this the firm supplies nothing. At the break-even point, the minimum of average total cost, the firm just covers all its costs.

This is the theory behind the upward-sloping supply curve of Chapter 2. Supply curves slope up because marginal cost rises, and marginal cost rises because of diminishing marginal returns.

docs.title: The market supply curve in the short run
docs.text: In the short run the number of firms is fixed. The market supply curve is the horizontal sum of the supply curves of all the firms. If there are 200 identical firms like ours, then at a price of ₹40 the market supplies \(200 \times 7 = 1{,}400\) units; at ₹30, \(200 \times 6 = 1{,}200\) units. The market price is where this supply curve meets market demand, as in panel (a) of Figure 8.1.

docs.title: 8.6 The long run: entry and exit
docs.text:
In the long run, firms can enter and leave the industry. This changes everything.

Profits attract entry. Suppose the market price is ₹40 and each firm earns an economic profit of ₹60. Since economic profit means earning more than the resources could earn elsewhere, entrepreneurs outside the industry want a share. New firms enter. The market supply curve shifts to the right, and the market price falls. Entry continues as long as firms earn economic profit, that is, as long as the price is above minimum ATC.

Losses cause exit. If the price is below minimum ATC, firms make losses. In the long run, some leave the industry. The market supply curve shifts left and the price rises, until the remaining firms no longer make losses.

So in long-run equilibrium, the price settles where firms make zero economic profit:

\[ P = \text{minimum ATC}. \]

In our example this is ₹31, at which each firm produces 6 units. If market demand at a price of ₹31 is 1,500 units, the industry settles with \(1{,}500/6 = 250\) firms.

Common mistake

Zero economic profit does not mean that firms are doing badly. It means they earn normal profit: their revenue covers all costs, including a return on the owner's time and money equal to what these could earn elsewhere. Accounting profit is positive. Firms stay in the industry because they are doing as well as they could do anywhere else.

docs.title: The long-run supply curve of the industry
docs.text:
Suppose demand for the good increases permanently. In the short run, the price rises, existing firms move up their MC curves, and they earn economic profits. Over time new firms enter, supply increases and the price falls back. If the entry of new firms does not change the costs of firms (so that minimum ATC stays at ₹31), the price returns all the way to ₹31, and the industry produces more with more firms. The long-run supply curve of such a constant-cost industry is horizontal at minimum ATC.

If instead the expansion of the industry raises input prices (for example, because the industry needs a specialised kind of labour or land that becomes scarcer as it grows), minimum ATC rises with industry output, and the long-run supply curve slopes upwards. This is an increasing-cost industry. In either case, long-run supply is more elastic than short-run supply, as Chapter 3 said.

docs.title: 8.7 Perfect competition and efficiency
docs.text:
The long-run equilibrium of a perfectly competitive market has two properties that economists regard as highly desirable.

Allocative efficiency: price equals marginal cost. The price measures what buyers are willing to pay for the last unit, its marginal benefit (Chapter 5). Marginal cost measures the value of the resources used to produce it. When \(P = MC\), the last unit is worth exactly what it costs; producing more would cost more than it is worth, and producing less would forgo units worth more than they cost. This is the same as saying that total surplus is maximised (Chapter 4).

Productive efficiency: price equals minimum ATC. In the long run each firm produces at the lowest point of its average total cost curve, so the industry's output is produced at the lowest possible cost per unit. Firms with higher costs cannot survive.

These results, together with the absence of economic profit in the long run, are why economists use perfect competition as the benchmark against which other market structures are judged. Monopoly (Chapter 9) and imperfect competition (Chapter 10) generally fail one or both tests.

Tip

Learn the two efficiency conditions by what they compare. Allocative: price (the value to buyers) against marginal cost (the cost to society) for the last unit. Productive: the cost per unit against the lowest possible cost per unit.

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Perfect competition has many small buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, and perfect information. Each firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve.
  • For a competitive firm, \(MR = AR = P\).
  • Every firm maximises profit where MR = MC; for a competitive firm this means P = MC on the rising part of MC. Profit equals \((P - ATC) \times Q\).
  • In the short run, a firm should produce as long as \(P \ge\) minimum AVC, even at a loss; below that it should shut down. Fixed costs do not affect the decision.
  • The firm's short-run supply curve is its MC curve above minimum AVC. Market supply is the horizontal sum.
  • In the long run, entry and exit drive the price to minimum ATC, where economic profit is zero. The long-run supply curve is horizontal for a constant-cost industry and slopes up for an increasing-cost industry.
  • Perfect competition achieves allocative efficiency (\(P = MC\)) and, in the long run, productive efficiency (\(P =\) minimum ATC).

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Using Table 7.2, find the profit-maximising output and the profit when the market price is ₹50.

Answer

Produce while MC ≤ 50: the 8th unit costs ₹48, so the firm produces 8 units (Table 7.2 stops at 8). \(TR = 400\), \(TC = 268\), profit ₹132.

Exercise 2

Using Table 7.2, what should the firm do at a price of ₹24? What is its profit or loss?

Answer

₹24 is above minimum AVC (₹20) but below minimum ATC (₹31), so the firm should produce, at a loss. Produce while MC ≤ 24: the 5th unit (MC ₹20) but not the 6th (₹26), so 5 units. \(TR = 120\), \(TC = 160\), loss ₹40, which is less than the fixed cost of ₹60 it would lose by shutting down.

Exercise 3

A competitive firm produces 200 units at its best output. The price is ₹12, average total cost is ₹15 and average variable cost is ₹10. Find its fixed cost and its profit or loss. Should it produce in the short run? What will it do in the long run if the price stays at ₹12?

Answer

Average fixed cost is \(15 - 10 = 5\) rupees, so fixed cost is \(5 \times 200 =\) ₹1,000. Loss \(= (15 - 12) \times 200 =\) ₹600. Revenue (\(12 \times 200 = 2{,}400\)) covers variable cost (\(10 \times 200 = 2{,}000\)) and contributes ₹400 towards the fixed cost, so the loss from producing (₹600) is smaller than the loss from shutting down (₹1,000). Since \(P > AVC\), it should produce in the short run. In the long run, if the price stays below ATC, it should exit the industry.

Exercise 4

Explain why a firm in a perfectly competitive industry earns zero economic profit in the long run, but why this does not mean its owners are unhappy.

Answer

Positive economic profit attracts entry, which increases supply and lowers the price; losses cause exit, which raises the price. Entry and exit stop only when \(P =\) minimum ATC, where economic profit is zero. Zero economic profit is normal profit: owners earn as much as their time and money could earn in the best alternative, so they have no reason to leave.

Exercise 5

The demand for a good increases permanently in a constant-cost competitive industry. Describe what happens to the price, the output of each firm, the number of firms and industry output, in the short run and the long run.

Answer

Short run: the price rises; each existing firm moves up its MC curve and produces more; firms earn economic profit; the number of firms is unchanged; industry output rises. Long run: profits attract entry; supply shifts right until the price returns to minimum ATC; each firm produces its original output at minimum ATC; there are more firms; industry output is higher than in the short run.

Exercise 6

What are allocative and productive efficiency? Which of them does a competitive firm achieve in the short run when the price is above minimum ATC?

Answer

Allocative efficiency: \(P = MC\), so the last unit is valued at exactly what it costs. Productive efficiency: output is produced at minimum ATC. In the short run with \(P >\) minimum ATC, the firm produces where \(P = MC\), so it is allocatively efficient, but at an output above the minimum of ATC, so it is not productively efficient. Entry in the long run brings it to minimum ATC.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text: What this book covers and how to get the most from it

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Every day you make economic decisions. You decide how to spend a limited allowance or salary, whether an extra hour of study is worth more than an hour of sleep, and whether a bus ticket or an auto-rickshaw ride is the better way home. Shopkeepers decide what to stock and what to charge. Farmers decide what to sow. Large firms decide whether to build a new plant, and governments decide what to tax and what to subsidise. Microeconomics is the study of these decisions and of how they fit together in markets.

This book is a first course in microeconomics. It begins with the idea at the heart of the subject, that resources are scarce and every choice has an opportunity cost, and then builds the main tools one at a time: demand and supply, elasticity, consumer and producer surplus, the theory of the consumer, production and costs, and the theory of the firm in different market structures. The later chapters use these tools to study the markets for labour, capital and land, the ways in which markets can fail, what behavioural economics adds to the standard theory, and why countries gain from trading with one another.

The book explains each idea in three ways: in plain words, with a diagram, and with numbers. Every chapter contains worked numerical examples whose arithmetic has been checked, and diagrams drawn to scale from the same numbers, so that you can see that the words, the picture and the calculation say the same thing.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The book is written for a reader meeting economics for the first time. It suits:

  • a student in a first university course in economics, commerce, management or the social sciences;
  • a student in the final years of school who wants a careful introduction;
  • a student of engineering, law or the sciences who needs to understand how markets work;
  • anyone preparing for an examination or a profession in which basic economics is expected.

No background is assumed beyond school mathematics. You should be comfortable with percentages, with straight lines on a graph and with solving a pair of simple equations. A few sections use the idea of a slope, and one or two optional boxes use a derivative; each of these is explained where it occurs, and none is needed to follow the rest of the book.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
Part Chapters What you learn I. Markets 1 to 4 Scarcity and opportunity cost; demand and supply; elasticity; surplus, taxes, subsidies and price controls II. Consumers and firms 5 to 7 Utility and consumer choice; indifference curves and budget constraints; production and costs III. Market structures 8 to 10 Perfect competition; monopoly; monopolistic competition, oligopoly and basic game theory IV. Beyond a single market 11 to 14 Factor markets; market failure; behavioural economics; international trade

Table P.1. The four parts of the book.

The chapters are meant to be read in order. Chapters 1 to 4 are the foundation for everything else. Chapters 5 and 6 (the consumer) and Chapter 7 (the firm) can be read in either order, but Chapter 7 must come before Chapters 8 to 11.

docs.title: How each chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter follows the same plan:

  • Learning outcomes at the top tell you what you should be able to do when you finish.
  • Numbered sections explain each idea, first by intuition and then precisely.
  • Worked examples show every step of a calculation. Cover the solution and try each one yourself first.
  • Figures are drawn from the numbers of the examples, so that you can read values off them.
  • Boxes pick out what matters most: a key idea to remember, a note that adds detail, and a caution that warns of a common mistake.
  • A summary collects the main points.
  • Exercises follow, each with its answer folded underneath. Try each exercise on paper before you open the answer.
  • A short quiz at the end lets you check your understanding; it can be answered on the page.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Economics is learned by doing problems. Reading a demand and supply diagram is easy; drawing one from a description of a market, and saying what happens when something changes, is the skill that counts. For each chapter:

  1. Read the explanation once, without stopping to memorise.
  2. Redraw every figure yourself, labelling the axes and the curves, and rework every example with a pencil.
  3. Attempt the exercises, then open the answers. Where your answer differs, find the step at which it went wrong.
  4. Take the quiz. If you miss a question, reread the section it comes from.

A few chapters contain short programs in Python that repeat a calculation of the text. They are optional. If you know a little Python, run them and change the numbers to see what happens; if you do not, skip them, because nothing in the book depends on them.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Prices in examples are mostly in Indian rupees (₹). The numbers are chosen to make the arithmetic clear; they are not data about any real market.
  • Names of firms, towns and people in the examples are invented, unless the text says otherwise.
  • When the text mentions real countries, markets or policies, it describes them only in general terms. Laws, tax rates and policies change, so check a current official source before relying on a detail.
  • \(P\) stands for price and \(Q\) for quantity. \(Q_d\) and \(Q_s\) are the quantities demanded and supplied. A symbol with a star, such as \(P^*\), is an equilibrium value.
  • "Per unit" amounts are written as ₹6 per unit; total amounts as ₹312.
  • On diagrams, price or cost is on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, as is customary in economics.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Production and Costs
docs.text:
How output depends on inputs, and how costs depend on output

Learning outcomes

After studying this chapter you should be able to:

  1. Distinguish explicit from implicit costs and accounting profit from economic profit.
  2. Distinguish the short run from the long run, and fixed from variable inputs.
  3. Calculate total, average and marginal product, and explain the law of diminishing marginal returns.
  4. Calculate fixed, variable and total cost and the average and marginal cost curves from a table.
  5. Explain why marginal cost cuts average variable cost and average total cost at their minimum points.
  6. Explain the long-run average cost curve, economies and diseconomies of scale, and returns to scale.
  7. State the condition for producing a given output at least cost.

docs.title: 7.1 The firm, its costs and its profit
docs.text:
Chapters 5 and 6 looked behind the demand curve at the consumer. This chapter and the next look behind the supply curve at the firm: an organisation that buys or hires inputs and turns them into goods or services for sale. Firms range from a single tailor with a sewing machine to companies employing hundreds of thousands of people. Economists usually assume that a firm's goal is to maximise profit:

\[ \text{profit} = \text{total revenue} - \text{total cost}. \]

Total revenue is the price times the quantity sold. To understand profit, we need to understand cost, and economists measure cost differently from accountants.

docs.title: Explicit and implicit costs
docs.text:
• Explicit costs are payments of money to people outside the firm: wages, rent, raw materials, electricity, interest on loans.
  • Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of resources the firm already owns, for which no money changes hands: the owner's own time, the owner's money invested in the business, a building the owner owns and could have rented out.

Accountants record explicit costs. Economists include both, because both are given up when the firm uses the resources in this business rather than in the best alternative (Chapter 1).

  • Accounting profit = total revenue − explicit costs.
  • Economic profit = total revenue − explicit costs − implicit costs.

Example 7.1 Accounting and economic profit

Sunita runs a tailoring business. In a year it earns revenue of ₹12,00,000. She pays ₹8,00,000 for cloth, wages, rent and electricity. She could instead have worked as a salaried designer for ₹3,00,000 a year, and she has ₹5,00,000 of her own savings in the business, which could earn 8 per cent a year in a bank deposit. Find her accounting profit and economic profit.

Solution. Accounting profit \(= 12{,}00{,}000 - 8{,}00{,}000 = 4{,}00{,}000\) rupees.

Implicit costs: forgone salary ₹3,00,000 plus forgone interest \(0.08 \times 5{,}00{,}000 = 40{,}000\) rupees, a total of ₹3,40,000.

Economic profit \(= 4{,}00{,}000 - 3{,}40{,}000 = 60{,}000\) rupees.

The business is worth continuing, but it is much less profitable than the accounts suggest. If her economic profit were zero, she would be earning exactly what she could earn elsewhere.

An economic profit of zero is called normal profit: the firm covers all its costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's time and money. A firm earning normal profit has no reason to leave the industry, and others have no special reason to enter. In this book "cost" always includes implicit costs, so "profit" means economic profit.

docs.title: 7.2 Production in the short run
docs.text:
A firm's production function shows the maximum output it can produce from each combination of inputs, given its technology. Economists distinguish two time horizons.

  • In the short run, at least one input is fixed: the firm cannot change it quickly. Typically the size of the factory, the number of machines or the area of land is fixed. Other inputs, such as labour, raw materials and power, are variable.
  • In the long run, all inputs are variable: the firm can build a new factory, buy more machines, or close down entirely.

The short run and long run are not fixed lengths of time. For a street food stall, the long run may be a few weeks; for a steel plant or a power station, it may be many years.

docs.title: 7.3 Total, average and marginal product
docs.text:
Consider a small workshop that makes chairs with a fixed set of tools and a fixed floor space. Only the number of workers can be changed. Table 7.1 shows how output (total product) depends on the number of workers per day.

Workers (L) Total product (TP, chairs) Marginal product (MP) Average product (AP = TP/L) 0 0 1 10 10 10.0 2 24 14 12.0 3 36 12 12.0 4 44 8 11.0 5 48 4 9.6 6 48 0 8.0

Table 7.1. Output of a chair workshop with fixed equipment.

  • Total product (TP) is the whole output.
  • Marginal product (MP) is the extra output from one more worker: \(MP = \Delta TP / \Delta L\).
  • Average product (AP) is output per worker: \(AP = TP/L\).
Figure 7.1 Total, marginal and average product. Top: total product rises quickly at first and then more slowly, levelling off at 48 chairs. Bottom: marginal product rises to 14 with the second worker and then falls to zero; average product reaches its peak of 12 where marginal product crosses it.

docs.title: The law of diminishing marginal returns
docs.text:
At first, adding workers raises output more than in proportion: the second worker adds 14 chairs, more than the first, because two people can divide the tasks (one cuts, one assembles) and use the tools better. But from the third worker on, each extra worker adds less than the one before: 12, then 8, then 4, then nothing. With fixed tools and space, workers begin to wait for equipment and get in one another's way.

This is the law of diminishing marginal returns: when more and more of a variable input is added to a fixed input, the marginal product of the variable input eventually falls. It is one of the most reliable regularities in economics. It applies to fertiliser on a fixed field (Chapter 1's farmer), to workers in a fixed factory, and to students in a fixed classroom. It is a short-run law: it arises because some input is fixed.

Common mistake

Diminishing marginal returns does not mean that total output falls, or that later workers are less able. Total output keeps rising as long as marginal product is positive. The extra output falls because each worker has less of the fixed input to work with.

docs.title: Marginal and average product
docs.text:
Figure 7.1 shows a relationship that holds between any marginal and average:

  • when MP is above AP, adding a worker raises the average (the second worker, with MP = 14, raises AP from 10 to 12);
  • when MP is below AP, adding a worker lowers the average (the fourth worker, with MP = 8, lowers AP from 12 to 11);
  • so MP crosses AP at the maximum of AP (between the second and third workers, where AP = 12).

The same logic applies to a cricketer's batting average: if her score in the next innings (the marginal) is above her average, the average rises; if below, it falls.

docs.title: 7.4 Costs in the short run
docs.text:
Every input has a cost, so the production function determines how cost depends on output. In the short run, costs divide into two kinds.

  • Fixed cost (FC) does not change with output: the rent of the workshop, the cost of the tools, insurance, the salary of a manager on a fixed contract. It must be paid even if output is zero.
  • Variable cost (VC) rises with output: wages of production workers, raw materials, power.
  • Total cost (TC) is the sum: \(TC = FC + VC\).

From these come four measures per unit of output:

\[ AFC = \frac{FC}{Q}, \qquad AVC = \frac{VC}{Q}, \qquad ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = AFC + AVC, \qquad MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q}. \]

Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit. Since fixed cost does not change, marginal cost depends only on variable cost.

Table 7.2 gives the costs of a small firm with a fixed cost of ₹60.

Output (Q) FC VC TC MC AFC AVC ATC 0 60 0 60 1 60 30 90 30 60.00 30.00 90.00 2 60 50 110 20 30.00 25.00 55.00 3 60 66 126 16 20.00 22.00 42.00 4 60 80 140 14 15.00 20.00 35.00 5 60 100 160 20 12.00 20.00 32.00 6 60 126 186 26 10.00 21.00 31.00 7 60 160 220 34 8.57 22.86 31.43 8 60 208 268 48 7.50 26.00 33.50

Table 7.2. Short-run costs of a firm (₹). MC is the cost of each additional unit.

Example 7.2 Reading the cost table

Using Table 7.2, find (a) the marginal cost of the 6th unit, (b) the output at which average variable cost is lowest, and (c) the output at which average total cost is lowest.

Solution. (a) \(MC = 186 - 160 = 26\) rupees. (b) AVC is lowest, at ₹20, at 4 and 5 units; the marginal cost of the 5th unit is also ₹20, equal to AVC there. (c) ATC is lowest, at ₹31, at 6 units. The 6th unit's marginal cost (₹26) is below the ATC of 5 units (₹32), so producing it pulls the average down; the 7th unit's marginal cost (₹34) is above the ATC of 6 units (₹31), so producing it pushes the average up.

docs.title: The shapes of the cost curves
docs.text:
Figure 7.2 Short-run cost curves. The short-run cost curves. Marginal cost (MC) falls and then rises steeply. It cuts average variable cost (AVC) and average total cost (ATC) at their minimum points. Average fixed cost (AFC) falls continuously. The gap between ATC and AVC is AFC, which narrows as output rises.
  • AFC falls continuously as output rises, because a fixed sum is spread over more units ("spreading the overhead").
  • MC is U-shaped. It falls at first, while marginal product is rising, and then rises because of diminishing marginal returns: each extra unit needs more and more of the variable input.
  • AVC and ATC are U-shaped. AVC falls while MC is below it and rises once MC is above it. ATC falls for longer than AVC, because falling AFC keeps pulling it down; its minimum is at a larger output than the minimum of AVC.
  • The vertical gap between ATC and AVC is AFC, which shrinks as output grows, so the two curves come closer together.

Key idea

Marginal cost cuts both average variable cost and average total cost at their lowest points. When the cost of the next unit is below the average, it pulls the average down; when it is above, it pushes the average up. This is the same rule that links marginal and average product, and it is the most important relationship among the cost curves.

docs.title: 7.5 Why costs and products mirror each other
docs.text:
Suppose labour is the only variable input and each worker is paid a wage \(w\). Producing one more unit needs \(1/MP\) extra workers, so

\[ MC = \frac{w}{MP}, \qquad AVC = \frac{wL}{Q} = \frac{w}{AP}. \]

When marginal product is high, marginal cost is low; when marginal product falls, marginal cost rises. Diminishing marginal returns is the reason marginal cost eventually rises. Similarly, AVC is lowest where AP is highest. The cost curves are the product curves turned upside down.

For example, in the chair workshop of Table 7.1, suppose a worker costs ₹280 a day. The second worker adds 14 chairs, so the marginal cost of those chairs is \(280/14 = 20\) rupees each. The fourth worker adds only 8 chairs, so their marginal cost is \(280/8 = 35\) rupees each. The fifth adds 4 chairs at \(280/4 = 70\) rupees each.

docs.title: 7.6 Production and costs in the long run
docs.text:
In the long run the firm can vary all its inputs, including the size of its plant. For each possible plant size there is a short-run average cost curve (SRAC). In the long run the firm chooses the plant that produces its planned output at the lowest cost. The long-run average cost curve (LRAC) shows the lowest average cost of producing each output when all inputs can be varied. It is the envelope of the short-run curves: it touches each SRAC at the output for which that plant size is best.

Figure 7.3 The long-run average cost curve. Three short-run average cost curves (SRAC), one for each plant size, and the long-run average cost curve (LRAC) that envelops them. LRAC falls while there are economies of scale, is flat around the minimum efficient scale, and rises when diseconomies of scale set in.

docs.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
docs.text:
• Economies of scale exist when long-run average cost falls as output rises. The LRAC slopes down.
  • Constant returns to scale (in the sense of costs) exist when long-run average cost is unchanged as output rises.
  • Diseconomies of scale exist when long-run average cost rises as output rises.

The sources of economies of scale include:

  1. Specialisation and division of labour. In a large firm, workers and managers can specialise in narrow tasks and become expert at them. Adam Smith's famous example in The Wealth of Nations was a pin factory, in which dividing the work into many separate operations multiplied output per worker.
  2. Indivisible inputs. Some inputs come only in large sizes: a blast furnace, an assembly line, a research laboratory, a national advertising campaign. Their cost per unit falls as output rises.
  3. Engineering relationships. The capacity of a tank or a pipe rises faster than the material needed to build it, so larger plants are often cheaper per unit of capacity.
  4. Purchasing and finance. Large firms can often buy inputs in bulk at lower prices and borrow at lower interest rates.

Diseconomies of scale arise mainly from the difficulty of managing a very large organisation: communication becomes slower, decisions pass through more layers, coordination is harder, and individual workers may feel less responsible for results.

The output at which LRAC first reaches its minimum is called the minimum efficient scale. It matters for the structure of industries. If the minimum efficient scale is small relative to the market (as in tailoring, hairdressing or vegetable farming), there is room for many firms. If it is large relative to the market (as in aircraft manufacture or the distribution of electricity in a city), only a few firms, or even one, can produce at low cost. Chapters 9 and 10 return to this.

docs.title: Returns to scale
docs.text:
Economies of scale are about costs. A closely related idea, returns to scale, is about the production function: what happens to output when all inputs are increased in the same proportion.

  • Increasing returns to scale: doubling all inputs more than doubles output.
  • Constant returns to scale: doubling all inputs exactly doubles output.
  • Decreasing returns to scale: doubling all inputs less than doubles output.

If input prices do not change as the firm grows, increasing returns to scale mean economies of scale, and decreasing returns mean diseconomies.

Caution

Do not confuse diminishing marginal returns with decreasing returns to scale. Diminishing marginal returns is a short-run idea: one input increases while others are fixed. Returns to scale is a long-run idea: all inputs increase together. A firm can have diminishing marginal returns to labour in the short run and constant or increasing returns to scale in the long run.

docs.title: 7.7 Choosing the cheapest combination of inputs
docs.text:
In the long run a firm can produce a given output with different combinations of labour and capital: more machines and fewer workers, or the reverse. Which should it choose? The answer is the producer's version of the equimarginal principle of Chapter 5. A firm produces at least cost when the marginal product per rupee is the same for every input:

\[ \frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r}, \]

where \(w\) is the wage and \(r\) the rental price of a unit of capital (a machine-day, for example).

If the extra output from the last rupee spent on capital is greater than from the last rupee spent on labour, the firm can produce the same output more cheaply by using a little more capital and a little less labour.

Example 7.3 Labour or machines?

A garment factory finds that one more worker-day adds 20 shirts and costs ₹400, while one more machine-day adds 50 shirts and costs ₹500. Is it producing at least cost? What should it do?

Solution. Marginal product per rupee: labour \(20/400 = 0.05\) shirts per rupee; capital \(50/500 = 0.10\) shirts per rupee. A rupee spent on machines produces twice as many shirts as a rupee spent on workers, so the factory is not at least cost. It should use more machines and fewer workers. As it does, the marginal product of machines falls and that of labour rises (diminishing marginal returns to each), until the two ratios are equal.

This rule explains why techniques of production differ between countries and change over time. Where labour is cheap relative to machines, firms use labour-intensive methods; where wages are high, they substitute machines for workers. When wages rise, the same calculation pushes firms towards more capital per worker.

docs.title: 7.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Economic profit is revenue minus all costs, explicit and implicit. Zero economic profit is normal profit: the owner earns as much as in the best alternative.
  • In the short run some inputs are fixed; in the long run all are variable.
  • Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of an input. The law of diminishing marginal returns: with some inputs fixed, marginal product eventually falls. MP cuts AP at the maximum of AP.
  • Short-run costs: \(TC = FC + VC\); \(ATC = AFC + AVC\); \(MC = \Delta TC/\Delta Q\). AFC falls continuously; MC, AVC and ATC are U-shaped.
  • MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points. \(MC = w/MP\), so diminishing marginal returns make marginal cost rise.
  • The long-run average cost curve is the envelope of short-run curves. It falls with economies of scale, is flat around the minimum efficient scale, and rises with diseconomies of scale.
  • Returns to scale describe how output responds when all inputs increase together.
  • A firm minimises cost when \(MP_L/w = MP_K/r\).

docs.title: 7.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

A doctor leaves a hospital job paying ₹18,00,000 a year to open a clinic in a building she owns, which she could have rented out for ₹2,40,000 a year. The clinic's revenue is ₹30,00,000, and she pays ₹9,00,000 a year for staff, equipment and medicines. Find her accounting profit and economic profit.

Answer

Accounting profit \(= 30{,}00{,}000 - 9{,}00{,}000 =\) ₹21,00,000. Implicit costs \(= 18{,}00{,}000 + 2{,}40{,}000 = 20{,}40{,}000\) rupees. Economic profit \(= 21{,}00{,}000 - 20{,}40{,}000 =\) ₹60,000.

Exercise 2

Complete the marginal and average product columns.

Workers Total product 1 8 2 20 3 30 4 36 5 40 Answer

MP: 8, 12, 10, 6, 4. AP: 8, 10, 10, 9, 8. Diminishing marginal returns set in with the third worker. MP (10) equals AP (10) at three workers, where AP is at its maximum.

Exercise 3

A firm's fixed cost is ₹100 and its variable costs for outputs 1 to 5 are ₹40, ₹70, ₹96, ₹128 and ₹170. Find MC, AVC and ATC for each output. At what output is ATC lowest?

Answer

TC: 140, 170, 196, 228, 270. MC: 40, 30, 26, 32, 42. AVC: 40, 35, 32, 32, 34. ATC: 140, 85, 65.33, 57, 54. ATC is lowest at 5 units (₹54) within this range; it is still falling because MC of the 5th unit (₹42) is below the ATC of 4 units (₹57).

Exercise 4

Explain why the marginal cost curve passes through the lowest point of the average total cost curve.

Answer

When the cost of an extra unit (MC) is below the average, producing it lowers the average; when it is above, it raises the average. ATC therefore falls while MC < ATC and rises while MC > ATC, so it is at its minimum where MC = ATC.

Exercise 5

A firm pays its workers ₹500 a day. The tenth worker hired adds 25 units of output. What is the marginal cost of output at this point? If the eleventh worker adds only 20 units, what happens to marginal cost?

Answer

\(MC = w/MP = 500/25 =\) ₹20 per unit. With the eleventh worker, \(MC = 500/20 =\) ₹25 per unit: marginal cost rises because marginal product falls.

Exercise 6

Distinguish diminishing marginal returns from decreasing returns to scale, with an example of each.

Answer

Diminishing marginal returns is short-run: adding more of one input (workers) to a fixed input (a kitchen of fixed size) eventually adds less and less output. Decreasing returns to scale is long-run: increasing all inputs in proportion (doubling the kitchen, the cooks, the stoves and the ingredients) raises output by less than in proportion, for example because a very large restaurant is harder to manage.

Exercise 7

At a firm's current input mix, \(MP_L = 30\), \(w = 600\), \(MP_K = 45\) and \(r = 900\). Is the firm producing at least cost?

Answer

\(MP_L/w = 30/600 = 0.05\) and \(MP_K/r = 45/900 = 0.05\). The ratios are equal, so the firm is producing its output at least cost.

docs.text:
Check your understanding of Chapter 7

Exercise 1

  1. wages paid to workers
  2. interest paid on a bank loan
  3. the salary the owner gives up by running the firm
  4. rent paid for the shop
Answer

Exercise 2

  1. only in the long run
  2. when at least one input is fixed
  3. when all inputs increase together
  4. only to agriculture
Answer

Exercise 3

Total cost rises from ₹250 to ₹285 when output rises from 10 to 11 units. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit, in rupees?

Answer

35 / ₹35

Exercise 4

Average fixed cost

  1. is U-shaped
  2. falls continuously as output rises
  3. rises with output
  4. equals marginal cost
Answer

Exercise 5

The marginal cost curve cuts the average total cost curve

  1. at the maximum of ATC
  2. at the minimum of ATC
  3. where ATC equals AFC
  4. nowhere
Answer

Exercise 6

If long-run average cost falls as output rises, the firm has

  1. diseconomies of scale
  2. economies of scale
  3. diminishing marginal returns
  4. normal profit
Answer
